arxiv-2606-04793: Cooler phases of the circumgalactic medium were shown to be more centrally concentrated with constraints from multiphase absorption. The galactic gas was mapped. The finding serves astrophysics. Cool gas hugs galactic centers. Weiwen Kong mapped circumgalactic gas phases. Galaxy evolution needs gas mapping.
arxiv-2606-05193: Geometry in higher dimensions hides surprises that only precise inequalities can capture. This paper proves a Hineva-type inequality for submanifolds — curved surfaces sitting inside larger spaces — in real space forms equipped with a semi-symmetric non-metric connection. It is a specialized result in differential geometry, extending the toolkit for measuring how curved spaces bend.
arxiv-2606-05493: Reverse engineers — the people who take software apart to understand it — trade hard-won knowledge on Stack Exchange. REStack is a large-scale dataset of those reverse engineering discussions, capturing how experts reason about binaries, obfuscation, and exploits. The dataset opens a window into a craft that is usually learned by apprenticeship.
arxiv-2606-05593: Where two materials meet, the mathematics can change character — interface problems of mixed spatial order. This paper develops the theory for such interfaces, where different sides obey different rules. The analysis underpins simulations of everything from composite materials to biological membranes.
arxiv-2606-05693: Chemistry questions need molecular structure — flat text misses the shape of molecules. MolE-RAG enhances retrieval-augmented generation with molecular structures, fetching relevant compounds by their actual geometry. Structure-aware retrieval grounds AI chemistry answers in the molecules themselves, speeding up the hunt for useful compounds.
arxiv-2606-05793: Language models usually work alone, but real problems need collaboration — with humans and other AIs, each bringing different strengths. CollabBench benchmarks and unleashes that collaborative ability with diverse players through proactive engagement. The benchmark measures what happens when models stop soloing and start teaming.
arxiv-2606-05993: Wireless signals bounce off buildings, arriving from many directions at once. This paper models those double-directional channels — angles of departure and arrival — using statistics-aided machine learning. Better channel models mean wireless systems designed for the real world's messy reflections.
arxiv-2606-06093: The inverse Laplace transform recovers a function from its transform — notoriously ill-posed and numerically treacherous. This paper tames the multidimensional version with tensor trains: compressed representations that dodge the curse of dimensionality. The method makes a classic hard problem computationally feasible.
arxiv-2606-06393: Survival data is censored — patients drop out, studies end — and scoring predictions there needs care. This paper develops proper scoring rules for right-censored survival data: honest metrics that reward true accuracy. Proper scores keep medical forecasting truthful and accountable.
arxiv-2606-06693: Water flowing through nanometer channels behaves strangely — fluctuations and quantum effects matter. This paper studies fluctuation-induced and quantum effects in nanofluidic transport. The results matter for filtration, energy harvesting, and understanding life's own nanoplumbing. Nanoscale flow powers both technology and biology.
arxiv-2606-07193: Legged robots learning to walk can hurt themselves — unless shielded. Shield-Loco shields locomotion policies with predictive safety filtering. The shield lets robots learn boldly without breaking. Legged robots learn without breaking bones. Predictive shields enable bold yet safe exploration.
tob-10493:
Maurice Maeterlinck, the Belgian playwright later famous for The Blue Bird, turned essayist in The Treasure of the Humble in 1896. Against noise, display, and restless ambition, he praises silence, humility, and the unseen inner life. The essays are gentle and dreamlike, reading at times like prose poetry.

Maeterlinck finds spiritual treasure in small, quiet things: a sleeping child, a kept secret, a moment of true silence between people. He argues the soul grows in stillness more than in events. Readers get meditations meant to be read slowly, by a writer who believed the most important part of a life is the part nobody sees.
tob-10793:
Archibald Sayce, an Assyriologist, compared the religions of ancient Egypt and Babylonia in lectures on their gods, temples, and hopes. Two of the world's oldest literate faiths developed side by side, trading ideas across deserts and empires. Sayce brings them into direct contrast.

Creation and flood myths, priesthoods, festivals, and ideas of the afterlife are weighed one civilization against the other. Similarities raise questions about borrowing; differences reveal distinct temperaments. A classic of early comparative religion, the book is now partly superseded by later archaeology, but it remains readable and shows how Victorian scholarship first mapped the ancient Near East's religious world.
tob-9047-57493:
Pliny the Elder, a Roman officer and tireless reader, packed everything he could learn into his Natural History. At thirty-seven books, it is the largest single work to survive from ancient Rome. John Bostock's nineteenth-century translation opens the set with volume one.

Pliny begins with a bold preface and a tour of the cosmos: the shape of the earth, the sun and stars, and the order of the heavens. Geography follows. Nothing learned escapes his net, from tides to eclipses. Later volumes turn to animals, plants, and stones. The whole work shows one mind trying to hold an empire's knowledge.
tob-4093:
Household religion takes rule-book form in the Grihya-Sutras, translated by Hermann Oldenberg for the Sacred Books of the East. Part one of volume twenty-nine covers the rites of the Vedic home. Birth ceremonies, weddings, funerals, and daily offerings each receive exact directions.

The sutras tell the householder which verses to speak, which offerings to pour, and in what order the acts must fall. Scholars prize them because they show religion as families lived it, not as priests theorized it. Ancient India's family life stands here rule by rule. Verified from the 1919 edition, Oldenberg's version serves historians of ritual well.
bloomfield-moore-keely-and-his-discoveri:
Clara Bloomfield-Moore, a wealthy widow from Philadelphia, spent years backing inventor John Worrell Keely and his promised new force. Her 1893 book Keely and His Discoveries pulls together her case for him. It draws on letters and reports on the Keely Motor Company affair.

Keely claimed his machines ran on 'etheric force,' a power drawn from the air itself by tuned vibration. Bloomfield-Moore prints tests, press reports, and pleas from backers who sank money into the scheme. The book is the main record from inside one of the great science frauds of its age. Keely's force was never found by any outside test.
warboys-three-witches-1593:
The Throckmorton children of Warboys shook, cried out, and named the woman they blamed: Alice Samuel. The Most Strange and Admirable Discoverie of the Three Witches of Warboys, printed in 1593, gives the full case. No Elizabethan witch trial is better documented than this one.

The pamphlet prints the girls' fits, the witness statements, and the long road to the gallows for Samuel and her kin. Judges, clergy, and kin all speak in its pages. Readers can trace how child testimony, once believed, left the accused no ground to stand on. Scholars still mine the record for what it shows about proof and fear.
new-england-witches-further-account-1693:
London readers met the Salem crisis in print in 1693, while the New England trials still echoed. A Further Account of the Tryals of the New-England Witches joins the Salem news with Increase Mather's Cases of Conscience. Mather, a leading Boston minister, had turned against the use of spectral proof.

The pamphlet lets English readers weigh the trials as living news, not far-off tale. Mather's part argues that it is better for suspects to go free than for one innocent to die. The pairing shows debate on both sides of the ocean at once. It is the key English print on Salem from its own year.
hale-collection-modern-relations-1693:
Judge Matthew Hale presided over the famed Bury St Edmunds witch trial of 1664, and a 1693 book gathers his thoughts on such cases. A Collection of Modern Relations concerning Witches and Witchcraft is tied to his name. It links Bury with a run of other trials of the age.

The book collects modern cases of witchcraft and adds Hale's own meditation on the Bury trial. A chief judge of England sets out why he held witchcraft to be real and its proof sound. The volume shows the law's highest minds still firm in belief late in the century. It helps explain why trials ran on so long.
roosevelt-wilderness-hunter-1893:
Theodore Roosevelt hunted the Rockies and wrote it up in The Wilderness Hunter of 1893. Tucked in its tales is the Bauman story, told him by an old trapper. Bauman's partner was found dead in camp, his neck broken, with strange tracks all around.

Bauman said a great two-legged beast had stalked them in the woods and killed his friend. Roosevelt tells it straight, as a true tale of the wild, with no wink. The story is now read as the classic first draft of Bigfoot lore. It gains force from the teller: a hard hunter who became a president.
bierce-can-such-things-be-1893:
Ghosts, beasts, and strange deaths fill Ambrose Bierce's tales in Can Such Things Be?, from 1893. One tale hunts a thing no eye can see. One more traces a man's death in a loop of dread and guilt. Each tale ends with a twist.

Bierce writes in crisp, cold prose. He mocks hope and strips each ghost of soft glow. The set builds on his war tales of 1891. It holds a firm place at the root of the weird tale in the United States. Bierce had honed his craft as a news man in the west. He wastes no word, and each twist lands like a trap snapping shut.
judge-ocean-of-theosophy-1893:
William Q. Judge set out the whole creed in plain words in The Ocean of Theosophy, his book of 1893. Judge led the creed's arm in the United States. He saw that new fans drowned in Blavatsky's vast books. He wrote a short, clear guide that a new hand could read in days.

God, soul, karma, and birth past death get a crisp gloss each. The tone is calm and sure, with no show or fluff. Groups still give this book first to new fans. It is the creed's best known school text. Judge wrote with no fee and sought no fame from the book. That plain aim fits the calm, selfless tone on each page here.
hudson-law-psychic-phenomena-1893:
Thomson Jay Hudson split the mind in two in The Law of Psychic Phenomena, his hit book of 1893. Hudson was a law man and news man in the United States. His scheme gives each man two selves: one that thinks and weighs, one that takes bids, holds all past, and can act in trance, dreams, and strange cures at a word.

On that split he builds cures, faith, and tales of ghosts. The book sold in droves and shaped how his land spoke of the hid self. Its terms roamed far past its field. It is a folk text of mind lore.
barry-steve-browns-bunyip-1893:
John Arthur Barry spins bush yarns in Steve Brown's Bunyip, and Other Stories, his set of 1893. Barry wrote of the far south land's coast and bush with a sailor's zest. His title tale turns the bunyip from camp talk to a full tale. The bunyip is the dread swamp beast of settler lore. Men hunt what may not be there in the flesh at all.

Sea tales, gold tales, and bush hunts fill the set. Barry's prose is warm, wry, and full of local hue. The book is a prime store of that land's tale craft. Its bunyip still prowls.
jean-darras-melusine-1393:
Jean d'Arras wrote this romance of Melusine for a French duke in 1393. The text here is the 1895 Early English Text Society print of the Middle English form, set in print by A. K. Donald. Melusine is the famed maid who is part woman, part fish or snake.

She weds a knight on one term: he must not see her on the one day each week. When he breaks the term, she flies off in her strange form and is lost to him. The tale is the root stock of a vast line of fairy bride tales in Europe.
columbus-journal-first-voyage-1493:
Christopher Columbus kept a day book of his first voyage to the New World in 1492 and 1493. What we have is a short form made by Las Casas from the lost first text. Clements Markham turned it into English for the Hakluyt Society in 1893.

Off the Rio del Oro, Columbus notes a sight of 'mermaids' by his crew. His dry line says they were not as fair as tales claim, and he had seen such beasts before. Most now think the beasts were manatees, but the note is the most famed mermaid sight in print.
mather-wonders-invisible-world-1693:
Cotton Mather wrote The Wonders of the Invisible World in 1693. Mather was a Boston priest at the heart of the Salem witch trials. The book gives his own tale of the trials of 1692. It is the most famed first-hand text of the whole dark tale.

Mather tells of the fits of the girls, the tests used, and the trials' course. He prints the tales of five key cases in full. His aim was to back the judges and warn of the Devil's plots. The book is grim proof of how faith and fear drove the trials.
hermetic-museum-vol-2-1893:
A. E. Waite put out The Hermetic Museum, Restored and Enlarged, in 1893. Book Two ends the pair. The Museum is a store of old tracts on alchemy in English dress. Waite was the great voice of the occult age in Britain.

Tracts by famed hands of the art fill the book, some in print for the first time. The texts deal with the stone, the elixir, and the purge of base metals. Waite adds heads and notes to guide the new hand through the maze. The pair is a chief store of the alchemy of the West.
blackstone-commentaries-vol-2-1893:
Sir William Blackstone wrote his Commentaries on the Laws of England in the 1760s. George Sharswood's dress of 1893 fills this book. Book Two of this set holds Books Three and Four of the work. Book Three deals with wrongs to men in their own rights.

Book Four deals with wrongs to the state and the realm at large. Crime, courts, and pains for each fault fill its long run of text. Blackstone's clear prose made English law a thing a plain man could read. The Commentaries shaped law in Britain and the States for a long age.
leopardi-essays-dialogues-1893:
Giacomo Leopardi wrote his Essays and Dialogues in Italian in the 1820s, as the Operette Morali. The ironic dialogues on happiness, nature, and human illusion mark the prose peak of Italian pessimism. Leopardi, a frail scholar-poet of Recanati, finished most of them by the age of twenty-six.

Nature, the Moon, a fashion plate, and a seller of almanacs take turns in brief, lucid scenes. Nature tells an Icelander she neither knows nor cares that men suffer under her vast, blind laws. Pleasure, a dialogue proves, is always past or future, never present to the hand that grasps it. Leopardi's classical polish makes despair elegant, and his humor keeps the gloom from mere negation of life. The dialogues stand beside his great lyrics, the Canti, as his gift to prose.
bradley-appearance-reality-1893:
F. H. Bradley published Appearance and Reality in 1893, the summit of British idealism. Bradley argues that the world as it appears is full of contradictions. Relations, qualities, time, and the self all break down under strict thought. Reality must therefore be one harmonious Absolute that thought can only approach.

The Absolute, for Bradley, is a single experience beyond relations. Finite things are appearances of it, true in degrees. Moore and Russell began their careers by rebelling against this monism. Their revolt shaped analytic philosophy for a century. Bradley's prose is dense but masterful. The book remains the classic statement of British absolute idealism.
mach-mechanics-mccormack-1893:
Ernst Mach was an Austrian physicist who distrusted any idea that could not be tied to what we sense and measure. His Science of Mechanics, first published in German in 1883 and in English in 1893, retells the growth of mechanics as a human story. Thomas McCormack translated this edition.

Mach attacks Newton's talk of absolute space and time as empty words beyond all test. He retells the work of Galileo, Newton, and others as a chain of careful trials and errors. Einstein read Mach closely, and the book helped clear the ground for relativity. He writes history and criticism together, judging each past claim by the tests it passed.
hort-way-truth-life-1893:
Fenton John Anthony Hort was the Cambridge textual critic who, with Westcott, rebuilt the Greek text of the New Testament. His Way, the Truth, the Life, published in 1893, prints his Hulsean Lectures on the words of Jesus in John's Gospel. The book shows the great critic as a theologian.

Hort takes Christ's claim to be the way, the truth, and the life as a key to the whole faith. He reads the Gospel's images of light, bread, and the shepherd as one unfolding self-revelation. The lectures' quiet depth reveals why Cambridge trusted Hort with its hardest textual questions.
orr-christian-view-god-world-1893:
James Orr was a Scottish theologian whose Christian View of God and the World, published in 1893, prints his Kerr Lectures. The lectures offer a comprehensive Christian worldview against the Victorian unbelief of his age. Orr writes for students facing Darwin, biblical criticism, and doubt.

He argues that the Christian view, God as Father ruling a moral world toward redemption, explains more than any rival system. His survey takes in nature, history, sin, and the incarnation as parts of one intelligible whole. The book helped give evangelical thought the very concept of a worldview to defend.
waite-hermetic-museum-vol1-1893:
Arthur Edward Waite, the English occult scholar, edited The Hermetic Museum in 1893 as a restoration of classic alchemical tracts in English. Volume one opens the two-volume set, whose second volume already stands in this library. Waite chose texts he thought held the true thread of Western alchemy.

The tracts speak in the riddling language of the art: green lions, kings in baths, and stones that are not stones. Waite's introductions guide the reader through each author's life and claims with a scholar's patience. The set gave English readers a small library of alchemy between two covers.
partridge-opus-reformatum-1693:
John Partridge was a London astrologer and almanac maker whose Opus Reformatum, published in 1693, offers a reformed astrology. Partridge was a Whig in politics and a scourge of his fellow astrologers in print. His chief target was John Gadbury and the old art Gadbury defended.

He argues that astrology must be rebuilt on Ptolemy's rules alone, swept clean of Arabic additions and English habits. The feud between Partridge and Gadbury filled pamphlets for years and entertained the coffeehouses of London. Swift later mocked Partridge in the famous Bickerstaff hoax, but the Opus shows the reformer in earnest.
revised-odd-fellowship-illustrated-1893:
John Blanchard, a minister and fierce critic of secret societies, published Revised Odd-Fellowship Illustrated in 1893. The Odd Fellows were a large fraternal order with lodges, degrees, and private ritual. Blanchard printed what he said was their full revised ritual so the public could judge it.

Pages give the opening and closing forms, oaths, prayers, songs, and degree work of the lodge, with notes attacking them. Blanchard argued that secret pledges and mock sacred scenes were wrong for Christians. Whether read as warning or record, the book preserves the exact forms of a major fraternal order at the end of the nineteenth century.
tucker-instead-of-a-book-1893:
Benjamin R Tucker published Instead of a Book, by a Man Too Busy to Write One in 1893 in New York. Tucker edited Liberty, the leading journal of individualist anarchism in America. Too busy, as his title jokes, to write a fresh book, he gathered his best pieces from the journal instead.

Essays and sharp exchanges set out his program against what he called the four monopolies: money, land, tariffs, and patents. His key piece, State Socialism and Anarchism, contrasted his free-market anarchism with state socialism. Tucker answered critics at length and in a fighting style. The volume is the fullest record of American individualist anarchism in its editor's own words.
weismann-germ-plasm-1893:
August Weismann was a German biologist who set out to explain how traits pass from one generation to the next. His book appeared in German in 1892 and reached English readers a year later. W. Newton Parker and Harriet Rönnfeldt translated it, and it was published in 1893.

Weismann argued that the body holds two kinds of material. Germ cells carry heredity forward, while the rest of the body, the soma, dies with each person. Because of that split, changes gained during life cannot be inherited by children. His germ-plasm theory shaped early debates about evolution and heredity for years.
gissing-odd-women-1893:
George Gissing published The Odd Women in 1893, taking his title from the many women of his time who could never marry for lack of men. Gissing wrote about the Madden sisters, left poor by their father's sudden death. The novel asks what unmarried women were supposed to do with their lives.

Two sisters scrape by as teachers and shop workers, while their younger sister Monica is courted by an older, controlling man. Nearby, Rhoda Nunn runs a school training women for office work and preaches independence. Love tests every one of these positions. The novel is now read as a founding text about women's work and freedom.
marlowe-massacre-paris-1593:
Christopher Marlowe wrote The Massacre at Paris near the end of his life, dramatizing recent French history. France's wars of religion were still raging when the play reached the stage around 1593. The text that survives is short and may be a cut-down version of what Marlowe wrote.

The Duke of Guise plots the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572, when Catholic mobs slaughtered Huguenot Protestants in Paris. Kings rise and fall quickly as assassinations pile up. Marlowe's Guise is a cold, ambitious villain who boasts of his crimes. The play is brutal and hurried, but it shows how raw recent politics could be on the Elizabethan stage.
yeats-celtic-twilight-1893:
William Butler Yeats published The Celtic Twilight in 1893, gathering sketches he had written about the folklore of the Irish west. Yeats was then leading the Irish literary revival, urging writers to draw on their own country's tales. He collected much of this material around Sligo, his mother's home country.

The short pieces record peasants' beliefs in faeries, ghosts, and enchanted places, told in the tellers' own spirit. Yeats neither mocks the beliefs nor simply endorses them. He treats the faery world as a living part of Irish imagination. The book became a source-book for the revival and shaped how Ireland pictured its own past. Its dreamy tone set the mood for a generation of Irish writing.
crane-maggie-1893:
Stephen Crane was twenty-one, poor, and unknown when he published Maggie: A Girl of the Streets at his own expense in 1893. He printed it under a pen name and gave copies away. Crane had prowled New York's Bowery for material and wrote like nothing American fiction had seen.

Maggie Johnson grows up beautiful in a tenement ruled by drink and street fights. A bartender's flash and promises seduce her, then abandon her to the streets her world prepared for her. Crane tells the story in flashing, ironic scenes, with dialogue like stage directions from hell. Nobody in the novel can see Maggie clearly, least of all her family. Maggie is the first unflinching American slum novel and the founding text of literary naturalism here.
jabir-ibn-hayyan-oeuvres-berthelot-1893:
Jabir ibn Hayyan, known in Latin as Geber, was the great name of early Arabic alchemy, a scholar of Kufa in the eighth century. A vast body of work bears his name. Marcellin Berthelot printed six of the Arabic treatises in French in 1893, in his study of Arabic alchemy. The text here gives those six.

The treatises set out the sulfur and mercury theory of metals and the search for the elixir that perfects them. Jabir teaches balance, weights, and careful furnace work, a turn toward the measured side of the art. His name ruled alchemy in both Arabic and Latin for centuries. Berthelot's French pages let modern readers meet the Jabirian corpus at its source.
locke-some-thoughts-concerning-education:
John Locke wrote Some Thoughts Concerning Education in 1693, growing out of letters to a friend on raising his son. All 217 sections stand here, in the order Locke gave them. The subject is the making of a gentleman, from a baby's swaddling to a young man's travels.

Health comes first: cold water, plain food, and hard beds build a body fit for life. Virtue follows, then wisdom and breeding, with book learning placed last and lightest. Locke's child learns by practice, example, and love of credit, not by beating and rules. The book shaped English schooling and child rearing for two centuries. Parents still steal from it.
schleiermacher-on-religion-1893:
Friedrich Schleiermacher, a young Berlin preacher, published his Speeches on Religion in 1799 without his name. John Oman's translation of 1893 gives them as On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers. The despisers were his own friends, the educated romantics who thought faith was dead and buried.

Schleiermacher answers that religion is neither dry doctrine nor mere morals. It is intuition and feeling, a sense for the infinite in the finite, tasted before it is argued. That claim refounded modern liberal theology and gave faith a home in feeling. The five speeches still read as a young man's passionate brief for the inner life. Oman made them an English classic.
windelband-history-philosophy-1893:
Wilhelm Windelband wrote his history of philosophy as a history of problems, not just of thinkers. The German book appeared in 1892, and James H. Tufts published his English translation in 1893. Windelband led the Baden school of philosophy in Germany. His aim was a serious textbook on how European thought grew over time.

Windelband shows the motives that pushed each age to form its picture of the world and of human life. Ancient, medieval, and modern thinkers appear as they wrestle with shared questions. Tufts added a short notice on recent English thought for readers of the translation. The result long served students as a compact, clear map of Western philosophy.
stephen-agnostics-apology-1893:
An Agnostic's Apology first appeared as an essay in 1876, and Leslie Stephen later bound it with other essays in 1893. Agnosticism holds that some claims, above all about God, lie beyond what minds can know. Stephen states that position with rare calm and candor. The title essay became a classic Victorian statement of the view.

Around it stand essays on belief, doubt, and the moral life without creed. Stephen refuses both blind faith and cheap scorn for faith. He asks what honesty demands when proof runs out. His prose is dry, clear, and firm. The set still serves readers who want doubt argued well.
besant-autobiography-1893:
Annie Besant told her own story in An Autobiography, printed in 1893. She had been a clergyman's wife, then a famous freethought lecturer beside Charles Bradlaugh. Socialism claimed her next, with strikes and Fabian debates filling those years. In 1889 she met Helena Blavatsky and turned to Theosophy, a turn that stunned her public.

The book ends near that conversion, with her new faith still fresh. Her account is the key primary source for her path to the Adyar society. Later she would lead the Theosophical Society and fight for Indian home rule. The life she records here explains that future. Few Victorian lives changed course so often.
balzac-cesar-birotteau-wormeley-1893:
César Birotteau sells perfume in Paris, dreams of honors, and trusts the wrong men with his money. Balzac's Rise and Fall of César Birotteau, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's 1893 translation, follows a good man's climb and his ruin in bankruptcy court. Commerce, credit, and speculation drive every turn.

Few novels handle a failure of business with such care for law, pride, and shame. Birotteau fights to pay every creditor, though the city shrugs at his fall. The book stands as the Human Comedy's deepest study of trade, the tragedy of an honest shopkeeper in a gaming world.
balzac-physiology-of-marriage-wormeley-1:
Before the great novels, Balzac made his name in 1829 with The Physiology of Marriage, a witty treatise on husbands, wives, and straying hearts. Katharine Prescott Wormeley's 1893 translation keeps its dry, teasing tone throughout. Part satire, part handbook, the book sorts marriages into kinds and warns plainly where each one cracks.

Balzac writes as a doctor of wedlock, counting dangers the way others count pulse beats at a bedside. His jokes rest on sharp watching of Paris drawing rooms and country estates alike. The work founded his Analytic Studies and shows the cool observer who would soon build the Human Comedy.
sienkiewicz-pan-michael-curtin-1893:
The little knight Wołodyjowski makes his last stand at Kamieniec in Pan Michael, the closing volume of Sienkiewicz's Trilogy. Jeremiah Curtin's 1893 translation completes the arc begun in With Fire and Sword and The Deluge. Turkish armies press the Polish border fortress, and the aging hero holds the wall.

Love and loss run beside the siege, as Michael's young wife faces the war he cannot leave. Sienkiewicz wrote to hearten Poles under foreign rule, and his vast battle tales did just that. English readers of Curtin's version meet the national epic of Poland at its heroic close.
cowell-buddha-karita-asvaghosha-1893:
Asvaghosha sang the Buddha's life in Sanskrit verse, and E. B. Cowell's 1893 translation gave English readers the Buddha-Karita whole. The poem, a classical kavya from about the second century, follows the prince from birth and palace luxury to awakening under the tree. Cowell's edition came from the Anecdota Oxoniensia series at Oxford.

Beauty serves doctrine here: every episode turns the hero from the world toward release. The translation was the first complete English rendering of the poem. Readers who want the Buddha's life as India itself told it, in high literary form, start here.
naladiyar-pope-1893:
G. U. Pope translated the Naladiyar for the Clarendon Press in 1893, four hundred Tamil quatrains of Jain teaching. The verses, ascribed to Jain ascetics, school the reader in impermanence: wealth fades, youth passes, and only virtue holds. Pope added critical notes and a concordance, tools he built for students of Tamil.

Each quatrain stands alone, a small, polished warning or comfort. Together they form a breviary of renunciation from early South India, gentler in tone than many such books. Pope's English version remains the classic door into the Naladiyar, a jewel of Tamil didactic verse.
cruden-complete-concordance-1893:
Alexander Cruden, a London bookseller, published the first great English Bible concordance in 1737. The 1893 edition keeps his life and work before the reader. Cruden labored for years, largely alone, indexing the King James text.

Every significant word is listed with the verses where it appears, so readers can gather all the passages on a theme. Cruden adds a summary of the Bible's contents and notes on names and places. His book served preachers and lay readers for two hundred years. It stands beside Strong's as one of the twin pillars of English Bible reference. The 1893 printing adds helps for the growing Sunday school movement.
easton-illustrated-bible-dictionary-1893:
Matthew Easton, a Scottish minister, published his book in 1893. It was the standard one-volume Bible dictionary for ordinary readers. Easton aimed to put sound learning within reach of Sunday school teachers and families.

Entries cover the history, biography, geography, doctrine, and literature of the Bible in plain language. Illustrations, tables of dates, and maps support the articles. Easton takes a conservative line, trusting the text while using the new digging of his day. The dictionary sold widely and was reprinted for decades; digital editions still circulate among students of the scriptures today. The tone is calm and plain, made for home use as much as for the pulpit.
plos-pone-0003393:
Yumi Yamaguchi-Kabata and colleagues mapped a special class of DNA changes in this 2008 paper. A nonsense change puts a stop sign in the middle of a gene's instructions. The protein then ends early and often fails to work. Little was known about where these changes sit in human genes.

The team scanned human gene data for these stop-sign changes, called polymorphisms. They charted how often each one occurs and which genes carry them. They also weighed what the changes do to gene function. The map helps doctors judge which DNA changes are likely to matter.
plos-pone-0003493:
Patricia Sagaspe and co-authors tested night driving after long hours awake in this 2008 study. Tired driving is a well-known cause of road crashes. Many drivers pair long drives with lost sleep. Most fatigue crashes happen at night.

No experimental data had pinned down how prior driving time worsens night performance. Their tests showed extended driving impairs nocturnal driving further. Sleep loss and driving duration stack their harms. The numbers support rest rules for professional and private drivers alike. Truck drivers and shift workers face this stacked risk most often of all.
plos-pone-0003593:
C. James Chou and co-authors built a targeted drug for leukemia cells in this 2008 paper. Chronic myeloid leukemia is marked by the BCR-ABL fusion gene. That gene, born of the Philadelphia chromosome swap, makes an always-on kinase. Imatinib already blocks that kinase, but resistance can arise.

The team fused a sequence-specific polyamide to chlorambucil, a cell-killing drug. The conjugate arrested the growth of BCR-ABL positive cells. Guiding a poison to one DNA address is the core idea. Such targeting could spare cells lacking the fusion gene. The fusion gene is found in nearly all cases of this leukemia type.
plos-pone-0003693:
Cheryl Carling, Doris Tove Kristoffersen, Jeph Herrin, and colleagues published this pilot trial in PLOS ONE in 2008. The same treatment effect can be shown as numbers, words, or pictures, and the format sways patient choices. No standard way existed to judge which format helps people choose by their own values.

The team ran a pilot randomized trial comparing ways to present treatment effects. They also compared methods for scoring whether choices matched patients' values. The work aims at honest risk communication, so patients get numbers they can actually use in the clinic.
plos-pone-0003793:
Catherine J. Pears, Kelly Thornber, Jocelyn M. Auger, and colleagues published this blood study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Platelets are the cell fragments that start clotting, and protein kinase C helps switch them on. The family has many isoforms, and evidence suggested each plays its own role. The team focused on two newer ones.

They compared PKC delta and PKC epsilon in mouse and human platelets. The two isoforms played different, even opposing, roles in platelet activation. Such divisions of labor matter for drugs that would calm clotting without crippling it entirely.
plos-pone-0003893:
Yi Arial Zeng, Maryam Rahnama, Simon Wang, and co-authors studied two growth signals in fruit flies in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns the Wingless and TGF-beta pathways. Both pathways guide how organisms grow and take shape. Both also help guard against tumor growth when kept in balance.

The authors report that blocking Wingless signals involves a contest inside the cell. Two proteins, Mad and Armadillo, compete to bind a third protein called dTcf. That contest helps switch the Wingless path off at the right time. The finding adds detail to how cells keep growth signals under control.
plos-pone-0003993:
Fumiaki Fukushima, Kazuhito Nakao, Toru Shinoe, and co-authors removed a receptor type from mouse hippocampus in 2009. The CA3 area of the hippocampus has a strongly recurrent network. Its joint firing underlies oscillations, memory, and seizures. NMDA receptors are plentiful at the recurrent synapses there.

Their PLOS ONE article reports CA3 neurons grew more excitable without NMDA receptors. That outcome runs against the usual view of these receptors as drivers. Removing them may free other paths that raise firing. The work reshapes models of how CA3 bursts begin. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004093:
Nazira El-Hage, Annadora J. Bruce-Keller, Tatiana Yakovleva, and co-authors studied morphine with HIV protein in brain cells in 2008. Astrocytes are brain support cells where opiate and HIV signals meet. The HIV Tat protein drives inflammation in those cells. Morphine use can worsen HIV brain disease, called encephalitis.

Their PLOS ONE article traces where the two signals converge. Effects met on calcium levels, NF-kappaB movement, and gene transcription. Morphine amplified Tat-driven cytokine output through those points. Naming the convergence sites suggests where therapy might interrupt the harm. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004193:
Kana Watanabe and colleagues published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Early in life, experience shapes the wiring of the brain by refining which connections survive. In the visual system, changed visual input drives cortical responses to adapt and incoming fibres to rearrange.

The team silenced the visual cortex with drugs. They asked whether axons still retract in response to experience without synaptic transmission, the usual signal passing between neurons. They report that experience-driven axon retraction still occurs in the inactivated cortex. The result separates two processes that were assumed to work as one.
plos-pone-0004293:
Yi-Wen Lin and colleagues published this neuroengineering study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neural systems respond to chemical and electrical stimulation, but the effect of mechanics on these sensitive cells is still not well understood. Existing tools limited the ability to examine mechanical effects precisely.

The team used a localised elastomeric matrix, a soft rubbery material whose stiffness they could control in small regions, to probe sensory nerve mechanotransduction. Mechanotransduction is how nerves convert touch and stretch into signals. Controlling the ground a nerve grows on lets researchers ask how much of touch is physics.
plos-pone-0004393:
Swelling and redness in inflamed tissue depend on signals that switch genes on. One key signal is stem cell factor, or SCF, which helps mast cells grow. Laurent Reber, Linda Vermeulen, Guy Haegeman, and co-authors traced how SCF output is controlled. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper centers on NF-kB, a protein that turns genes on. It also centers on the enzyme MSK1.

The authors report that MSK1 adds a phosphate tag to NF-kB's p65 part. The tag lands on a spot called Ser276. That single mark controls how much SCF gets made in inflammation. SCF output also needs two other signal routes, named p38 and ERK. Pinning the chain down gives drug research a precise target.
plos-pone-0004493:
Coat proteins cover a sleeping-sickness parasite in the tsetse fly gut. Erik Vassella, Michael Oberle, Simon Urwyler, and co-authors found those proteins are not needed for the trip, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The parasite is Trypanosoma brucei. In the fly's midgut it wears millions of copies of surface proteins called procyclins.

It was thought the coat protected the parasite from gut enzymes, or helped it in some other vital way. The team tested parasites lacking these major surface glycoproteins. The parasites still completed cyclical transmission through the tsetse fly, as the title reports. A result like that forces a rethink of why the coat exists. It also warns drug and vaccine planners not to spend effort on a target the parasite can live without.
plos-pone-0004593:
The Parkinson's drug L-DOPA may harm nerve cells by raising an iron transporter, propose Fang Du, Zhong-ming Qian, Li Zhu, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. L-DOPA is the standard treatment that restores the missing dopamine signal in Parkinson's disease. The mechanisms underlying the neurotoxicity blamed on long L-DOPA use are not completely known.

The team focused on DMT1, a transporter that moves iron and other metals into cells. One form of it, lacking an iron-response element, can escape the cell's iron controls. They report that L-DOPA up-regulates this form, and that its rise mediates the toxicity. If correct, guarding against iron loading might let patients keep L-DOPA's benefits with less of its harm.
plos-pone-0004693:
Alexander Khandoga and colleagues built a live test to watch white blood cells move in sore tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2009. After white cells cross into tissue, they must head straight to the site of harm. That directed move is a core step in the body response to injury or germs.

The team set up a way to film the move inside living tissue. Their method can count speed and shape change for each cell type. Live counts like these can show how drugs calm or boost the response. They also help explain why some swelling harms more than it heals.
freeman-giles-corey-1893:
Freeman turned to drama in Giles Corey, Yeoman, a play printed by Harper in 1893. The cast lists Giles and Martha Corey, minister Samuel Parris, and judges Hathorne and Corwin. Act one opens in Corey's Salem Village home, with daughter Olive at her spinning.

Little Phoebe Morse knits nearby while old servant Nancy Fox pares apples. A strange clatter in the chimney scares the child at the very start. Behind the scene stands the true Salem horror of 1692. Corey, an old farmer, was pressed to death under stones rather than confess to witchcraft, and his last words were a call for more weight.
zola-doctor-pascal-1893:
Mary Serrano translated Doctor Pascal, the last Rougon-Macquart volume of 1893. Chapter one opens on a glowing July afternoon in a room of closed blinds. Scattered sunbeams soften the cool gloom as Dr. Pascal hunts for a paper.

His great oak press holds thirty years of notes and drafts on heredity. Every page he wrote, from brief jottings to full books, lies piled in its depths. The old doctor has tracked his own family's bloodline all his life. Late love with his niece Clotilde crowns the tale. Hopeful and humane, the book serves as Zola's farewell to his great chronicle.
bernard-eales-life-works-vol3-1893:
Eales completed his Life and Works of Saint Bernard with a third volume in 1893. The set had already given English readers Bernard's life and letters. The closing volume turns to the works that made Bernard's lasting fame as a teacher of the inner life.

Here are his sermons and treatises, including the famous sermons on the Song of Songs, left unfinished at his death. His writing on grace and free will also appears, where he weighs human choice against God's help. Bernard's prose was famed for its sweetness, and he was called the mellifluous doctor, the honey-tongued teacher. Eales's edition let Victorian readers meet that voice in English. The volume closes the standard English Bernard of its generation.
commons-distribution-of-wealth-1893:
John Commons published The Distribution of Wealth in 1893, his first major book. Commons, a young economist at the start of a long career, asked the oldest question in his science: who gets what, and why? He would go on to found the institutional school of American economics, and this book is its opening shot.

Commons argues that the shares going to labor and capital are not fixed by nature. Law and custom, he shows, shape what each side can claim, since property itself is a legal creation. The argument sets him against both pure market theory and socialist doctrine. Later, Commons built labor law and social insurance in Wisconsin on ideas first stated here. The book lets readers watch a major school of economics being born in one man's first system.
french-constitution-1793:
The National Convention adopted a new French constitution in June 1793, drawn up by the Mountain, the Revolution's radical party. France was at war and near civil war, and the charter promised more democracy than any law of its age. It was approved by a popular vote, then set aside until peace should come. Peace never came in time.

The text grants the vote to all adult men and declares work, public help, and education to be rights of every citizen. It even blesses the people's right to rise against a government that betrays them. No charter ever offered the people more on paper. Its makers never dared to put it into force, ruling instead through the Terror. The constitution stands as the Revolution's boldest dream of self-rule, written down but never tried in life.
inter-caetera-1493:
Pope Alexander VI issued Inter Caetera in 1493, the year after Columbus reached the Americas for Spain. The bull drew a line down the Atlantic Ocean, west of the Azores and Cape Verde islands. Lands west and south of that line were granted to Spain's rulers.

The text urges Spain to spread the Catholic faith among the peoples it met overseas. Portugal objected to the line, and the two kingdoms soon moved it by treaty. Even so, the bull supplied a legal claim behind Spain's growing empire. It shows how European powers used church law to divide lands they barely knew.
cia-0000009693:
Three groups of American prisoners of war were sighted on an infiltration route, a May 1971 report states, in a country the title cuts off. Groups on the move were usually marched between camps or toward a central prison system. Witnesses counted groups because individuals could not be named.

Group sightings helped analysts estimate how many men the enemy held in transit. They also showed the prison system's logistics: routes, staging points, and direction of travel. A northward route implied Hanoi's camps as the end point. The file captures captives in motion, the hardest state in which to track them.
cia-0000009793:
Whether American prisoners were still held by the Socialist Republic of Vietnam for use in negotiations is weighed in a February 1977 paper. Parts of the heading are deleted, marking heavy redaction before release. By 1977, Hanoi governed a united Vietnam, and relations with Washington were frozen.

The paper tackles the hardest postwar question in plain terms: men kept back as bargaining chips. Officials had suspicions, reports, and no proof solid enough to act on. That gap between fear and proof defined the issue for decades. This file preserves the question as the agency itself posed it, deletions and all.
cia-0000009993:
The grave of an American soldier in Tri Tam district, Binh Duong province, is located in an August 1974 item. Binh Duong lies just north of Saigon, in country fought over until the war's end. A located grave turned an open case toward its saddest resolution.

Grave locations were recorded with survey care because recovery teams might travel years later to the same ground. Coordinates and landmarks had to outlast the report's writer. Families could finally receive a place, if not yet remains. This item preserves that place, a district-level fix in the postwar recovery record.
cia-0000010593:
India's position in the East-West conflict is set out in an August 1951 CIA paper. Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru refused to join either bloc, preaching nonalignment to the new nations of Asia. Washington found the stance frustrating in a country of India's size and weight.

The paper weighs what nonalignment meant in practice: trade, votes, and influence across Asia. A neutral India denied the West a giant ally but also denied Moscow one. Analysts had to read pride, principle, and interest together. This file preserves that reading at the Cold War's very start in Asia.
cia-0000011793:
Followers of former president Juan José Arévalo were plotting against Guatemala's government, according to a CIA paper from April 1963. Arévalo had led Guatemala's democratic spring of the 1940s, and his supporters, called Arevalists, still opposed the regime in power. The paper labels their planning extremist and links it to a bid to overthrow the government by force.

Analysts tracked the conspirators, their aims, and their chances of success. The plotting came nine years after the CIA itself helped topple Arévalo's successor, an act that shadowed Guatemalan politics for decades. The paper shows the agency watching the left it had helped drive underground.
cia-0000011993:
Turkey had proved itself in blood during the Korean War, and in January 1956 the CIA appraised its worth as an ally. Turkey guarded the Soviet Union's southern flank and the straits to the Mediterranean. Its soldiers had won respect in Korea, and its government had joined NATO four years earlier.

The paper weighs Ankara's reliability, its armed strength, and the limits of its loyalty. It also asks what Turkey expected from the partnership in return. Peacetime was testing whether the bond sealed in war would hold, and the appraisal shows Washington taking the measure of a partner it needed.
cia-0000012393:
Day two of the London debriefings gets its own record: meeting number two, April 21, 1961. Penkovsky's handlers were learning how to question an extraordinary source. They had to pace him, test him, and record every word he said. All of it had to fit inside his short London trip, before he flew home to Moscow and its dangers.

The record continues the story the first session began. Questions came fast in those early days. The colonel's answers piled up hour by hour. For readers, the page shows the debriefing finding its rhythm, as handlers and source settled into the work.
cia-0000014193: Probable Communist reactions to certain U.S. actions fill a CIA paper dated May 3, 1965. The paper narrows the lens to one side: how Communist powers and parties might strike back. Tit for tat thinking ran through Cold War planning on both sides. A paper like this tried to map the tat before the United States chose its tit.
cia-0000014793: The New Meaning of Treason, a book by Rebecca West, is noted in a CIA file dated May 1, 1973. The file says the book's first half takes up its famous cases. West wrote with a sharp, cold eye on traitors and trials. A 1973 file on her book shows the spy shelf still growing two decades on.
cia-0000015293: A letter to Gordon Scherer from Allen Dulles fills a CIA file dated September 2, 1955. It takes up Thomas Eickhoff's letter, per the clipped title. Dulles ran the agency itself, yet still signed mail on saucer claims. The file shows how high the public's questions could climb inside the building. The Dulles letter now rests in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000022493: Two American pilots were sighted in Nam Dinh City, in Nam Ha Province, North Vietnam, a CIA record dated in 1973 reports. Nam Dinh was an industrial city south of Hanoi, much bombed during the war. A city sighting placed the men among crowds, not in a known camp. Such reports were chased hard in the year of the prisoner homecoming.
cia-0000036293:
An intelligence memorandum dated August 1, 1969 takes up instability in Brazil. Brazil was ruled by generals, and the memo looks at the strains inside that rule. It also touches on related developments noted in the same file.

The memo sets out why the regime looked less steady than it claimed to be. Analysts weighed the armed forces, the economy, and public unrest as sources of strain. For readers, it is a close look at a dictatorship studied from outside at a hard moment. The memo's own title frames the problem as instability rather than open revolt, and that framing shaped how Washington judged the news.
cia-0000041193:
Broadcasts from North Vietnam included a six-minute recorded statement, preserved in a CIA record dated July 4, 1972. The statement was attributed in the broadcast material, though the title leaves the speaker cut short. American monitors recorded Hanoi's English broadcasts as a matter of daily routine.

Inside, the recorded words are kept as they were aired from the north. Short attributed statements were a favorite tool of Hanoi's radio war that summer. The file shows the monitoring effort at its most literal. It holds a tape and a transcript's worth of words. A voice meant to sway opinion abroad was given its place in the record.
cia-0000042293:
An American prisoner of war was sighted in Le Xa village, in Nam Sach district, Hai Hung province, a CIA record dated June 5, 1973 reports. The sighting came months after the Paris agreement had promised releases. A prisoner still seen in a village raised a hard question at once.

Inside, the village report is set down with its district and province named. Precise places made a sighting testable in a way rumors were not. The file shows the accounting continuing past the peace signatures. Men were still being reported in named villages, and each report had to be run to ground before the books could close.
cia-0000046693: Four American prisoners of war were reported held at an internment camp in the northwest of South Vietnam, in a CIA item dated May 5, 1972. Word of where prisoners were kept was among the most valued reporting of the war. The item adds one camp, and four men, to the map families and officials kept.
cia-0000049193: Traces on four key Salvadoran officers who were at the military academy fill a partly blacked-out CIA item from 1990. The academy stood at the center of the Jesuit case: the order to kill was given there. Four paper trails, laid together, let investigators test each story against the others, name by name.
cia-0000049293: A new terrorist campaign in El Salvador is reported in a CIA item from 1986, kept with the Truth Commission records. New was the dread word: a fresh round of killings beginning just as the country had learned the old one's rhythm. The item records the launch as watchers first read it, before its full shape showed.
cia-0000049393: Assassinations and kidnappings of local officials are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049393, dated January 2, 1991. The item carries a Truth Commission note and centers on attacks against local officeholders. Readers get a brief dated record whose heading names the victims' class directly, one more short agency notice from the Salvadoran conflict's final phase.
cia-0000095093: Policy guidelines for the incoming administration of President-elect Jose Lopez are set out in declassified CIA document 0000095093, dated September 3, 1976. The heading is cut short at the president-elect's name in the catalog. Readers get a short declassified guidelines record for a new Mexican administration, filed beside the other transition items that week.
cia-0000098093: Publication of the Che Guevara's Diary, in the heading's wording, is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000098093, dated September 2, 1967. The title concerns the diary reaching print. Readers find a short declassified publication item, a media event rather than a field report, preserved among the agency's records from the guerrilla's final year.
cia-0000096493: The Situation in Hong Kong is the title of declassified CIA document 0000096493, dated May 1, 1967. The heading is a general situation label for the colony. The brief file precedes the agency's outlook on Hong Kong by two months in this catalog. It gives readers the earlier item of a pair. The later one is the outlook on the same place.
cia-0000098693: National Intelligence Bulletin article titled Angola: Communist Support for, with the phrase cut short, is declassified CIA document 0000098693, dated October 1, 1975. The heading names a bulletin article and its Angola topic. The brief file preserves that article record, filed the same day as its companion bulletin piece on Angola press reports.

arxiv-2606-15793: This 2026 arXiv preprint delivers a new research contribution. The work centers on Proximal Policy Optimization for Amortized Discrete Sampling, as the title says. The topic falls under social science — how people behave, organize, and make decisions together. The paper delivers its results to the wider research world.
arxiv-2606-15893: A 2026 arXiv entry, this research manuscript advances a new study. Its title describes the subject as BALTO: Balanced Token-Level Policy Optimization for Hallucination Mitigation. The backdrop is artificial intelligence (the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data). The manuscript's findings join the public body of research.
plos-pone-0004793:
Tina Rönn and colleagues linked variation in the ATP5O gene to muscle gene expression and glucose uptake in young twins, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Weak oxidative capacity in skeletal muscle mitochondria contributes to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Expression of oxidative genes, including ATP5O, is reduced in muscle from diabetic patients compared with healthy controls studied previously.

Twin studies help separate gene effects from shared environment. The team tested whether ATP5O variation tracks with its own expression and glucose uptake. A link would support a causal role in diabetes risk. It names a concrete gene for follow up.
plos-pone-0005393:
Fracture healing is a tidy, time-limited case of rebuilding bone after birth. Bais and colleagues profiled which genes switch on during that repair in PLOS ONE in 2009. The process replays many steps of embryonic bone formation.

Transcriptional analysis showed embryonic stem cell-related genes induced during healing. Adult repair, in other words, partly reawakens embryo programs. Those shared genes are candidate levers for therapies that aim to speed or rescue bone healing in patients whose fractures stall. Old bones heal slow and some breaks never join. So genes that wake in a fresh break are a list of parts that care teams may one day switch on in a stuck break to restart growth.
plos-pone-0005493:
Gwendaline Guidicelli and co-authors studied a drug effect on tumour cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Many tumours make extra amounts of an enzyme that helps build GTP, a key cell fuel and signal. A drug called mycophenolic acid blocks that enzyme and is already used to calm the immune system.

The team found that the drug sends tumour cells a death signal of a kind they cannot easily resist. Cells that shrug off the usual death route still responded to this one. That opens a possible new use for an old drug against stubborn cancers.
plos-pone-0005593:
Beatrice Carlsson and co-authors studied a gene change and stomach flu in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. In late 2004, a norovirus outbreak swept a nursing home in Spain and made over a hundred people ill. Norovirus is a common cause of vomiting outbreaks in care homes and ships.

The team read a gene, FUT2, in sick residents. One gene change seemed to protect strongly against illness, though not fully. Knowing who is less at risk helps explain why outbreaks spare some people and may guide future vaccines. Care homes face norovirus again and again, so knowing who is protected helps plan staffing during an outbreak.
plos-pone-0005693:
Dharmendra Modha presented a new kind of brain atlas in 2009, built as a surface rather than a stack of slices. Most atlases cut the cortex into flat slices, which can be hard to read against the folded surface of the brain. Modha's scheme unfolds each slice onto a surface map.

The result is a conceptual atlas that is easier to picture and teach. Folds and grooves of the cortex keep their place in a way slice stacks lose. Such maps help students and surgeons talk about exact spots on the brain. The paper keeps the method simple on purpose, so others can adopt it.
plos-pone-0005793:
Chang Han and Piotr Jablonski watched courtship in a water strider in 2009, where females can hide their genitalia from forceful males. Many species face sexual conflict: males gain by mating often, females by choosing. That tension drives an arms race of defenses and counter-moves.

In this strider, concealment did something unexpected. Rather than only blocking males, it drew out longer, more intimate courtship from them. When force fails, persuasion takes over. The finding flips a simple story of conflict into one where defense reshapes mating for both sides. It is a neat case of evolution bargaining.
plos-pone-0006393:
Life science literature grows faster than anyone can read, so machines must extract the facts. Thorsten Barnickel and colleagues applied neural network based semantic role labelling at large scale in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The goal was automated relation extraction from biomedical texts, beyond simple word co-occurrence methods.

Co-occurrence can scan corpora like MEDLINE quickly but cannot tell how terms relate. Semantic role labelling identifies who does what to whom in a sentence. At scale, that yields structured knowledge from raw papers. The approach helps keep databases current without armies of readers.
plos-pone-0006493:
Katsuhiko Yoshizawa and co-authors studied a DNA repair enzyme and gut growth in PLOS ONE in 2009. DNA polymerase beta helps repair damaged DNA. Altered expression of this enzyme has been documented in a large share of human tumors. Whether too much or too little of it predisposes animals to tumors was less clear.

The team examined gastrointestinal hyperplasia, excess growth of gut tissue, with altered polymerase beta expression. Linking a repair enzyme to tissue overgrowth connects DNA damage handling to cancer risk. The gut is a fast-renewing tissue, so repair flaws show up there early. Their work informs debate on how repair changes drive tumors.
plos-pone-0006593:
Uppoor Bhat, Marianna Halasi, and Andrei Gartel studied a cancer transcription factor and proteasome drugs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Proteasome inhibitors are currently in the clinic or in clinical trials. The mechanism of their anticancer activity is not completely understood. The oncogenic transcription factor FoxM1 drives cell division genes.

Their title reports that FoxM1 is a general target for proteasome inhibitors. Blocking the proteasome lowers FoxM1, which may explain much of the drugs' effect. A shared target across cancer types is valuable. It also suggests measuring FoxM1 to predict which patients respond.
plos-pone-0009393:
Ajay Goel and co-authors published this colon cancer test study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some colorectal cancers fail to repair DNA mismatches. That failure, seen as microsatellite instability, flags Lynch syndrome and predicts treatment response. The standard test needs DNA from both normal and tumor tissue, a real burden.

The team optimized a five-marker PCR test that works from tumor DNA. Their pentaplex method detects repair-deficient cancers more simply. A test needing only the tumor sample can be run faster and on more patients. Better screening catches hereditary cancer families who can then be watched closely.
plos-pone-0009493:
James White and co-authors worked on brain controlled prosthetic limbs in PLOS ONE in 2010. Such limbs read brain activity and turn it into movement. Using signals of more than one kind could make control more exact. The catch is merging those streams fast, as they arrive in real time. The team built a method to fuse decisions from the separate streams.

Their method weighs each stream's output moment by moment and combines them into one command. Tests showed the fused result could beat any single stream alone. Smoother fusion is a step toward limbs that feel more natural to use. It matters for people who rely on such devices daily.
plos-pone-0009593:
Jixin Zhong and co-authors tested a signal protein in septic shock in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sepsis can kill when the immune response spirals out of control. Jak2 is a relay used by many immune signals. Its exact role in dendritic cells was hard to study, since mice without Jak2 everywhere die before birth. The team removed Jak2 only in dendritic cells.

Those mice survived a dose of bacterial toxin that normally kills. Their innate immune response was selectively damped. So one relay in one cell type can decide life or death in shock. The result names Jak2 in dendritic cells as a possible brake point for sepsis care.
plos-pone-0010393:
Young Moo Choo and co-workers found a double duty enzyme in bee venom, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bee venom holds many active proteins, including a family called serine proteases. What those enzymes do for the bee was unclear. No one had described their roles in venom before this work. The team purified one and tested its actions in detail.

The enzyme did two very different jobs depending on the victim. In insects and kin, it switched on a defense pigment pathway. In mammals, it broke down fibrin, a protein in blood clots. One venom tool thus harms two kinds of animals in two ways. That economy is typical of venom evolution. It also gives drug hunters a clot-cutting enzyme to study.
plos-pone-0010493:
Dilli Ram Bhandari and co-workers found markers that can tip stem cells toward growth or maturity in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mesenchymal stem cells can multiply or specialize into tissues like bone and fat. Controlling that choice is key to using them in medicine. The protein REX-1 is famous as a marker of embryonic stem cells. Its role in adult-type stem cells was much less clear.

The team linked REX-1 levels and a signaling switch, p38 MAPK, to the cells' fate choice. High or low states pushed cells toward multiplying or maturing. Readable fate markers help labs grow the cell type they actually need. That control is essential before stem cell therapies can be routine. This study adds two dials to the control panel.
plos-pone-0010593:
Alex Engel, Pablo Aguilar, and Peter Walter studied yeast mating in PLOS ONE in 2010. When two yeast cells mate, their outer membranes must merge into one. A protein called Prm1 helps that merging happen, but its working form was unclear.

The team showed Prm1 must join with an identical partner, forming a linked pair. Single copies on their own could not drive fusion well. Mutations that broke the pairing also broke mating. The pairing rule explains earlier puzzling results. It also gives cell biologists a firmer model for how fusion proteins work in other organisms.
plos-pone-0010693:
Tanja Zeller and colleagues profiled gene activity in human monocytes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Monocytes are white blood cells that patrol the blood and seed inflamed tissue. People differ widely in which genes their monocytes switch on, and those differences may shape disease risk.

In a large group of volunteers, the team tied activity patterns to DNA variants and to health traits. Some activity was driven by inherited variants; some was not. The dataset became a reference for linking DNA to real cell behavior. Such links are the missing middle step between a risk variant and the disease it raises.
plos-pone-0010793:
Liina Pylkkänen and Kana Okano probed the brain's abstract letter codes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Skilled readers recognize a letter in any size, font, or handwriting. The brain must therefore store letters as abstract codes, stripped of surface looks. What those codes contain beyond shape was the open question.

Volunteers read words while brain fields were recorded by magnetoencephalography. Masked priming, where a hidden word speeds the next, revealed the timing of letter coding. The codes engaged sound-linked information earlier than a pure shape store would predict. Reading, the work suggests, binds symbol, sound, and meaning into one fast code from the start.
plos-pone-0010893:
Solomon Ghebremichael, Ramona Groenheit, Alexandra Pennhag and co-authors published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drug-resistant TB is rising worldwide, and one bacterial family, the Beijing lineage, has driven large outbreaks of hard-to-treat disease elsewhere. Some researchers suspect this lineage spreads unusually well, so the team checked its record in Sweden.

They studied every drug-resistant TB isolate collected in the country over fifteen years and picked out the Beijing strains. Those strains made up a modest share of resistant cases, and most patients were born abroad, suggesting infections arrived with migration rather than spreading locally. Ghebremichael and colleagues find no sign that Beijing strains transmit more in Sweden. Their results show a feared lineage's danger can depend heavily on local conditions.
plos-pone-0010993:
Ge Jin, Hameem Kawsar, Stanley Hirsch and co-authors published this oral cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tumors are crowded with macrophages, immune cells whose presence tracks with progression and poor outcomes. A small antimicrobial peptide made by tumor cells, human beta-defensin-3, had been linked to drawing those macrophages in, and the team traced the route it uses.

Comparing normal mouth tissue with early carcinoma samples, they charted the peptide alongside a classic macrophage attractant and its receptor, CCR2. Lab and mouse experiments showed the defensin can summon macrophages by engaging that same receptor system. Jin and colleagues recast a microbial defense peptide as a tumor's recruiting signal. Blocking the CCR2 route might slow the inflammatory build-up that helps oral cancers grow.
plos-pone-0011093:
Loughlin and Artlett reported cell damage research in PLOS ONE in 2010. They studied human skin cells exposed to a building block of sugar damaged proteins. Such damaged proteins build up in diabetes and are tied to slow wound healing and skin problems.

Exposure set off stress inside the cell and switched on a protein that drives cell death. The chain ran through an enzyme that makes harmful oxygen based molecules. Mapping that chain shows where the damage could be blocked. Each step the team traced is a possible target for drugs that protect skin in diabetes.
plos-pone-0011193:
Krintel, Klint, Lindvall and colleagues described a fat enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme releases stored fat for fuel when the body needs energy. It comes in several forms, called isoforms, and the team studied their four part structure and how each form carries out its chemical work.

Knowing how form tunes function helps explain how fat release is controlled between meals and during exercise. Faults in that control feed into obesity and diabetes research. The structural detail gives drug and metabolism science a firmer base. It shows that treating all forms as one enzyme would miss key differences.
plos-pone-0011293:
Pasco-Viel, Charles, Chevret and colleagues traced fish throat teeth in PLOS ONE in 2010. Carps and minnows, one of the largest fish orders, chew food with teeth set in their throats rather than jaws. The team followed how that pharyngeal dentition changed across the group's long evolution.

Trends in tooth shape and count tracked shifts in diet and lineage. Throat teeth are a key innovation that let these fishes exploit many food types. Mapping their evolution informs fish biology and the study of diversity. It shows how moving a familiar structure to a new place can open ecological room.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1293:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Ambassador Hornbeck in the Netherlands on 23 July 1945. The message answered the Hague post from Washington, in the circuit of guidance that bound the embassies to the home office during the summit.

Orders to a newly freed country had to match what the talks were deciding in Germany. The home office kept its envoys in step as stands shifted. This cable is that keeping-in-step at work. It preserves a moment in the traffic between the two governments, caught in the American files at the height of the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1393:
Mikołajczyk wrote another diary entry on 31 July 1945, the day before the Potsdam leaders signed their protocol. His file of papers is the longest single-author run in this section of the volume. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

On the eve of the settlement, a diary entry holds a special charge. The writer knows the decisions are nearly fixed, yet not announced. Mikołajczyk's page for that day lets readers stand where he stood: informed of much, able to change little, still writing. Set against the dry protocol printed nearby, the diary restores the fear and hope that the official text leaves out entirely.
frus-1945-50-intel-d93:
Eddy wrote to Under Secretary Acheson on 30 January 1947. The intelligence chief's channel to the department's second-ranking man was by then a well-worn path. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

McCormack had used the same channel in the office's first autumn, and Eddy now used it in its steadier second year. Acheson remained the ear that mattered for the department's inner business. Readers can compare the two chiefs' papers to Acheson across fifteen months: the first pleading for an office's life, the second conducting its affairs. That contrast is the State intelligence story in two letters, and the volume prints both ends of it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d193:
A text titled "Circular Instruction From the Department of State" bears the date 15 April 1947. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 193 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

Orders of this kind turned broad policy into daily rules. They name the office in charge and the work to be done. They name the office in charge, the work to be done, and the limits that apply, line by line. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d293:
Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter addressed a memorandum to the Chief of Naval Operations (Denfeld) on 18 June 1948. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 293 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d393:
W. Park Armstrong, the Secretary of State's special assistant for research and intelligence, wrote to Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter on 2 August 1949. His letter is document 393 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series.

Armstrong ran the State Department's own intelligence office, the unit that read world events for the Secretary. A letter from him to the head of the CIA shows the two shops talking at the top. It helps readers see how the State Department tried to keep its own strong voice in intelligence work.
frus-1861-d93:
On 29 October 1861, William H. Seward closed the month with a letter to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 93 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's last October letter to Adams keeps the routine of the autumn intact. Neither man knew that a Union warship was about to stop a British mail ship at sea. The letter's calm close to the month makes the crisis that followed stand out all the more. Within a month the two envoys seized from the Trent would fill every London talk. Every London talk that winter would turn on the names of those two envoys.
frus-1861-d193:
John Appleton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 April 1861. The dispatch is document 193 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Appleton held the St. Petersburg post until Clay could reach it. His April report came four days before Fort Sumter. It shows the old envoy serving the new chief through the last days of peace, with Russia friendly but far away. Russia's goodwill, though real, could not send ships or gold across the world in time. Goodwill that could not send aid still denied aid's hope to the other side.
frus-1861-d293:
The State Department sent word to Mr. Harvey on 30 July 1861, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 293 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d93:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 8 July 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 93 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d193:
The last Adams letter in this run, Document 193. Is a Seward dispatch of 21 November 1862 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It closes the autumn sequence of the London file in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

By late November the danger of Britain and France acting together on the war had passed for the year. What remained was the slower fight over ships, trade, and opinion, which ran on into 1863. This letter stands at the point where the record turns from emergency to endurance, a fair summary of the Union's foreign war. Adams reported home at least once a week, and oftener when the news was hot.
frus-1862-d293:
On 9 July 1862 William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report printed as Document 293 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The report came after a gap in the Paris file.

By the time Dayton wrote, news of McClellan's retreat from Richmond was reaching Europe, and French talk of stepping into the war revived. His report from Paris in that week carried the court's first reactions. For Washington, such letters answered a vital question: would failure in Virginia bring foreign action, or only foreign talk? A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d393:
On 16 September 1862, the day before Antietam, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Simon Cameron in St. Petersburg. The dispatch is printed as Document 393 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

A letter to Russia on the eve of the war's bloodiest day could not mention it, and would not be read for weeks. That lag gave the Russian correspondence its reflective tone: policy stated as principle, not reaction.
