This dispatch closes the Seward-Cameron run in the file, written at the hinge of the autumn campaign. The Russian route was the longest in the file, crossing an ocean and then half of Europe.
frus-1862-d493:
On 8 April 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. It is Document 493 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

Seward wrote two days after Shiloh, though full word of that battle had yet to settle. His orders to The Hague that spring kept returning to the same Dutch questions. Those were port rules and colonial harbors. They also included the standing of Confederate agents in Europe. Pike's task was to be pleasant, exact, and immovable on the Union's rights. The dispatch is one of a steady spring run in the Dutch file, in which neither side let a month pass in silence.
frus-1862-d593:
On 28 June 1862 Thomas Corwin sent this report from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 593 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Corwin's end-of-June report came as the Seven Days battles opened in Virginia, though no word of them could reach him for weeks. In Mexico his subject was the French advance and the endurance of the Juárez government, which the Union supported in word. The isolation of his post is part of the record's interest: a minister arguing America's case with month-old news, in a capital itself under threat. His letters home remain the volume's fullest American account of the Mexican crisis of 1862.
frus-1862-d693: On 23 May 1862, a Mr. De Long sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 693 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, his first letter in the file since March of that year. The evidence gives the writer, the date, and the place in the volume, but not his post or what the letter covers.
frus-1863p1-d93:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 February 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date, and a Seward letter shares it too. Adams was the American minister in London; this letter is document 93 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late February was one of the thickest points in the whole file, with both men writing in bunches. Adams's sheets reported the London scene as the month closed: officials, papers, and Southern men all in motion. This one opens his set of three for the day. The pile itself tells the story of a post at full stretch.
frus-1863p1-d193:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 May 1863. It is document 193 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Adams dealt most often with Lord John Russell, Britain's foreign secretary. His letters home summed up those talks and the mood of the British government. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d293:
The mail from London dated 17 September 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 293 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

British yards were building two ironclad rams for the Confederacy in the summer of 1863. The fight to stop those ships reached its peak that autumn, filling the London mail. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d393:
A note dated 18 February 1863 carried the British position from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 393 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d493:
Among the day's business on 7 May 1863 was a letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d593:
In the flow of wartime mail, Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington wrote to Secretary William H. Seward on 22 July 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d693:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, on 12 November 1863. The letter stands as document 693 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863, part one of that year's printed papers.

By mid-November the two men had a set rhythm of notes, replies, and fresh notes. That rhythm was itself a kind of peace work. It gave both capitals a calm way to raise sharp points about the war at sea and on land. For the reader, this dispatch fills in one more day of that rhythm. Its plain, brief form is typical of how the work got done.
plos-pbio-0020393:
Mathew T. Pletcher, Philip McClurg, Serge Batalov, and a large team offered a shortcut for mouse genetics in PLOS Biology in 2004. Mapping a trait to a gene in mice normally needs many bred crosses. Their method uses a dense map of DNA markers and computer models to predict the gene's place from strain data alone.

In silico mapping, as they call it, mines the rich records already held on standard mouse strains. It can narrow a trait's location before any new mice are bred. That saves time, money, and animals. The approach works best for traits measured across many strains, and it has become a first pass in mouse gene hunts.
plos-pone-0000093:
Hassan Lemjabbar-Alaoui, Vijay Dasari, Sukhvir S. Sidhu, and their team linked cigarette smoke to lung cancer pathways in PLOS ONE in 2006. Two signal systems, Wnt and Hedgehog, guide lung growth before birth. The team found both systems switched back on by smoke exposure in lung cells, in ways tied to cancer growth.

Dormant growth programs waking up is a common cancer theme. If smoke wakes these two, they become candidate targets for prevention or treatment. The result also helps explain, at the molecular level, why smoking is so potent a cause of lung cancer. It gives tobacco research specific switches to watch in smokers' lung tissue long before tumors form.
plos-pone-0000193:
Michael A. Brockhurst, Nick Colegrave, David J. Hodgson, and colleagues published this experimental evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Working with microcosms, small lab ecosystems of microbes, they test what limits adaptive radiation, the rapid splitting of one lineage into many forms. Their answer is in the title: niche occupation, when the available roles are already filled.

A lineage can only diversify into open ecological space. The authors show experimentally that filled niches block further radiation. The result speaks to grand patterns in evolution, from island finches to bacteria. It does so with a controlled lab test rather than fossil inference alone.
plos-pone-0000293:
Li Chen, Rulong Shen, Yin Ye, and colleagues published this cancer stem cell paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Precancerous stem cells sit at the border between healthy tissue and cancer. The authors report that these cells have the potential for both benign and malignant differentiation: they can mature into harmless tissue or into cancer.

A cell that can go either way is both a risk and an opportunity. Understanding what tips it toward cancer could allow prevention at the earliest stage. The paper supports the stem cell model of cancer, in which a small pool of versatile cells drives the disease.
plos-pone-0000393:
Fanny Tzelepis, Pedro M. Persechini, and Mauricio M. Rodrigues examined timing in the immune response in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. CD8 killer T cells destroy infected cells, but they develop with help from CD4 T cells. The team asked how the moment when pathogen numbers rise affects the making of those killer cells.

When an infection grows fast or slowly, the immune system may build its killer force at a different pace or quality. The study varies the timing of the increase in pathogen load and measures the effect on T cell growth and specialization. Results like these matter for vaccine design, where the size and timing of the dose shape the defense that forms.
plos-pone-0000493:
Robert Andrews and Julie Ahringer watched the early sorting machinery of worm embryos, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Endosomes are the cell's sorting stations for material taken in from outside. In embryos of the worm C. elegans, the team found an asymmetry of early endosome distribution: the stations are not spread evenly but placed unevenly between the embryo's regions.

Asymmetry is how a one-cell embryo begins building a body with a head end and a tail end. If sorting stations are unevenly placed, the daughter cells may inherit different processing power. The finding adds cell logistics to the list of things embryos set up unevenly from the very first divisions.
plos-pone-0000593:
Sam P. Brown and François Taddei modeled how the lifespan of shared goods changes cooperation, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Public goods, from clean water to microbial secretions, invite free-riders who benefit without paying. The authors show that the durability of public goods changes the dynamics and nature of social dilemmas.

A long-lasting good keeps rewarding the group, altering whether cooperation pays and whether cheats prosper. That twist matters from bacteria, where shared enzymes are literal public goods, to human commons like fisheries. Durability is a design lever: goods built to last may sustain the cooperation that produces them.
plos-pone-0000693:
Thomas Efferth, Marco Giaisi, Annette Merling and colleagues tested a malaria drug against resistant leukemia cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Drug resistance is a major obstacle in cancer treatment, as tumor cells learn to survive chemotherapy. New drugs are urgently needed that hit tumor cells hard while sparing normal cells. Artesunate, a drug known from malaria care, was their candidate.

The title states their finding: artesunate triggers apoptosis, programmed cell death, in T leukemia cells that resist doxorubicin. The killing runs through ROS, reactive oxygen species that damage cells from inside. Repurposing a known drug for resistant cancers could shorten the road to the clinic.
plos-pone-0000793:
Michel A. Slotman, Aristeidis Parmakelis, Jonathon C. Marshall and colleagues searched mosquito genomes for signs of an arms race, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Plasmodium parasites and their mosquito vectors coevolve, which can leave adaptive changes in genes central to the vector's defense. By checking which genes show positive selection in malaria vectors, but not in close non-vector relatives, the team could spotlight the defenses under pressure.

Their title reports evidence for adaptive evolution in LRIM1 in Anopheles arabiensis, one such vector. A gene evolving fast under parasite pressure is a target for intervention. That kind of target hunting is the study's wider promise.
plos-pone-0000893:
Stefan Jonsson, Rebecca LaRue, Mark Stenglein and colleagues tested how a human protein blocks a pig retrovirus, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The protein, APOBEC3G, is part of the body's built-in defense against viruses. It can stop some retroviruses, including ones that live permanently in animal genomes.

The virus in focus, PERV, lives in pigs and is a concern for transplanting pig organs into people. Using long term cell cultures, the team asked whether APOBEC3G can restrict its spread between species. The work bears on xenotransplantation, using animal organs for human patients. Safety there depends on knowing which human defenses actually hold.
plos-pone-0000993:
Gordon Louie, Thomas Baiga, Marianne Bowman and colleagues solved the structure of basil eugenol synthase, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Phenylpropenes are plant scents that defend leaves and draw pollinators. Eugenol, the scent of cloves and basil, is made by an enzyme that trims a side chain on its starting material.

The team present both the enzyme's structure and its reaction mechanism, how it performs that trim. A structure turns a black box into a machine with visible parts. Plant scent enzymes are also targets for farming and fragrance work. Knowing the mechanism could let growers or chemists tune how much scent a plant makes.
plos-pone-0001093:
Derek Nancarrow, Herlina Handoko, Mitchell Stark and colleagues built a tool to score DNA copy number changes in chip data, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genome wide SNP chips can now find where cancer genomes gain or lose DNA stretches, with fine sensitivity. In some tumors those changes are so complex that scoring them by eye fails.

Their tool, SiDCoN, aids that scoring. Copy number changes are not small print: whole gene doses shift, and with them cell behavior. A consistent scorer helps compare tumors across studies. Cancer genome projects produce data faster than humans can grade it, so assistive tools are part of the science, not an extra.
plos-pone-0001193:
Hidden inside many bacterial genomes sit prophages, the dormant genomes of viruses that once invaded the cell. K. V. Srividhya and colleagues present a computer method for finding them in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Prophages help make strains differ, and many genes for bacterial virulence are carried by them.

Their method uses dinucleotide relative abundance difference, a numeric fingerprint of DNA makeup that differs between a bacterium and its prophages. Current methods look for possible viral genes or binding sites and can miss cases. A makeup-based approach offers another way to spot these stowaways. The method needs only the genome sequence itself.
plos-pone-0001293:
Some genes are expressed from only one of the two copies a person carries, the other copy staying silent. Jinhui Wang and colleagues searched the mouse central nervous system for such monoallelic expression, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Genes like these are hard to detect, yet the inheritance patterns of several major disorders hint that they are involved.

DNA methylation in regulatory regions is often a mark of the silent copy, which the authors used as a guide. Finding multiple genes with monoallelic expression in the CNS widens the known reach of this phenomenon in the brain. It may matter for disorders with puzzling inheritance.
plos-pone-0001393:
Renat Shaykhiev, Jürgen Behr, and Robert Bals published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how airway cells heal. The cells that line the airways meet germs each day and sense them with alarm proteins. Those alarms are often tied to swelling and harm. The team asked whether the same alarms also help repair.

They found that germ patterns sensed by two such alarms aid growth and repair of the airway lining. The signals helped cells close wounds and stay alive. That dual role shifts the view of these alarms as pure threats. It suggests future drugs might boost the repair side while still curbing harm from infection.
plos-pone-0001493:
Fiona Thompson and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a malaria shot that mixes two plans. Past work held that the best shot would hit the parasite at more than one life stage. This phase 2a trial was the first to merge two such plans in one shot. Volunteers were then exposed to malaria in a controlled test.

The team report signs that the shot worked at the blood stage of the parasite. Blood stage action is what stops illness once infection starts. Even partial proof at this stage is a gain for the field. It backs the multi stage tack for the next round of shot design.
plos-pone-0001593:
Zoltán Bochdanovits and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on guessing gene pairs that work as a team. Our genome holds few genes for the vast range of traits we show. Gene teams that interact could explain that range. The team sought such teams in patterns of gene change between mice and men.

Pairs whose change patterns track each other are flagged as likely partners. The method scans the whole genome at once, not pair by pair in the lab. Its calls give bench labs a short list to test. True pairs found this way would enrich the map of how traits are built.
plos-pone-0001693:
Momiao Xiong, Frank C. Arnett, Xinjian Guo, and their co-authors studied skin cells from scleroderma patients in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Scleroderma hardens skin and connective tissue. Diseases in general arise when whole biological systems, not single parts, are pushed off balance by environmental triggers, and those systems keep changing over time.

The team disturbed fibroblasts, the cells that build connective tissue, with changes in their environment and tracked how patient and healthy cells responded. They found the dynamic responses differ, per the paper's title. The full text gives the perturbation tests and the response patterns. Distinct response dynamics could become a way to spot the disease's state or test drugs, beyond static gene lists.
plos-pone-0001793:
Kristoffer Ström, Ola Hansson, Stéphanie Lucas, and their co-authors studied fat cells in mice lacking a fat-splitting enzyme, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Hormone-sensitive lipase, or HSL, works mainly in adipose tissue. There it breaks down stored triglycerides and diglycerides to mobilize fatty acids when hormones call for energy. It also acts on a broad range of other substrates.

In mice with no HSL, white adipocytes, the usual storage cells, attained features of brown adipocytes, the heat-producing kind. The full text gives the fat tissue measurements and gene markers. White fat turning brown-like is a sought-after effect in obesity research, since brown fat burns energy as heat.
plos-pone-0001893:
Haoran Wang and co-authors studied the high squeaks mice make during courtship, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Adult mice call at pitches too high for human ears when they seek mates, yet the genes that steer such calls were little known. The team worked with mice that lack one of several signal proteins in the brain.

They tested mice missing muscarinic receptors M2, M4, or M5, and mice missing the D2 dopamine receptor. Sex cues and a dose of amphetamine were used to prompt calls. By counting calls in each line, the study ties brain signal paths to a basic social act. That helps map how genes and brain chemistry shape voice and courtship.
plos-pone-0001993:
Anna Roukens and co-authors tested a smaller dose of yellow fever vaccine, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Yellow fever vaccination is held back by short supply of the vaccine. Giving each person less, if it still protects, would stretch stocks across far more people.

The team tried a new route: injecting a reduced dose into the skin, rather than under it. Their randomized trial was built as a non-inferiority test. It was meant to prove the low dose is not worse than the standard by more than a set margin. As the title states, the reduced dose induced a protective immune response.
plos-pone-0002093:
Liang Li, Simon Norrelykke, and Edward Cox studied how cells roam when no signal guides them, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cells such as amoebae, fibroblasts, neutrophils, and growth cones can sense a chemical gradient across their own length and steer toward it. Far less was known about how they move when there is no external signal at all.

The team tracked persistent cell motion in that blank setting, cell by cell. A cell that keeps a heading without cues may be running a search strategy, covering ground well while waiting for a scent. The work defines the baseline that all guided motion builds on.
plos-pone-0002193:
Oswald Crasta, Otto Folkerts, Zhangjun Fei, and co-authors sequenced the genome of a cattle vaccine strain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Brucella abortus strain S19 has been used for six decades to vaccinate cattle against brucellosis, a disease that also infects people. S19 lost its power to cause disease on its own, but the changes behind that weakening were unknown.

The team read the strain's full genome and compared it with virulent relatives. Differences between them point to candidate genes that make the wild strains dangerous. Knowing exactly what S19 lacks could lead to safer vaccines and better tests that tell vaccinated cattle from infected ones.
plos-pone-0002293:
Yann Saint-Georges, Mathilde Garcia, Thierry Delaveau, and co-authors studied how yeast park certain messenger RNAs at their mitochondria, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Where an mRNA sits inside a cell helps coordinate what happens after genes are read. Many mRNAs for mitochondrial proteins are made in the nucleus but localize near mitochondria, so their proteins can be imported on the spot.

The team examined the role of Puf3p, an RNA-binding protein of the PUF family, in that localization. They tested how changes in the binding context affect the parking of these messages. The work details one layer of the logistics that keep a cell's power plants supplied.
plos-pone-0002393:
Sussman and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Meir Sussman, Bette L. Willis, Steven Victor, among others. Its subject is coral Pathogens Identified for White Syndrome (WS) Epizootics in the Indo-Pacific.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work. Each claim is tied to the work the team did, and the text keeps facts apart from the views of the authors.
plos-pone-0002493:
Beer, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Shelly Beer, Kimberly Komatsubara, David I. Bellovin, among others. Its subject is hepatotoxin-Induced Changes in the Adult Murine Liver Promote MYC-Induced Tumorigenesis. Overexpression of the human c-MYC (MYC) oncogene is one of the most frequently implicated events in the pathogenesis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002593:
Scholl and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Hendrik P. N. Scholl, Peter Charbel Issa, Maja Walier, among others. Its subject is systemic Complement Activation in Age-Related Macular Degeneration. Dysregulation of the alternative pathway (AP) of complement cascade has been implicated in the pathogenesis of age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002693:
In 2008, Julie Doostzadeh and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about high throughput automated allele frequency estimation by pyrosequencing. Authorship is credited in the record to Julie Doostzadeh and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Pyrosequencing is a DNA sequencing method based on the principle of sequencing-by-synthesis and pyrophosphate detection through a series of enzymatic reactions. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002793:
Michel Gohar and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of the PlcR virulence regulon of bacillus cereus. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Michel Gohar, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. PlcR is a Bacillus cereus transcriptional regulator, which activates gene expression by binding to a nucleotidic sequence called the ‘PlcR box’. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002893:
Ildiko Somorjai and Alfonso Martinez-Arias watched Wingless signaling at work in fly wing discs in 2008. Wingless is the fly form of the Wnt signal, a major guide for growth. Its partner protein Armadillo both carries the signal and helps E-Cadherin hold cells together at their edges.

Using third-stage larval wing tissue, the PLOS ONE study tracks how the signal changes the levels, place, and movement of both proteins. Without the signal, Armadillo is marked for breakdown. Developmental biologists get a close view of how one protein balances signaling and cell adhesion in a growing wing.
plos-pone-0002993:
Natarajan Singaravelan, Isabella Grishkan, Alex Beharav and co-authors studied UV response in a soil fungus at Evolution Canyon in Israel in 2008. Adaptation tailors traits in a population to local challenges through natural selection. Mount Carmel's canyon offers sharply different sun exposure on opposing slopes in a tiny area.

The fungus Aspergillus niger makes melanin, a dark pigment that can shield against ultraviolet radiation. The team examined its adaptive melanin response to UV stress between slopes. Published in PLOS ONE, the site acts as a natural lab for fast, local evolution. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003093:
Keith Bradnam and Ian Korf showed in 2008 that first introns tend to be longer across eukaryotes. Many properties of gene structure are well characterized, yet differences between introns at different positions in a transcript were less understood. Intron length variation by position was a specific open point.

Longer first introns are a general property of eukaryotic gene structure, the title concludes. Published in PLOS ONE, a genome-wide regularity like this constrains theories of gene evolution. First introns often hold regulatory elements, so their extra length may be functional, not filler. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003193:
Melissa A. Penny, Nicolas Maire, Alain Studer and colleagues simulate malaria vaccine effects in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A number of malaria vaccine candidates were in pre-clinical or clinical development. They vary greatly in their traits, and it is unlikely any will provide long-lasting sterilizing immunity against the parasite. There was great interest in what developers should ask before trials.

The authors simulate the effectiveness of malaria vaccines to guide those questions. Readers see how modelling can compare partial protection scenarios in advance. Simulations cannot replace trials, but they can stop weak designs early and highlight which outcomes matter most.
plos-pone-0003293:
Sergey Gavrilets, Edgar A. Duenez-Guzman and Michael D. Vose model alliance formation in human history in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Arguably the most influential force in human history is the formation of social coalitions and alliances, meaning long-lasting coalitions, and their impact on individual power. Understanding the dynamics of alliance formation and its consequences for biological, social and cultural evolution is a major goal.

The authors model how alliances form and how they may have driven an egalitarian revolution, the levelling of dominance. Readers get a formal account of how weak individuals can jointly restrain the strong. That idea is central to theories of human cooperation.
plos-pone-0007393:
Philip Rhodes, Jim Craigon, Clint Gray, and colleagues studied prenatal nutrition and adult obesity in sheep in 2009. Obesity triggers many metabolic disturbances. A shift from poor nutrition before birth to excess afterward may worsen adult metabolic dysfunction, a pattern called developmental programming seen across many mammalian species studied.

The authors restrict maternal nutrition during gestation in sheep. They then examine glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity in adult male offspring that became obese. Adult-onset obesity revealed prenatal programming effects from late gestation restriction. Their results warn that early deprivation plus later plenty is a risky combination.
plos-pone-0007493:
Beata Ujvari and Thomas Madsen published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on telomeres in tropical pythons. Telomeres are the protective caps at chromosome ends, and they shorten as cells divide. Length has been tied to lifespan in birds and humans. The team measured telomeres in red blood cells of hatchling snakes. They then considered what the values mean for the snakes' long lives ahead.

Even at hatching, the pythons' telomeres were already short. That complicates the simple story that longer telomeres always mean a longer life. Snakes manage longevity with a different starting point than birds or people. The study tracks how erythrocyte telomeres change as the snakes age. It widens the telomere debate beyond the usual warm-blooded models. Simple rules drawn from humans do not travel well across species.
plos-pone-0007593:
Wan-Suk Oh and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the pinewood nematode, a tiny worm devastating pine forests worldwide. The worm feeds on fungi and on pine tissue itself. It drives the pine wilt epidemic now threatening forests on several continents. Control options exist but are limited, and resistance is a worry. The team identified and characterized a compound that attacks the nematode through two actions at once.

A dual-acting agent is harder for the pest to resist than a single-action one. If one mechanism is dodged, the other still lands. That property is prized in protecting a resource as vast as pine forests. The study characterizes the compound's actions against the worm. It offers forest managers a candidate weapon where few exist. Two blows in one molecule is a sound strategy against an adaptable pest.
plos-pone-0007693:
Grant Trobridge, Robert Wu, Brian Beard and their co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on gene therapy for AIDS. No effective AIDS vaccine exists, which pushes researchers toward other approaches. One landmark case involved a patient given blood stem cells that naturally lack a doorway the virus uses.

The team tested a related strategy in a primate model. They gave stem cells a protective change, let the cells produce immune cells, and then selected for those cells inside the body. The protected cells survived and multiplied. That result supports stem cell therapy as a possible route against HIV.
plos-pone-0007793:
Jennifer Campos and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It compares real movement through space with movement that is only imagined. Do the two share one inner picture in the mind? Scientists had argued that point for years. Few tests had set whole-body motion beside imagined motion in a direct way.

The team used a new pointing task that runs without pause. People pointed as they moved, and then as they just pictured the same move. The imagined path did not match the felt path. That gap matters for coaches who train athletes by mental rehearsal. It also matters for builders of flight simulators and virtual worlds.
plos-pone-0007893:
Kengo Uemura and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It links the shape of an Alzheimer's-related enzyme to the mix of amyloid it makes. The enzyme, gamma-secretase, cuts amyloid protein into pieces of various lengths. Its catalytic part is presenilin 1, or PS1.

Longer amyloid pieces, especially Abeta42, are more harmful. Patients with inherited Alzheimer's make more of those longer forms. The authors show that allosteric drugs shift the enzyme's conformation. That shift correlates with the ratio of Abeta42 to Abeta40. Tuning the enzyme's shape offers a drug strategy gentler than blocking it outright.
plos-pone-0007993:
Mark Dessing and colleagues tested how lung harm from a bacterial toxin unfolds in mice, for PLOS ONE in 2009. The toxin is pneumolysin, made by the germ behind much pneumonia. Two sensors on immune cells, the Toll-like receptors numbered 2 and 4, spot germ patterns and raise the alarm.

Mice work showed both sensors help drive the lung swelling and injury the toxin causes. The alarm saves lives in true infection, yet here it adds to the damage. The finding suggests that softening this alarm, at the right moment, might limit lung injury in severe pneumonia without leaving the germ unchecked.
plos-pone-0008093:
Ji Sohn and colleagues worked out how a hepatitis kin builds its lasting DNA form in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hepadnaviruses, the family that includes hepatitis B, copy their genome in an odd way. To persist in the liver, the loose circle of viral DNA must be rebuilt into a tight closed circle.

That closed form is the virus's long-term archive, the reason infections can return after years. The team traced which enzymes do the rebuilding, host repair crews or the virus's own. Naming the crew names a choke point where a drug might erase the archive at last.
plos-pone-0008193:
Jean-Charles Ceccato and co-authors studied trunk movement in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Starting to walk and walking steadily both demand balance. The trunk muscles help keep that dynamic posture stable. The team compared trunk activity during gait initiation with activity during ongoing walking in humans.

They recorded trunk motion and the electrical activity of the erector spinae muscles. These muscles run along the spine and help hold the body upright. A dynamic analysis joined the two kinds of data. The comparison shows how the trunk works differently when a step begins. That matters for research on balance and falls.
plos-pone-0008293:
Rachel E. Horton and colleagues compared immune cells from two body sites in PLOS ONE in 2009. Studying immunity in the female genital tract is critical for vaccines against sexually transmitted infections. Microbicides also depend on that knowledge. Sampling this site is difficult, so most studies use blood cells instead. Whether blood reflects the genital tract was the open question.

The team compared gene expression and cell phenotypes between cervical and blood cells. Differences would mean blood studies miss local features. The comparison guides how future studies should sample. It supports better design of prevention tools for women.
plos-pone-0008393:
Evangelos J. Giamarellos-Bourboulis and colleagues studied pandemic influenza immunity in PLOS ONE in 2009. The novel H1N1 pandemic created a need to understand its effects on host immunity. Blood was sampled within the first two days of symptoms. Volunteers included healthy people and cases of flu-like illness. Patients with confirmed novel virus were also sampled.

Comparing immune markers across these groups showed how the new virus perturbs the immune system. Early changes may predict who becomes severely ill. The work was done during the pandemic itself. It gave clinicians timely information about the new strain.
plos-pone-0008493:
Suhail Mithani and co-authors scan mitochondrial DNA in salivary tumors in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a cancer of the salivary glands. No prior study had looked at mitochondrial mutations in this cancer. Mitochondria are cell units with their own small genome. The team use the MitoChip, an array that reads that whole genome. It allows accurate, complete sequencing in one run.

They sequence the mitochondrial genomes of tumors in their sample. They catalog mutations that differ from normal sequence. Such changes may affect how tumor cells make energy. The work opens a new line of inquiry for this hard-to-treat cancer.
plos-pone-0008593:
Tohru Hasegawa and co-authors test an antibody in Alzheimer mice in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Alzheimer disease is a brain disorder of old age that causes dementia. Its exact causes remain unknown. The team had reported a compound called homocysteic acid as a marker in Alzheimer brains. That compound may help drive nerve cell damage. They treat male mice bred to model the disease with an antibody against it.

The antibody helps the immune system clear the compound. The team then check symptoms and brain changes in treated mice. If the marker is truly harmful, clearing it should help. The study tests a therapy aimed at a marker, not at amyloid.
plos-pone-0008693:
Claudine James, Lee-Anne Stanton, Hanga Agoston, and coworkers charted how cartilage turns into bone. Their mouse study was published in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most bones start as a cartilage model that is slowly replaced. Bone builders, bone removers, and blood vessel cells work together in sequence. A full gene-by-gene picture of that relay had been missing.

The team measured which genes switch on or off at each stage. Their genome-wide survey follows the whole change from soft model to hard bone. The resulting lists name new candidate genes for further tests. Such a map can inform work on growth defects and bone healing.
plos-pone-0008793:
Jasper Simon and Michael Dickinson built a better stage for watching fruit fly behavior. Their methods paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drosophila is a workhorse of genetics, with powerful tools for changing genes. Tools for measuring the resulting behavior lagged far behind. Slow, subjective scoring wasted the genetic precision available. A general arena for many behavior tests was needed.

Their chamber records fly movement quickly and objectively. The design is simple enough for any lab to copy. Better behavior measurement sharpens every gene-behavior claim built on it. The chamber helps close the gap between fly genetics and fly behavior science.
plos-pone-0008893:
Valerie Ugo, Sylvie Tondeur, Marie-Laurence Menot, and colleagues validated a mutation test across several laboratories. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Polycythemia vera is a blood disorder of runaway cell production. Most cases carry an activating mutation in the JAK2 gene. A second mutation site, in exon 12, accounts for the rest. Detecting it reliably is essential for diagnosis. The HRM method scans DNA by how it melts.

Labs in the network ran the method on shared patient samples. Results agreed well enough to trust the test clinically. A validated multi-lab test can spread to routine hospitals. Patients gain faster, surer diagnosis of their blood disorder.
plos-pone-0008993:
Dara Orbach and co-authors asked whether a tipsy bat can still fly straight, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fruit- and nectar-eating bats often feed on fermenting food in the wild. Fermentation makes alcohol, so these bats may take in doses that could intoxicate them. The study species were phyllostomid bats, a big family from the Americas.

The team fed bats alcohol and tested their flight through an obstacle course. They also checked echolocation, the sound-based sense bats steer by. Measuring both skills showed whether alcohol costs bats food or safety. The work links diet, fermentation, and the daily survival of wild bats.
plos-pone-0009093:
Ana Paula de Barros and co-authors rebuilt a corner of bone marrow in three dimensions, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Blood stem cells live in marrow, where their movement and growth are stage-managed. Osteoblasts, the bone-building cells, help control the stem cell pool. Flat lab dishes cannot mimic marrow's real three-dimensional neighbourhood.

The team grew stem cells with osteoblasts and marrow stromal cells in 3D. Together, the support cells governed how stem cells migrated and multiplied. The model behaves more like real marrow than flat cultures do. Better marrow models help test blood diseases and transplant ideas safely.
plos-pone-0009193:
Ilan Ben-Zvi and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It concerns lupus, a disease where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. Overactive dendritic cells, which sound the alarm for immune attacks, are thought to drive lupus. Many lupus patients also run low on vitamin D.

In healthy people, vitamin D calms dendritic cells and blunts their response to interferon signals. The team studied whether vitamin D does the same in cells from lupus patients. That matters because a cheap vitamin could, in principle, help quiet the disease. The study tests that hope directly in patient cells.
plos-pone-0009293:
Yiannis Kourmpetis and co-authors published this computational biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Guessing what each protein does is a central task in biology. Genomic experiments produce far more proteins than labs can test one by one. Automated prediction methods must fill the gap.

The authors present a Bayesian Markov random field method that works from network data. Proteins that interact tend to share jobs, so the network itself carries clues. Their statistical method spreads those clues across the network in a principled way. Better predictions help researchers choose which proteins deserve costly lab attention.
plos-pone-0011393:
Matthias Dehmer, Laurin Mueller, and Armin Graber introduced new math descriptors for molecules in 2010. Chemists give each molecule a numeric code so computers can compare structures and predict behavior. Many existing codes collide, giving near-identical values for clearly different molecules, which blurs computer predictions used in drug screening.

The authors built codes from a new graph polynomial drawn from how a molecule's atoms are arranged, then derived added measures from that formula. Their codes stay distinct across different structures far more often than older ones. Sharper codes mean screening software can rank candidate drugs with less confusion. The paper is a methods advance for chemistry: a quiet upgrade to the labels on which large parts of computer-aided drug design depend.
plos-pone-0011493:
Astanand Jugessur and co-authors searched in 2010 for mothers' genes that raise the chance of facial clefts in their children. Cleft lip and palate arise early in pregnancy, and most studies test the child's genes. Yet the womb environment is built by the mother's body, so her genes could shape the risk even when the child does not inherit a risk form directly.

Using two large population-based studies from Scandinavia, the team ran a comprehensive search for maternal genetic associations with clefts in offspring. Scandinavian registries give such a search unusual statistical power and clean records. Whether the hunt finds strong hits or rules regions out, it settles how much of cleft risk sits in the mother's genome. That answer guides counseling and tells researchers where the remaining risk must be hiding.
plos-pone-0011593:
Louise Rodrigues and co-authors forced a rodent malaria parasite to evolve drug resistance in the lab, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria control now leans heavily on artemisinin combination treatments. Losing those drugs to resistance would be a disaster, yet how resistance to the combined therapy arises was poorly understood.

Exposing the parasite to the drug pair over generations produced resistant lines. In those lines, the mdr1 gene had been copied many extra times. That gene copying shows one concrete route by which resistance can emerge. Health teams can watch for the same change in real outbreaks as an early warning sign.
plos-pone-0011693:
Raffi Bekeredjian and co-authors built a mouse model of reversible heart failure, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The heart's response to low oxygen is controlled by a factor called HIF-1. The team engineered mice in which a stable form of its alpha subunit could be switched on in heart muscle cells only, on demand.

With the switch on, heart function steadily declined into cardiomyopathy. Turning it off let the heart recover, making the failure reversible. A failure model that can be undone offers a rare window for studying how heart muscle repairs itself and which changes cause lasting harm.
plos-pone-0011793:
Jacques Demongeot and co-authors proposed a mathematical gauge of biological robustness, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Living systems are strikingly robust, resisting perturbations and constraints imposed from outside or at their boundaries. That apparent toughness has drawn a decade of research, but measuring it in complex systems remains difficult.

The authors use attraction basins, the sets of starting states that flow to a stable outcome, as the gauge. Larger basins mean a system shrugs off boundary conditions more easily. Their yardstick gives modellers a principled way to compare resilience across tangled living networks.
plos-pone-0011893:
Dieter Vanderelst and co-workers examined in 2010 the odd flaps of skin on the noses of bats that call through their nostrils. These noseleaves shape the beam of sound a bat sends out, much as a horn shapes a note. Yet no species had been studied with both its hearing and its sound emission fully measured, leaving the flap's exact job unclear.

Comparing FM bats, which sweep their call pitch downward, the team found that what a noseleaf does depends on how specialized the bat's senses are. A shape that helps one hunting style may matter little to another. The finding ties a visible facial feature to each species' way of life, from gleaning insects off leaves to chasing them in open air.
plos-pone-0011993:
Thomas Lettner and co-workers found in 2010 a gene that a harmful fungus needs in order to turn risky. The fungus, Candida albicans, does its harm when it grows long threads called hyphae and when it shrugs off drugs. The team tied its gene AGE3 to a yeast gene named GCS1, which codes for a protein that trims the action of other proteins.

By swapping genes between the two fungi, the team showed that AGE3 does the same job as GCS1, and that Candida cannot grow its threads or hold out against drugs without it. A gene that both invasion form and drug strength rest on makes a fine target: block it, and the fungus may be weakened on two fronts at once.
plos-pone-0012093:
April Rose, Matthew Annis, Zhifeng Dong, and co-authors reported in PLOS ONE in 2010 on a protein found in many breast cancers. The protein sits in the cell membrane and helps cancer cells move, spread, and invade new tissue. The team studied an enzyme that can snip off the part of the protein that sticks out of the cell, setting that piece free in the fluid around it.

Once freed, that piece can help new blood vessels grow, the authors show. Tumors need such vessels to feed themselves and expand. Naming both the cutting enzyme and the freed piece gives cancer research two fresh points of attack: block the cut, or block what the freed piece does next.
plos-pone-0012193:
Sayaka Saito, Kei Mukohara, and Seiji Bito surveyed Japanese doctors about drug company representatives for PLOS ONE in 2010. Sales visits, gifts, and sponsored talks are a routine part of medical life in many countries, and earlier surveys on the subject were often small or weak. Their national survey of practicing doctors aimed to measure how deep that involvement runs.

They recorded how often doctors meet representatives, what they accept, and how they view the relationship. Solid numbers give medical ethics debates a factual base instead of anecdotes. They also help hospitals and medical schools in Japan write gift and visiting rules that match real practice rather than guesswork.
plos-pone-0012293:
Jie Chen, Ana Gomes, Lara Monteiro, and co-authors studied a growth-control protein in breast cancer tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The PI3K-Akt pathway drives tumor growth and helps cancers resist chemotherapy, which is why patients whose tumors resist treatment face so few options. FOXO3a is a brake protein in that same pathway, and where it sits inside the cell, in the nucleus or outside it, decides whether it can work.

Tumors keeping the brake in the nucleus, where it should protect, were paradoxically tied to poorer survival and to a more active growth signal. That twist suggests the brake's presence alone is not protection; its wiring matters. Such markers help predict which breast cancers will behave worst and resist standard drugs.
plos-pone-0012393:
Eva Cernuda-Morollón, Jaime Millán, Mark Shipman and co-workers watched T cells stop moving on cue in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. T cells patrol the body, but when their receptor spots a target, they must halt and engage with the cell showing it. The authors traced how a switch protein called Rac, once thought to drive movement, instead helps deliver the stop order.

Turning on the T cell receptor activated Rac, and that activation shut down migration rather than speeding it. The stop lets the T cell form a tight contact and do its job of killing or signaling. Misread stop signals could help explain immune diseases where T cells wander or attack at the wrong place.
plos-pone-0012493:
Li-Ching Wu, Hsin-Hao Chen, Jorng-Tzong Horng and colleagues cleaned up protein mass spectrometry data with a signal method, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Mass spectrometry reads thousands of protein peaks fast, and comparing peak patterns between healthy and sick samples can reveal disease markers. Raw spectra are noisy and warped, so preprocessing decides whether real markers survive.

Their method, built on the Hilbert-Huang transform, adapts to each signal's own wiggles instead of forcing a fixed filter. Cleaner spectra mean more reliable peak lists for diagnosis studies. Better preprocessing is unglamorous but decisive work, since every downstream cancer marker claim rests on it.
plos-pone-0012593:
Yonglan Yu, Haili Zhang and Guan Zhu found a plant-style sugar pathway in a gut parasite, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Trehalose is a stress-protecting sugar made by bacteria, fungi, plants, and many invertebrates, but vertebrates lack the pathway entirely. Cryptosporidium, a diarrheal parasite, belongs to the apicomplexans, a group better known for malaria.

The team showed Cryptosporidium and some relatives carry the plant-type version of the trehalose pathway. A pathway humans lack but the parasite needs is an ideal drug target, since blocking it should spare the patient. The plant-like signature also raises evolutionary questions about where these parasites picked up their chemistry.
plos-pone-0012693:
Fridley, Jenkins and Biernacka compared ways of reading gene-set results from expression data. Gene-set methods ask whether a whole group of related genes, taken together, links to a trait or disease. Their 2010 paper reviews existing tools and tests new ones that keep the analysis inside the data itself.

Head-to-head tests show which methods hold up and which overstate their case. Analysts face a shelf of similar tools, so fair trials prevent wasted effort. Better gene-set reading sharpens almost every large gene study that follows.  Their tests span both real and simulated expression data sets.
plos-pone-0012793:
Becker, Siems, Kluge and co-authors gave an old enzyme a new job description in body weight control. The enzyme, NEP, was known for trimming small signal peptides around the body. Their 2010 study used mice that lack NEP entirely and watched their weight over life.

The mice developed obesity late in life, even though the enzyme had no known fat role before. Late onset makes the finding relevant to the slow weight gain of middle age. NEP joins the list of possible targets for obesity research.  Their mouse line offers a new handle on a very common condition.
pmc-1904193:
Schardt, Adams, Owens, and co-authors test whether the PICO framework improves searching PubMed for clinical answers. Modern evidence-based care needs quick access to trusted medical knowledge at the point of care. Many bedside questions go unanswered, though, often because searches are poorly framed.

PICO breaks a question into patient, intervention, comparison, and outcome parts before searching. The authors studied whether teaching that structure helps searchers find better evidence faster. Clearer questions lead to cleaner searches, which matters when a clinician needs a solid answer during a busy clinic.  Better searches mean fewer missed papers when evidence is gathered under time pressure.
pmc-2443193:
Hagmann, Cammoun, Gigandet, and co-authors map the structural core of the human cerebral cortex. The cortex is divided into specialised regions, yet those regions are joined by a dense web of fibre pathways. Using diffusion spectrum imaging, the team traced those pathways without surgery.

Their scans covered links within each hemisphere and across to the other side. From the full web, they identify a core set of highly connected regions that may anchor brain communication. A structural backbone helps explain how separate brain areas act as one system, and what fails when core links are damaged.
pmc-3965093:
Orchard and many co-authors reported the MIntAct project in 2013. At its heart is IntAct, a free and open database of how molecules interact inside cells. Its records come from careful reading of published papers and from data sent in by research groups.

MIntAct made IntAct the shared editing platform for eleven interaction databases at once. One web-based curation tool lets all partner groups enter and check records in the same way. That shared work cuts repeat effort and keeps records in a common form. Users gain a larger, cleaner pool of interaction data for studies of cell pathways and disease.
pmc-4342193:
Chang, Chow, Tellier, and their co-authors released a second generation of PLINK in 2015. PLINK is a widely used open source toolset for genome-wide association studies and population genetics. Data from imputation and whole genome sequencing had grown so large that the first version strained.

The new version was rebuilt for speed and scale on larger, richer datasets. It keeps the familiar commands that labs rely on while handling far bigger files. Association studies test millions of DNA variants against a trait or disease. Faster tools mean bigger studies can be run and re-run as methods improve, which sharpens the search for genetic effects.
pmc-5998893:
Chao Zhang, Maryam Rabiee, Erfan Sayyari, and coauthors presented ASTRAL-III in 2018. Genes within a genome can tell conflicting stories about how species split. A good species tree must allow for that discord rather than ignore it.

ASTRAL builds the species tree from many gene trees while modeling the conflict. The third version handles gene trees that are only partly resolved, a common real-world case. It also runs fast enough for large data sets. Evolutionary biologists use it to place new species and test how sensitive a tree is to gene choice.
pmc-6098093:
Henrik Roager and Tine Licht reviewed microbial products of tryptophan in health and disease in 2018. Tryptophan is an amino acid from food protein. Gut microbes turn part of it into small compounds that signal to the host.

Growing evidence links these compounds to immune balance, gut barrier strength, and even mood pathways. Some products calm inflammation, while others may harm when levels go wrong. The review sorts what is known from what is still guesswork. Diet researchers read it to see how protein choices ripple through microbial chemistry. Several of these compounds also reach the blood, which extends their reach beyond the gut wall.
plos-pone-0359793:
Hay Mar Myat Kyaw and colleagues studied in 2026 how COVID-19 infection related to reading skills among elementary school children in Hong Kong. The study looks at proficiency in both Chinese and English reading, the two languages of the children's schooling. It also sets two ways of judging that proficiency side by side.

One measure comes from parents reporting how well their children read, and the other from direct, performance based reading tests given to the children. Comparing the two shows how far parent judgment and tested skill agree after illness and disrupted schooling. The question matters for schools deciding which returning students need reading support, and for researchers choosing how to measure learning loss after the pandemic.
plos-pone-0360393:
Fenfen Lan and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about babies born too early. Once premature infants leave hospital, their main caregivers at home face many care needs. The authors set out to analyze those needs in a structured way.

Their study is cross-sectional, gathering responses at one point in time, and it uses the Kano model, a tool that sorts needs by how much meeting them satisfies people. Sorting needs this way helps nurses decide which support to offer families first. The results speak to hospitals planning discharge teaching and follow-up for parents of premature babies.
plos-pone-0341693:
Ana Jovančević, Izabel Cvetković, Jasper Van Assche, Mladen Popović, and Eva Bittner published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their topic is public attitudes toward ChatGPT, the well-known AI chatbot. The title poses the tension directly: some see such tools as a threat, others as a helpful assistant and learning aid.

The authors set out to learn what predicts these attitudes, meaning which traits or experiences push people toward fear or toward welcome. Knowing the predictors helps explain why reactions to AI differ so sharply between groups. Educators and policymakers introducing AI tools can use that knowledge to address the concerns people actually hold.
plos-pone-0359293:
Md Atiqur Rahman and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on computer vision. Their system, FUSED-Net, detects traffic signs in images. The setting is limited data, meaning few example pictures to train on, which is common outside wealthy countries with huge image collections.

Traffic sign detection supports driver assistance and road surveys, but models usually demand thousands of labeled photos. A network designed to learn from less data could serve regions whose signs differ from standard sets. The authors offer FUSED-Net as a candidate for that job, and vision researchers can compare its data thrift against bigger models.
plos-pone-0357293: Ráčková and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE trial on quick ways to calm stress at work. After a bout of acute stress, volunteers tried slow, steady breathing, blue light, or both. Sleepiness and the body's stress response were then measured. The trial was randomized, double-blind, and cross-over, so each person served as their own control. Simple tools that work could help staff recover during hard shifts.
plos-pone-0348693:
Jorge Artur Peçanha de Miranda Coelho and three colleagues count children living with vision, hearing, and intellectual disabilities across Latin America and the Caribbean, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Drawing on Global Burden of Disease estimates for twenty-five countries, they cover roughly one hundred forty-nine million young people aged five to nineteen. These conditions quietly block schooling and future earnings, yet regional totals are rarely assembled in one place.

About nine point three million children and teenagers, just over six in every hundred, were affected. Hearing loss was the most common, hitting more than five million, and most cases were mild to moderate. Intellectual disability followed, then vision loss, nearly nine tenths of which could be fixed with ordinary glasses. Rates rose with age, and boys carried more intellectual disability than girls. The authors pair the headcount with a steep economic cost, arguing for earlier screening in schools.

plos-pone-0358993:
Zheyao Gu, Ting Xi, and Xiangying Luo report real world results for an eye injection drug in stubborn diabetic swelling, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Diabetic macular edema blurs central vision when fluid leaks into the retina. Faricimab is a newer antibody treatment. The team reviewed one hundred ten treated eyes over a year of loading and flexible dosing. Some eyes were new to therapy. Others had already failed different drugs.

Retinal thickness fell significantly in both groups, and scans showed fewer cysts, less fluid, and fewer warning spots. Vision, though, only improved clearly in eyes new to treatment; eyes that had resisted earlier drugs gained little sight despite looking better on scans. Those hard cases also carried more structural damage at the start. The gap between anatomy and eyesight, the authors note, should temper promises to long standing patients.
plos-pone-0355693:
Abby Dunn led a team of six authors setting out a study protocol on family support in psychiatric care, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. When a parent is admitted to a psychiatric ward, they are separated from their children at the worst possible moment. The planned study will investigate family rooms and support for these parents and children.

Dunn's mixed methods protocol asks what truly keeps families connected through a crisis. Family rooms sound simple, but their value and best use need evidence. The protocol defines who will be studied and how, in advance. Findings could guide wards across the country on a low-cost change with large human effects: letting children visit a parent safely, in a space designed for families.
plos-pone-0358593:
Victor Moses Musyoki led a team of eight authors studying blood sugar during tuberculosis treatment, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. TB can push blood sugar up even in people who never had diabetes, and that rise may worsen treatment results. The team followed patients over time in a prospective cohort, tracking when the sugar rise appears.

Musyoki's group tied those temporal patterns to treatment outcomes. Their findings argue for routine glucose checks as part of TB care, timed to when the risk peaks. Sugar problems can quietly undo good TB treatment, causing relapse or complications. Adding a cheap glucose test to TB programs is an easy step if the timing is right, which is what this study supplies.
plos-pone-0357793:
Kexin Wei and fellow researchers evaluate nine famous former homes in Yangzhou, China, that now welcome visitors, in a 2026 heritage study. They ask a practical question: do online reviews and paper surveys tell managers the same things about what needs fixing? Their design links the two sources in sequence, letting review themes shape the survey that followed.

Review coding produced five broad complaint areas, and survey scoring then weighed how severe each problem was. Both sources agreed that cultural displays, hands-on features, access, and signs were the weakest points. They split on staff attitude, which drew frequent online complaints but scored well in surveys. Blending both views, the authors argue, gives site managers a fuller and fairer picture.
plos-pone-0357593:
Do-Eun Lee and a large team lay out a trial plan, published in 2026, testing a Korean traditional therapy for trauma stress delivered through virtual reality. The therapy aims to calm over-strong emotions by working with opposing feelings, and its meditation part may be easier to deliver evenly inside a headset. The plan assigns adults with the disorder by chance to headset therapy, standard therapy, or a waiting list.

Both therapy groups will meet for sixteen sessions over eight weeks, with symptom checks at the end and a month later. The team will also track safety, body measures such as brain waves and heart rhythm, and costs against quality of life. Lee and colleagues designed the trial to show whether the headset version works as well as the human-led one.
plos-pone-0356693:
Aisha Abdul Haq and colleagues compare two ways of teaching brain anatomy to medical students. One way uses a three-dimensional digital dissection table alone. The other uses the same table inside a flipped classroom, where students prepare before class. Digital tables can lack fine relational detail, so the team suspected the teaching format around the tool matters. Second-year students were split into two groups and tested before and after the teaching block, and also surveyed on their experience.

The study tracks score gains in each group and gathers student views on the flipped format paired with the digital resource. Abdul Haq and colleagues frame the question for anatomy departments everywhere. Does costly viewing hardware pay off best as a display? Or does it pay off as the hub of an active, prepared classroom?
plos-pone-0353293: Potentially toxic elements hide in the surface soils of townships across northwest Hebei. This paper identified their sources and assessed the health risks. The source-to-risk assessment gives local authorities the evidence to protect residents.
plos-pone-0357093:
Amnart Chaiprasert and colleagues investigated phycocyanobilin, a pigment compound from the blue-green alga Arthrospira platensis, as a possible lead against systemic lupus erythematosus. Their 2026 computational study began from the compound's close structural resemblance to bilirubin, a molecule already known to calm immune activity, and screened it against proteins tied to the disease.

Docking simulations placed the compound snugly against several targets, and prediction tools singled out LYN, a kinase that helps control immune cell signaling. In motion simulations the compound stayed bound to LYN about as steadily as a known strong binder used for comparison. The work is entirely in silico, so it marks a starting point for lab studies rather than any treatment claim.
plos-pone-0355293:
Muhammad Zubair Gul and co-authors flooded young wheat plants for a week. They then let the plants recover for another week. The aim was to see what waterlogging does to growth and to the fatty acids in plant tissues. Their 2026 experiment used a local Pakistani variety, Atta Habib. It tracked root and shoot size, water content, and a protective enzyme. It also tracked the mix of fatty acids at each stage.

Flooding barely slowed the shoots but cut root weight sharply. Recovery restored only part of the loss. One fatty acid, linolenic acid, rose during flooding and fell during recovery. The protective enzyme's activity dipped after the water drained. With floods striking wheat regions more often, such measurements help breeders judge which varieties cope and which falter.
plos-pone-0356793:
Cinthya Vásquez-Velásquez and colleagues studied 317 infants in Puno, Peru, a city high in the Andes. National rules require iron treatment for anemic babies. They require preventive micronutrient powders for the rest. Their 2026 study compared two periods. One came before clinics began strictly following up each baby's supplementation, and one after. The follow-up ran for six months, with hemoglobin measured at both ends.

Only about one baby in seven gained a full point of hemoglobin. But strict follow-up roughly tripled the odds of that gain in the main analysis. Babies also gained more on average overall. The effect softened when many social factors were added. That is a reminder of how much poverty shapes the outcome. The message: handing out supplements is not enough without follow-through.
plos-pone-0355393:
Connor A J Rossel and colleagues took apart a worrying resistance package in gut germs. Fourteen drug resistance genes keep turning up side by side across Dutch outbreaks. Their 2026 study gathered long DNA readouts from six lands. It sorted the genes by the mobile bits flanking them. Those bits are the cut-and-paste tools that move resistance between germs.

The fourteen genes fell into nine distinct groups. Shuffled like mosaic tiles, they formed more than a hundred forms with no fixed order. Yet a few favored pairings kept coming back. Set genes sat beside set partners in most readouts. That kept core amid the shuffling suggests the groups travel as semi-stable kits. It helps explain how multi-drug resistance builds so fast.
plos-pone-0356493:
Sharmin Sultana Shoma and Janine Barden-O'Fallon interviewed married couples and family planning providers in two rural communities of Cumilla district, Bangladesh. They asked why the most reliable contraceptives remain rarely chosen. These methods include long-acting implants and permanent options. Their 2026 study sorted the answers across four levels: individual, family, community, and health system.

Fear did much of the work. People feared infertility, devices wandering the body, and impotence after vasectomy, all fed by anecdotes. Husbands and elder relatives often decided. Son preference loomed. Providers added bias, rushed counseling, and thin staffing. The authors argue no single fix will move uptake. Counseling quality, male engagement, and myth-busting have to advance together, with consent protected throughout.
plos-pone-0356393:
Osamah Azzam and five colleagues document thinking problems among older Palestinians for the first time across two living situations, in this 2026 study. More than four hundred adults aged fifty-five and over took part, recruited from ten charitable nursing homes and from primary healthcare centers across the West Bank, between May and October 2024. Each participant's cognition was screened with a validated Arabic mental state exam, alongside detailed social, clinical, and lifestyle information.

The two groups differed markedly. Nursing home residents were older, more often women, and far more likely to have had no schooling. Clinic attendees carried heavy rates of diabetes and high blood pressure. In both settings, cognitive impairment was significantly tied to gender, smoking, education, and speaking only one language. The authors call the results a baseline for Palestinian geriatric care and argue for investment in long-term studies and risk-factor management.
plos-pone-0353193:
Juan Cosin-Sales and colleagues modelled cholesterol care for high-risk Spanish heart patients who stay above target on standard drugs. Their 2026 simulation used real records from nearly thirty-five thousand adults. It compared treatment paths that add bempedoic acid, a newer tablet, before moving to costly injections.

Adding the tablet brought about a third more patients to their cholesterol target. Later injections lifted control further still. Going straight to injections reached the same final control rates, but cost more. Placing bempedoic acid first cut yearly treatment costs by almost a third. The authors present that order as a way to protect health budgets without losing control of cholesterol.
plos-pone-0356293:
Xu Guan and colleagues checked whether young people in the United Kingdom feel worse in winter than in other seasons. Their 2026 study used a large national household survey from the early twenty-twenties. It compared winter months with the rest of the year on three complaints: low mood, low energy, and worry-disturbed sleep.

Winter scores were modestly worse overall. The clearest gaps were in low energy and low mood. The sleep difference was smaller and less certain. Results held across different methods and across the years checked, with winter at the top of the seasonal pattern. Guan and colleagues suggest making light-touch mental health support easier to find during winter months.
plos-pone-0345893:
Selomon Afework Yenesew inventoried ancient Ge'ez manuscripts held by a church in northwest Ethiopia and graded their condition. Ge'ez is Ethiopia's classical written language, and its church manuscripts carry centuries of religious and cultural history. The 2026 study examined seventy-one manuscripts and tested which visible damage signs tracked with poor condition.

Most manuscripts dated from the seventeenth century, with smaller shares from the three centuries around it. About seven in ten were in good or better shape, while a small share sat in dangerous condition. Insect attack, damp damage, rodent gnawing, and plain frequent handling each tracked strongly with worse condition. Yenesew calls for routine condition checks, better storage, and gentler handling to keep the heritage alive.
plos-pone-0354593:
Adel Alshahrani and colleagues measured balance and trunk movement in adults living with long COVID. Lingering muscle and nerve problems after infection are increasingly reported, but posture control is rarely tested directly. Their 2026 study compared sixty-four patients with matched healthy adults using a computerised balance platform and strength tests.

Patients swayed more, especially with eyes closed on soft foam, and their stability scores ran lower. Trunk bending range and trunk muscle strength were both reduced. Fatigue scores were far higher than in controls. Statistical modelling tied weaker trunk extensors and heavier fatigue to poorer balance. Alshahrani and colleagues argue rehabilitation for long COVID should train the trunk and manage fatigue together.
plos-pone-0354293:
Hamza Abu Owida and co-authors built an explainable machine learning workflow that sorts liposome drug carriers by how fast they leak their cargo. Release speed decides whether a liposome medicine works, yet it depends on many recipe and test settings at once. Their 2026 proof-of-concept study reworked a public dataset of accelerated release experiments.

Simulated standard curves were clustered into slow, moderate, and fast release families. A gradient-boosted classifier performed best at separating the extreme slow and fast groups, though the authors call performance preliminary. Explanation tools ranked test acidity and drug loading among the most informative features. Abu Owida and colleagues aim to guide formulation choices before bench work begins.
plos-pone-0355493:
Elvira Sattarova and co-authors built carbon balance models for pigs at three life stages. Pig farming accounts for nutrients like nitrogen in detail, but carbon flows are rarely folded into the same ledger. Their 2026 study combined published prediction equations and standard constants to estimate carbon eaten, excreted, breathed out, and retained in body tissue.

Grower-finisher pigs showed the closest match between predicted and reported balances. Intake and breathing losses estimated well across stages. Dung, urine, and gut methane outputs strayed further from reported values, flagging where the equations need work. Sattarova and colleagues present the models as a workable frame for adding carbon to farm nutrient accounting.
plos-pone-0354893:
Chloe Lee and co-authors measured leg and hip muscle activity while lifters varied their barbell back squat technique. Coaches tweak bar position, stance, load, and repetitions to target muscles, but the size of each tweak's effect needed numbers. Their 2026 study wired eighteen healthy lifters with surface sensors and motion tracking across the variations.

A wide stance raised both peak and total activation of the inner front-thigh muscle. Heavier loads raised total activation in the outer front thigh and one hamstring muscle. Repetition scheme and bar placement were also compared across seven muscles in total. Lee and colleagues give coaches evidence for matching squat settings to the muscle they most want to train.
plos-pone-0355193:
Heeseung Cho, Yiyu Chen, and Christian Wallraven check in 2026 whether computer rankings of personality traits match older statistical measures of group difference. They trained several learning models in two very large surveys. Each model guessed a person's self reported gender from personality trait scores. Rankings from the models were then compared with classic effect sizes and with combined distance measures.

 Rankings stayed stable across many model runs. In one survey they matched simple effect sizes almost perfectly, while in the other they matched only the combined measures well. The split, the authors argue, comes from how traits overlap with each other, not from hidden new patterns in the data.
plos-pone-0354793:
Tian Tan and Jiangcai Li published this 2026 language study of three Mandarin Chinese verb patterns that add a sense of downward or onward direction after an action. The three look similar, so the authors measured statistically which verbs each pattern attracts and how strongly, then mapped how their meanings branch from a core sense.

One pattern drew the widest verb range and was most productive, while another stayed narrow but tightly bound to its favorite verbs. Core meanings held together strongly for all three. Tan and Li chart the networks as webs rather than simple lists.
plos-pone-0353693:
Scully and colleagues, in a 2026 study, profile the microbes living in processed colostrum, the first milk fed to newborn calves on a dairy farm. Colostrum carries antibodies and seeds the calf's gut, but on real farms it is often chilled and reheated before feeding, which may change its microbes. Samples came from one spring-calving herd just before feeding.

Twenty-one samples, each from at most two donor cows, were read by gene sequencing. Breed and whether a cow was a first-time mother made no difference to the microbial mix. Overall diversity was low and uneven, and the mix varied a lot from sample to sample. Among the archaeal microbes, one methane-making genus overwhelmingly dominated. The authors say farm handling leaves colostrum with a patchy microbial fingerprint, a baseline for judging whether processing helps or harms the calf's first meal.
plos-pone-0353393:
Kier Mitchel Pitogo and seven colleagues audit a century of species records from the Philippines to show how sampling habits distort the biodiversity map, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. They focused on frogs and scaly reptiles across the archipelago's conservation areas. Preserved museum specimens made up almost all records, so what science 'knows' largely mirrors where collectors happened to go.

Citizen-science reports piled onto already well-sampled places, while old literature quietly filled some gaps. Bigger areas held more recorded species, but steep terrain weakened that pattern. The authors warn planners: an empty spot on the map may mean nobody looked, not that nothing lives there.
plos-pone-0353993:
