Naung Latt Htun and three colleagues survey a hidden public-health problem in Yangon, Myanmar: sex combined with stimulant drugs, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Four hundred and fifteen gay and bisexual men answered an anonymous online questionnaire recruited through social media and dating apps in late 2024. About a quarter reported having taken part in drug-fuelled sex at some point, and a fifth within the past six months.

Methamphetamine dominated the drug choices, sessions often lasted many hours, and consistent condom use was rare — reported by only about one participant in ten. Group encounters were common. The authors call the pattern alarming and argue for harm-reduction services designed for this community, which stigma keeps out of reach of ordinary clinics.
plos-pone-0352793:
Dongzhen Liu and three colleagues build a lean neural network for understanding three-dimensional point clouds, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Point clouds — swarms of measured dots from scanners — drive robot vision and self-driving systems, but reading the whole shape at once is usually expensive. Their design borrows a memory network from language processing and reads the points in sequence, in both directions, capturing long-range structure at a fraction of the usual cost.

A training trick that shuffles point order taught the model not to depend on any fixed sequence. On three standard benchmarks it matched heavier rivals while running markedly faster and using less memory — a practical step toward real-time 3D perception on modest hardware.
plos-pone-0349693:
Efendi and colleagues set out a plan in 2026 to review all reviews of resuscitation training for health workers. Reviews on teaching life-saving skills have multiplied, but weak methods can bias their advice. Under the plan, the team will search eight databases for reviews covering training for professionals and students, not lay rescuers.

Each review found will be mapped by topic and scored for method quality. The team will also test which settings or methods link to stronger reviews. A clear map of what has already been reviewed, and how well, can stop wasted repeats and point training research toward the gaps that matter for patient survival.
plos-pone-0352693:
Alam and colleagues measured chemical elements across tissues in mice modeling a genetic condition in a 2026 study. The condition, Fragile X syndrome, silences a protein that helps control other proteins, including some that move ions. The team compared ten elements in brain and body tissues of normal mice and mice lacking the gene.

Most differences were between tissues rather than between mouse types. Still, normal mice had more magnesium and sodium in droppings and more potassium in fur than the gene-lacking mice. Element balance may thus shift subtly with the condition. Such shifts could hint at body-wide effects beyond the brain, the usual focus of Fragile X research.
plos-pone-0343793:
Valentina Todisco and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of the Old World swallowtail butterfly. The team traced its family history across the Palearctic. That vast region runs from Europe to East Asia. They assembled nearly six hundred samples. They sequenced four genes in a subset. Then they used machine learning to check whether body traits matched the genetic groups.

Three named forms proved to be close sister lines of the main species. Distinct genetic lines appeared in the Himalayas and Central Asia. A further line ran across North Africa. Image-based clustering lined up well with the genetic and map patterns. Screening also found a bacterial infection in females of one relative. The authors close with a scenario for how this butterfly group spread across the region.
plos-pone-0352893:
Arsalan Yousafzai and five colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One laboratory study on making wood glue from lignin, the natural polymer left over in plant material, instead of petroleum-based phenol. They extracted lignin from three Pakistani biomass sources: chir pine needles, eucalyptus sawdust, and sugarcane bagasse. Each lignin was reacted with formaldehyde to form a resin for wood panels.

The resins cured properly under hot pressing and held workable properties, though a conventional phenol glue control still bonded strongest in dry and wet tests. Among the lignin glues, the pine version performed best even though it did not have the most reactive chemical groups, showing that lignin structure matters as much as chemistry counts. The authors see real potential for lower-phenol adhesives from local farm and forest waste.
plos-pone-0352993:
Alper Kartal and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One experiment on soccer warm-ups. It tests whether a few heavy lifts after a soccer warm-up can prime players to jump higher and run faster. Coaches call this boost post-activation performance enhancement. Seventeen male amateur players took part. Sessions compared heavy hip thrusts, heavy back squats, and a plain warm-up. Players then took jump, sprint, and agility tests.

Neither heavy routine improved any test result. Neither hurt results either. Gaps between players swamped any effect of the routine itself. The authors conclude that heavy lifts added to a soccer warm-up do not deliver the expected boost. At least, they do not under these realistic field conditions. Coaches, the authors say, should not count on the trick.
plos-pone-0352593:
Isaiah Osei Duah Junior and three colleagues set out a 2026 study plan in PLOS One for a scoping review on eye testing and early brain decline. Their tool is electroretinography, a painless test that records the retina's electric response to light. The retina grows from the same tissue as the brain, so its signals might flag dementia risk early, cheaply, and without scans. Early studies hint at such links, but the findings are scattered and hard to compare.

The review will map what studies exist on adults aged fifty and older. It will sort them by design, test type, and thinking outcomes, and note how eye disease and other illnesses were handled. It will also look for long-term studies and mark where the evidence is still too thin to trust.
plos-pone-0352193:
Aselefech Wotango and six colleagues turn slaughterhouse waste into sugarcane plant food in this 2026 study. Meat waste pollutes badly when dumped. It is also rich in organic matter that tired soils crave. The team fermented collected waste in a controlled pit. Acid, alkali, and phosphate treatments prepared it, and germs finished the breakdown. The product was tested for nutrients and dangerous elements. Sugarcane field trials then tested it alone and blended with chemical feed.

Safety numbers came back reassuring. Mercury, lead, cadmium, and arsenic all registered at very low levels. Organic carbon content was strikingly high, far above typical soil levels. Microbial profiling described the fertiliser's living community. The integrated approach matters for farms near meat plants. Waste becomes an input, pollution becomes yield, and chemical fertiliser bills can shrink. Studies like this give regulators and farmers the composition data needed before trusting waste on food crops.
plos-pone-0351693:
Jia Jun Chew and Chong Han Ng compared how coronaviruses spell their spike gene, the gene that builds the protein used to enter host cells. Viruses often favor certain codons, the three-letter words of genes, and those habits reflect mutation pressure and selection. The team analyzed spike genes across all four coronavirus genera and many host groups.

Codon habits differed clearly between genera on some measures, while the base composition at one codon position barely varied. The pattern points to family history, more than raw letter makeup, as the main organizer of spike spelling. Knowing which codons a virus prefers hints at how it adapts to hosts and may help researchers design lab versions of viral genes that cells read efficiently.
plos-pone-0351293:
Mikayo Toba and colleagues mined a national database of more than a hundred fifty-six thousand Japanese women given a labor-slowing drug for preterm labor, asking how practice changed over eleven years. World guidance says such treatment should last about two days at most, buying time for steroids and transfer. Japanese practice long ran longer, so the team measured the short-protocol share and what predicted it.

Short treatment rose from about sixteen percent to about twenty-four percent across the period, but the spread between hospitals widened too. University hospitals and perinatal centers, and cases with ruptured membranes or pregnancy hypertension, leaned short; twin pregnancies and some combined treatments leaned long. Practice, the authors conclude, follows institutional habit and case mix as much as evidence, which is where guideline campaigns should aim.
plos-pone-0349293:
Students rarely decide to quit university in one moment; the intention builds over time. Yaranay López Angulo and colleagues built a questionnaire, UDIFP-29, to measure how that intention forms, and they describe its testing in this 2026 PLOS One paper.

Focus groups with first-year students shaped an early model of the process. Experts then reviewed the draft questions for clarity and fit. Hundreds of survey answers were checked with statistical methods that confirm whether questions group as expected. The final tool proved steady and matched related measures in sensible ways. The authors hope campuses use it to spot unhappy students early enough to help.
plos-pone-0330793:
Who develops long COVID may partly depend on health before the infection ever happened. Kristen Kehl-Floberg and colleagues used records from a large American research program covering more than sixty-five thousand adults who had COVID-19, in this 2026 PLOS One cohort study.

The team checked whether symptoms common in long COVID, or limits on daily functioning, appeared in the five years before infection. They then compared who later showed lasting symptoms against who recovered cleanly, adjusting for other illnesses and background traits. A second aim tested whether everyday health records can estimate a person's functioning well enough for this kind of research.
plos-pone-0350993:
Dangerous heart rhythms after a heart attack leave telltale abnormal signals inside the heart, but spotting them by eye is slow and disputed. Marco Orrù and colleagues built ARGO, a free dataset of nearly two thousand heart signal recordings from nine patients, described in this 2026 PLOS One paper.

Three expert heart specialists labeled each signal independently, then agreed a final answer together. The set includes surface heart tracings and maps of timing and voltage inside the left ventricle. The authors also measured how much even experts disagree on exact start and end points, giving software builders honest error bars. Automated detectors can now be trained and compared on shared ground.
plos-pone-0351493:
Tuning a large language model for a new task often makes it overconfident and forgetful. Yumeng Ma and colleagues propose a tuning framework that tracks the model's own uncertainty and gives it an external memory to consult, in this 2026 PLOS One computer science paper.

Uncertainty is estimated feature by feature and carried across layers so noisy signals sway training less. The memory stores reusable context that the model retrieves and blends in through a gate. Tests on text sorting and name-finding tasks across three base models, from small to large, beat several standard methods. Removing either part weakened results, suggesting both pieces earn their place.
plos-pone-0350393:
Tommy Dharmawan and colleagues assessed how Indonesia organizes health research in 2026. Strong research systems help governments base policy on evidence, but the country's system had never been fully mapped despite recent reforms.

The team held an expert panel and interviewed thirteen leaders from agencies, research bodies, and universities, judging the system against a World Health Organization frame. Formal structures exist, yet weak coordination between national and local levels keeps the system fragmented. Money, skilled staff, and the use of findings also lag. The report gives reformers a clear list of weak points to fix first, starting with governance.
plos-pone-0349393:
FuGuo Liu and co-authors built a computer framework in 2026 for naming the jobs of viral proteins found in wastewater. Watching sewage for viruses only helps if the proteins in broken gene scraps can be identified, and viruses change fast.

Their system combines short gene fragment patterns with meaning based codes drawn from protein records, then squeezes a big teacher model into a fast student. Trained on a large coronavirus data set drawn from wastewater, it named protein jobs with high scores and held up on newer variants. Faster, trustworthy naming strengthens the early warning value of sewage monitoring.
plos-pone-0350093:
Yuriy Prysiazhnyi and co-authors tested lignin, the woody waste of paper making, as an addition to road bitumen in 2026. Long stored Ukrainian lignin piles are a disposal problem, and oil based bitumen is costly, so a marriage of the two tempts.

Stored lignin and its bitumen mixes were examined by heat analysis, infrared light, and electron microscopy. Despite changes from years outdoors, the lignin bonded actively with bitumen into fairly stable links. The basic chemistry works, the authors argue, so pilot road mixes are a fair next step. Turning a landfill burden into road material is the circular economy in literal form.
plos-pone-0349793:
Maureen Tissink and co-authors reported early results of the RiMini trial in 2026, comparing two forms of a one join gastric bypass for obesity. Adding a ring around the new stomach pouch may prevent later weight regain, an idea tested in other bypass types but not this one.

Two hundred fourteen patients were randomised evenly between ring and standard operations in 2022 and 2023. This report covers safety around surgery, early complications, and weight at one year, analysed as randomised. Long term weight data will decide the ring's worth, but short term safety must clear first, and reporting it separately keeps the trial honest about harms.
plos-pone-0350293:
Emily Hemendinger, Rachel A Davis, and co-authors asked people with severe obsessive-compulsive disorder how brain stimulation changed their daily lives, not just their symptom scores. Deep brain stimulation can help when medicines and therapy fail, but numbers alone miss how life actually feels afterward. Their 2026 study followed ten patients receiving the treatment, combining quality-of-life surveys with personal accounts coded for shared themes.

In most patients with full data, better quality of life tracked with milder symptoms, though the link was firm in only two. Patients generally described better mood and day-to-day functioning after surgery. Social life lagged behind: many still struggled with relationships and moving toward independent living. The authors suggest adding social skills and independence support to stimulation care could lift the gains further.
plos-pone-0350193:
Weeraphol Saengpanya and Ratchaneekorn Upasen measured thinking ability and creativity among school students across Thailand and asked how the scores vary between groups. Schools worldwide are pressed to build problem-solving and inventive skills, yet who gains them unevenly is poorly mapped. Their 2026 study used staged random sampling to test nearly fifteen hundred elementary and secondary students from several regions.

Overall scores landed in the low to moderate range. Both thinking and creativity differed significantly across demographic groups, forming distinct patterns rather than a single national picture. The authors recommend teaching matched to developmental stage, more inquiry-based and creativity-focused lessons, and policies aimed squarely at narrowing group gaps. They frame the results as a practical guide for teachers, school leaders, and curriculum planners.
plos-pone-0349593:
Log Young Kim and Young Seok Kim led a study of liver cancer risk in fatty liver disease. They used health screen data from more than a million Korean adults. The goal was to spot who will get liver cancer years ahead. Most patients never do, so blanket checks waste effort. The team trained learning models on 2017 screen data. They then tracked cancer over six years.

About two thousand people got liver cancer. The best model split future cases from the rest with high skill. Age, sex, liver enzymes, and total illness load drove its calls most. A tool that shows each factor's weight made the logic plain. The top risk group faced about seventy-five times the risk of the lowest. The team says such groups merit close watch.
plos-pone-0349193:
Hikaru Koike, Hirohito Okano, and Michio Nomura used language analysis to map urami, a Japanese emotion of lingering resentment after unfair treatment that outlasts ordinary anger. Earlier studies of its makeup were small. Their 2026 study collected free written descriptions of urami and anger from nearly five hundred adults and let a topic-modeling algorithm extract the recurring themes and situations.

The analysis separated the emotion's conceptual parts, including injustice, unforgiveness, and helplessness, and the settings that breed it. Compared with anger, urami stood out for sheer persistence over time. It arose most characteristically when the wrongdoer was someone close. Certain personality traits, including narcissism, tied into particular situation clusters. The authors say the large-sample map firms up a culturally specific emotion for wider psychological research.
plos-pone-0348593:
Kimsey Zajac, Louisa Peters, and Lutz Maria Kolbe ran a computational text analysis over thirteen recent national digital health strategies from African countries. They asked how much attention each pays to people at risk of digital exclusion. Digital health promises wider access, but strategies written around the connected can deepen inequality. The team measured how often women, children, and older people appear, and in what context.

Most strategies centered on system strengthening, infrastructure, and coordination between stakeholders. Women and children were mentioned, but usually in passing, without concrete plans, budgets, or dedicated actions. The gap between naming a group and planning for it is exactly where exclusion hides. The analysis gives ministries and donors a method for auditing the next round of strategies before they are finalized.
plos-pone-0348293:
Kumar Sekhar Roy and colleagues designed a network control system meant to survive both today's hackers and tomorrow's quantum computers. Their design lets managers state what the network should achieve while the system enforces it. It uses digital signatures that quantum machines cannot forge, certificate-based identity for every device. Tiered access rules are backed by extra login factors. Machine learning watches traffic for devices behaving oddly.

On a controlled test network, every quantum-safe signature checked out correctly, access rules held, and the anomaly detectors caught planted misbehaviour. Tamper-proof chained logs keep an audit trail. The team tested scaling as workloads grew and frame the system for sensitive settings such as hospitals, where a breached device can endanger patients as well as data.
plos-pone-0348193:
Mathias Boyer-Brosseau, Simon Rigoulot, and Sébastien Hétu ran a controlled experiment on a subtle facial feature: how much of the white of the eye shows. One hundred and sixty-two participants rated fifty neutral faces twice, with each face digitally altered to show a small or a large amount of eye white. They judged trustworthiness, attractiveness, friendliness, and social rank.

Larger eye-white exposure won on every dimension, with the same faces rated more favourably when more white showed. The effect did not depend on the sex of the face or of the rater, suggesting a general perceptual habit rather than a social stereotype about one group. The authors claim the first experimental proof that this overlooked feature steers first impressions, and they connect it to how humans read attention and health from the eyes.
plos-pone-0349093:
Yuening Yang and co-workers work out how tightly bolts should hold a common power-line fitting while current is flowing. Heat and magnetic forces from live wires change the pressure where a clamp grips a cable. Their 2026 paper builds a combined physics model that links electric, magnetic, and heat effects, then solves it step by step.

Checked against lab tests from a power testing institute, the method's average error was fairly small. It clearly beat simpler methods that ignore the linked effects. Crews who service live lines need clamps that grip neither too loose nor too tight. A sharper way to set bolt tightness makes that everyday work safer and more reliable.
plos-pone-0347893:
Guang Sheng Zhao and co-workers review a radiation treatment for cancer that has spread to bone and no longer responds to standard care. Tiny radioactive seeds are placed inside the bone tumors through a printed guide matched to each patient's scans. Their 2026 study pools two hundred fifty-three patients treated at five Chinese hospitals and tracks pain, tumor size, and immune measures.

Every patient completed the planned placement. Pain scores, painkiller use, daily function, and quality of life were compared before and after treatment, along with tumor response on scans. Blood tests tracked immune cell shifts that might hint at wider effects. Full results run through the paper; the method offers a targeted option when bone pain resists other care.
plos-pone-0347193:
Evgeny A. Podolskiy and colleagues lowered a camera and microphone to the floor of a glacial fjord in northwest Greenland and simply watched. Almost nothing was known about daily life near the bottom of such fjords, two hundred sixty metres down. Their 2026 paper reports what the instruments recorded in Inglefield Bredning, from drifting particles to passing animals.

The seabed scene was turbulent, thick with suspended fibres and marine snow whose flow swung with the tide. Of nearly five hundred creatures detected, most were tiny crustaceans and jelly-like drifters. Shrimp, snailfish, comb jellies, and even narwhals also swam past. The team shows that cheap, portable moorings can open up hidden Arctic ecosystems.
plos-pone-0348493:
Alessandro De Cassai and colleagues present the plan for NEURAL, a nationwide Italian study of rare but serious complications after regional anaesthesia, the numbing injections used instead of general anaesthesia. Injuries to nerves, bleeding, collapsed lung, and drug toxicity all occur occasionally, but their true rates are murky because past data came from patchy registries. The 2026 paper is a prospective study protocol.

More than forty Italian centres will record outcomes for thousands of patients, with checks from the first day up to a year for lingering nerve problems. The goal is trustworthy rates and a list of risk factors doctors can actually modify, feeding into updated guidelines and better warnings for patients.
plos-pone-0324893:
Yasmine N. Bire and her team spent a year on the hunt for young dengue gnats. Their ground was six small towns in and near Cocody-Bingerville, a zone in the south-east of the Ivory Coast nation. A dengue wave had just made thousands ill there. Past work had skipped the towns at the zone's edge. The team checked one hundred homes in each town, in all four rains and dry spells.

One gnat type ruled both town types. Old tyres and small pots bred most of the young. Counts of young per home and per head ran two to three times as high in the in-zone towns. Rain drove all the counts up and down.
plos-pone-0347293:
Note on status: this is a study protocol, a plan for a trial not yet run, by Long Qian and colleagues, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The planned trial at Guanyun People's Hospital in China asks whether anesthesia delivered entirely through a vein gives urology patients a smoother recovery than the usual inhaled gases.

Eighty adults scheduled for endoscopic kidney-area surgery will be randomly split into two equal groups, one receiving propofol-based intravenous anesthesia and one inhaled anesthesia. The team will compare recovery quality scores and blood levels of inflammation markers after surgery. Intravenous anesthesia already seems to cut nausea and fuzzy thinking after operations; this trial tests whether those gains hold for this surgery type.
plos-pone-0346593:
Aman Matebie Dagnaw and colleagues test whether teaching grammar from real language data beats the textbook, in this 2026 PLOS ONE education study from Ethiopia. The topic was tricky: past simple forms used for habits, such as used to, which learners often misuse or stretch to single events.

One class spent two weeks learning from a corpus, a searchable collection of authentic text, while a comparison class had conventional instruction. Both groups improved on writing tests, but the corpus group improved significantly more and made fewer errors, with some overgeneralization and agreement slips remaining. Comparing learner writing with a British reference corpus pinned down the typical mistakes, showing teachers exactly where to aim.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The Cyprus force entered the 1970s with this renewal of May 1971. On the twenty-sixth, the Council adopted Resolution 293 without dissent. The Secretary-General reported that the force was still needed. Cyprus agreed it should stay past mid-June.

The text restates the full series of Cyprus decisions through 1970. It urges the parties to use the hopeful climate for joint work. It also asks for the utmost restraint from all sides. The posting then runs to 15 December 1971. The standing hope closes the text once more. Progress toward a final deal might let the force shrink or leave.

Iraq's oil plants were falling apart under sanctions in 2000. The oil-for-food plan let Baghdad sell crude for aid goods. Spare parts for pumps and pipes needed cash too. The chief's report of 10 March 2000 backed a raise. Resolution 1293 passed on 31 March 2000.

Up to six hundred million dollars could now be drawn. The cash sat in a UN-held account fed by oil sales. It could pay fair costs from signed spare-part deals. Costs owed inside Iraq were barred. The Council said it hoped to renew the step. It also vowed to weigh the rest of the chief's advice fast. The text shows sanctions at their most fine-grained: a world body pricing the bolts of a broken oil field.

Resolution 393, adopted in July 1976 by fourteen votes to none with the United States abstaining, condemns a South African attack on Zambia. Zambia's foreign minister had addressed the Council, and its ambassador's letter laid out the charge: South Africa was using Namibia, which it occupied illegally, as a base for hitting neighboring African countries.

The Council strongly condemned the armed attack as a flagrant violation of Zambia's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It demanded that South Africa respect Zambia's independence, sovereignty, airspace, and borders scrupulously. It further demanded that South Africa stop using Namibia as a launching pad for attacks. The text also backed the Namibian people's struggle to free their country from illegal occupation.

Resolution 1693, adopted on 30 June 2006, extends the Congo mission through election season. The Democratic Republic of the Congo was a month from voting for a national assembly and, in a first round, a president, on 30 July. The Council underlined that elections were the foundation for restoring peace, reconciliation, and the rule of law, and thanked donors bankrolling the process.

MONUC's mandate was extended to the end of December 2006. The temporary troop increase authorized that April, linked to a European force deployed for the elections, was also kept in place for the polling period. Security sector reform was flagged as the long-term task, with the UN mission and European advisers both contributing.

Resolution 93 passed on 18 May 1951. Ten members backed it, and one did not vote either way. It guards the bare zone between Israel and Syria. Both states had laid charges in the hall. A land firm was draining swamps inside the zone, a UN truce chief said. He and the truce board's chair had asked Israel more than once to halt the work. It should wait for a deal struck through the board.

The 1949 truce pact bars any armed gain in the zone. On that rule, the Council told Israel to stop the firm's work there. The ditch row had sparked gun fights that spring. A swamp drain had thus grown into a test of the truce itself.

Resolution 993, adopted unanimously on 12 May 1995, extends the UN observer mission in Georgia while scolding the Abkhaz side over refugees. Progress toward a political settlement of the Abkhazia conflict was insufficient, the Council said. A 1994 Moscow agreement promised refugees and displaced people a safe return home, but Abkhaz authorities kept obstructing it, above all in the Gali region, where a first return would matter most.

The observer mission, UNOMIG, was kept in place for a further period. The Council backed consultations on a new Georgian constitution built on federal principles, as part of a comprehensive settlement, and warned that humanitarian programs faced critical funding shortages. Both parties were reminded to obey humanitarian law.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 293 (IV), adopted on 21 October 1949, kept the United Nations Commission on Korea in being. The Assembly noted that Korea stayed split and unity had not been reached. It noted that the Commission had checked the withdrawal of United States forces. It had not been allowed to check the reported Soviet withdrawal.

The Commission, with one state swapped in its seven-member makeup, was told to watch for any move that might lead to fighting. It was told to work to ease the split's effects and help toward unity. It was told to check the Soviet pullout where it could. The Assembly also voiced worry that the state of affairs could put Korea's safety at risk and lead to open war.

Resolution 53/93 of the General Assembly, adopted on 7 December 1998, extends the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala into another year of checking that the country's peace settlement is being honored. It follows fresh reporting from the Secretary-General, Guatemala's peace commission, and the mission's own verification work.

The mission's mandate is renewed for 1 January to 31 December 1999, and the Secretary-General is asked to report again and advise on the mission's future beyond 1999. The Assembly repeats its thanks to Guatemala's government and former guerrilla movement for cooperating. Keeping international monitors in place through 1999 gave the still-new peace process steady outside pressure to deliver on its promises.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Georgia's stalled peace process for Abkhazia is taken up on 31 January 2002. The United Nations Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, worked alongside a peacekeeping force from the Commonwealth of Independent States. Months earlier, a UNOMIG helicopter had been shot down, killing the nine people on board, and those responsible were still unknown.

The lack of progress toward a full settlement is called unacceptable, and renewed talks between the sides are backed. Breaches of the 1994 Moscow ceasefire deal are condemned, with a demand that they stop. Both parties are urged to rebuild trust, restart joint bodies, act on confidence measures agreed at Yalta, and improve safety and law enforcement in the Gali district.

Congo's United Nations mission, MONUC, is extended until 30 July 2004 by this text of 28 July 2003. A global transition deal signed in Pretoria in December 2002 had produced a Government of National Unity and Transition. Yet fighting and grave abuses continued in the east, above all in Ituri and the Kivus.

A stronger supporting role for the transition is given to the mission, coordinating United Nations work across the country. The new government is urged to put human rights, the rule of law, and an independent judiciary among its highest priorities. Congo's sovereignty over its natural resources is restated, and their continued illegal exploitation, linked to the war's persistence in the east, is condemned.

Darfur is referred to the International Criminal Court on 31 March 2005. A world commission of inquiry had reported grave violations of human rights and aid law in Darfur. Sudan is not a party to the court's treaty, so only the Council could give the court authority over the case.

Acting under Chapter VII, the situation in Darfur since 1 July 2002 is referred to the court's Prosecutor. Sudan's government and all parties to the Darfur conflict are ordered to cooperate fully with the court. Personnel of non-party states taking part in authorized operations are shielded from the court's reach. Four Council members abstained, including the United States and China.

Sierra Leone's integrated office, UNIOSIL, is extended for nine months on 21 December 2007, until 30 September 2008. Sierra Leone had held peaceful parliamentary and presidential elections in August and September 2007. Local elections were due in June 2008, and the country's president had asked for the office to stay.

The peacebuilding office stays in place to help the government consolidate peace and prepare the local polls. All parties are called on to ensure the 2008 elections are peaceful and widely accepted. Reports are due from the Secretary-General starting in January 2008. The extension is framed as the office's final phase, preparing the ground for a smaller follow-on presence after September.

Côte d'Ivoire's sanctions are renewed until 31 October 2010 on 29 October 2009. The measures are the arms embargo and travel and financial measures set in 2004, plus the ban on importing rough diamonds from the country set the year after. Expert reports in April and October 2009 informed the renewal, as did the approach of long-delayed presidential elections.

The measures would be reviewed against progress in the elections and the peace process, with mid-course reviews of the diamond ban and the targeted measures set. Continuing abuses against civilians, including sexual violence, are noted with concern, despite a better overall human rights picture. Pressure stays on all Ivorian parties to complete the peace agreement's steps, above all disarmament and voter identification.

Fighting in Cyprus was getting worse in the summer of 1964, and the Council adopted Resolution 193 on 9 August that year. Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots were fighting on the island. Turkish planes were bombing positions there. A United Nations peacekeeping force was already on the ground.

The Council repeated an urgent appeal that its president had just made to Turkey and Cyprus. Turkey was to stop the bombing and any use of military force against Cyprus at once. Cyprus was to order its own forces to stop firing. The text called for an immediate cease-fire by everyone involved. It also asked for full cooperation with the commander of the peacekeeping force, and for restraint by all states so that the fighting would not spread.
un-sc-res-293:
Peace on Cyprus still depended on foreign troops in the spring of 1971. On 26 May 1971 the Security Council voted to keep the United Nations Peace-keeping Force in Cyprus on the island. The Secretary-General had reported that the force was still needed. The government of Cyprus agreed that it should stay past 15 June.

The Council renewed the force until 15 December 1971. It restated its long line of Cyprus resolutions going back to 1964. It also urged all sides to show restraint and to use the calm period well. The text voices hope that progress toward a settlement would soon let the force shrink or leave.
un-sc-res-1293:
Iraq's oil industry needed spare parts that sanctions had long blocked. The oil-for-food program let Iraq sell oil for civilian goods. On 31 March 2000 the Security Council freed money for the oil sector itself. Up to 600 million dollars from the escrow account could pay reasonable costs. Those costs covered parts and equipment for raising oil exports. Earlier resolutions had set the account and its rules.

The Secretary-General's March report had recommended the step. More oil exports meant more money for food and medicine. The Council said it would weigh his other ideas quickly. It also kept the wider sanctions review in view. The text shows the program shifting from relief alone toward the industry that funded it.
un-sc-res-393:
A South African attack on Zambia brought strong condemnation from the Security Council in July 1976. Zambia's representative had written to the Council, and its foreign minister addressed the chamber. South Africa was using Namibia, an international territory it occupied illegally, as a base for attacks on neighboring African countries. The Council held that the worsening situation in southern Africa could threaten international peace.

The Council strongly condemned the armed attack as a flagrant breach of Zambia's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It demanded that South Africa respect Zambia's independence, air space, and borders in full. South Africa had to stop at once the use of Namibia as a launch base against Zambia and other African states. The Council praised Zambia and the other front-line states for backing Namibia's liberation struggle. It declared that freeing Namibia and Zimbabwe and ending apartheid were needed for lasting peace in the region.
un-sc-res-1693:
MONUC's election boost was held in place a little longer on 30 June 2006. Congo's national assembly vote and the first round of the presidential election were set for 30 July 2006. Militias and foreign armed groups in the east still threatened the polls. Security sector reform was judged key to the country's long-term calm. The Secretary-General's report of 13 June guided the step.

The Council extended the temporary increase in MONUC's military and police strength, granted in resolution 1621 (2005), to 30 September 2006. The short-term character of the rise was underlined again. Transitional bodies and all Congolese parties were called once more to keep the elections free, fair, and on time. Parties had to shun incitement to hatred and violence during the campaign. The Council recalled MONUC's power to use all necessary means, within its mandate, to protect civilians under threat.
un-sc-res-93:
Drainage works in the Israel–Syria demilitarized zone were ordered halted on 18 May 1951. The truce chief of staff had asked Israel in March to stop the Palestine Land Development Company's digging in the zone. The chairman of the Mixed Armistice Commission held charge of the zone under article V of the armistice. Israel had let the work go on.

The Council backed the requests of the truce chief of staff and the commission chairman. It called on Israel to comply with them. The disputed works had to stop until the commission chairman arranged terms for the project to go forward. Arab landowners driven from the zone by the fighting were to be allowed back to their lands. The Council also declared that no work in the zone could change the rights of either side under the armistice. The ruling shaped the zone's tense life until 1967.
un-sc-res-993:
UNOMIG was renewed as Georgia's settlement talks crept on 12 May 1995. The Secretary-General's report of 1 May lay before the Council. The Moscow ceasefire of 14 May 1994 had generally held for a year, with CIS peacekeepers and UNOMIG watching. Talks on a new constitution on federal lines formed part of the settlement effort. Aid programs faced critical funding shortages.

The Council extended UNOMIG's mandate for a further period ending 12 January 1996. The extension could be reviewed if the CIS force changed. Full support went to the Secretary-General's drive for a comprehensive settlement, on Georgia's status question above all. The parties were called to make real progress in the talks, with Russia's help as facilitator. The Abkhaz side was pressed again to speed the voluntary return of refugees, starting with the Gali region. Extra steps by UNOMIG and the CIS force to make return safer were welcomed.
europmc-pmc10025693:
Khan and co-authors examine how ChatGPT is reshaping medical education and patient care in a 2023 paper. Chatbots powered by large language models had just reached the public, and medical schools were weighing their promise and risks. The authors write from inside that debate, as teachers and clinicians.

The paper reviews uses of chatbots in study, diagnosis support, and record keeping. It weighs gains in speed and access against risks of error and bias. It closes with advice on safe use. Readers get an early, balanced view of AI's entry into medicine.
europmc-pmc10079493:
Lotfy, AboQuella, and Wang review clinical trials of exosomes derived from mesenchymal stem cells in a 2023 paper. Mesenchymal stem cells are repair cells found in many tissues. Much of their healing effect comes from signals they release, packaged in tiny parcels called exosomes, rather than from the cells themselves.

The review gathers trials that gave these parcels to patients for a range of conditions. It covers how the parcels are made, dosed, and checked for safety. The authors weigh early promise against the need for standard methods and larger trials.
europmc-pmc10166793:
De Angelis and colleagues warn that ChatGPT and other large language models could fuel a new wave of false health information, in a 2023 perspective. ChatGPT's release brought fluent AI text to the public at huge scale. The authors trace how these models grew and why their smooth style makes errors hard to spot.

They argue that health agencies must prepare for AI-driven infodemics, floods of false claims that spread fast. The paper suggests checks on sources, swift official replies, and public training in spotting fakes. It is an early call for readiness.
europmc-pmc10365993:
Schoeler and colleagues showed in 2023 that who joins a gene study can warp its results. UK Biobank is a huge volunteer health study used for gene research. Its members are not a fair cross-section of the public. They tend to be in better health than most people.

The team worked out join rates from 14 traits shared with a fair public sample. They then re-ran gene scans for 19 traits with those rates used as weights. Effect sizes shifted, and new gene links turned up for 12 traits. Behaviour and social traits showed the biggest warps in later tests. Schoeler urges the field to recruit samples that match the public more closely.
europmc-pmc10400493:
Győrffy built a large gene data bank in 2023 to rank survival marks in ovarian cancer. This cancer is often found late, and care gains lag behind other tumours. Good marks could help doctors pick the right chemo or targeted drug for each patient. The data bank holds 1,816 samples from 17 data sets.

Each gene was tested for a link to how long patients lived. Győrffy found 2,468 genes tied to time without the disease getting worse. A set of 704 genes tied to overall survival. Top genes for the first outcome were WBP1L, ASAP3, CNNM2, and NCAPH2. All scores are shared so future mark claims can be ranked fast.
europmc-pmc10407193:
Strizova and co-authors asked in 2023 if a neat split of immune cells is a myth. Macrophages are white blood cells that guard tissues and clear debris. Lab work sorts them into two poles: M1, which stirs attack, and M2, which calms it. Each pole has its own look and set of jobs.

In real bodies, Strizova finds a wide range between the poles. Cells blend traits of both, shaped by local signals. Germs can push the blend to aid their own survival. In tumours, M2-like cells tend to help growth, while M1-like cells can help or hinder. The same blend shows up in heart plaques and in grafts. The authors urge the terms M1-like and M2-like instead.
europmc-pmc10468393:
Willett and colleagues built a speech device in 2023 that reads brain signals from a person who can no longer speak. Their patient had ALS, a disease that wastes muscles, and could not form clear words. Tiny probes in the brain logged spikes as the patient tried to speak. Software then turned those spikes into text.

Speed reached 62 words per minute, 3.4 times the prior record. Willett reports an error rate of 9.1% on a 50-word set. On a vast 125,000-word set, errors were 23.8%, the first success at that scale. Natural talk runs near 160 words per minute. Brain maps showed that mouth and speech zones keep rich sound codes years after speech loss.
europmc-pmc10767893:
Harrison and a large Ensembl team gave the 2024 update of Ensembl, a free genome resource. Ensembl labels genes on genome builds for backboned animals and model species. It has run for more than two decades. The count and spread of fine genome builds have surged in recent years.

The Rapid Release site now tops 1,700 labelled genomes, double the past count. Harrison ties that jump to joint work with species diversity projects, Darwin Tree of Life among them. Farm species gained their first gene control builds. A key tool, the Variant Effect Predictor, was updated as well. All data, code, and tools stay free to the world.
europmc-pmc10821893:
Jiménez-Loygorri and colleagues studied cell clean-up and ageing in mice and human cells in this 2024 paper. Mitophagy is the process where cells break down worn-out mitochondria, the parts that make energy. A broader clean-up process fades with age, and the team asked whether this selective one fades too. They tracked clean-up across organs in a special reporter mouse that marks the process.

Clean-up held steady or rose with age, they found, rather than falling. Old retinas showed a strong alarm response, a rise in loose mitochondrial DNA, and a fired-up defence pathway. Lab drug treatment that boosted clean-up calmed the alarm and slowed loss of brain function in old mice. The authors suggest boosting this clean-up could cut age-linked swelling and extend healthy life.
europmc-pmc10954893:
Di Vincenzo and colleagues review how a weak gut wall can drive body-wide illness in this 2024 paper. The gut wall is the largest border between the body and the outside world. Its seal depends on gut microbes, on joints between gut cells, and on signals from nerves, hormones, and food. When the seal breaks, a state often called leaky gut, germ products slip into the blood.

One such product is lipopolysaccharide, a piece of germ cell walls that sparks swelling. The review ties seal loss to infections, cell stress, high-fat diets, alcohol, and an off-balance microbe mix. It then traces links to obesity, fatty liver disease, heart disease, bowel disease, and type 1 diabetes. Brain decline is also covered. The authors sort the ways the seal is kept and lost, organ by organ.
europmc-pmc11183193:
Shen, Sipos, and Zhao present the second version of a popular sequence toolkit in this 2024 paper. High-throughput sequencing is now routine, and labs need tools that are fast, broad, and easy for novices and experts alike. SeqKit, the original tool, was already widely used for handling sequence and alignment files. This article introduces its successor, SeqKit2.

SeqKit2 adds 19 subcommands, taking the total to 38 across eight categories, the authors report. New commands process amplicons, short targeted DNA reads, and parse sequence records with tolerance for errors. Three commands support real-time analysis, streaming live data from several files at once. Benchmarks against the old version and three rival tools showed SeqKit2 consistently faster, at a small memory cost. Other speed results stayed competitive. The subcommand layout of the original is retained.
europmc-pmc11564093:
Shen and colleagues chart how molecular ageing speeds up at two life stages in this 2024 study. Ageing is tied to nearly all diseases, and disease risk accelerates after specific ages rather than rising evenly. The team profiled many molecular layers in 108 California participants aged 25 to 75. Follow-up ran a median of 1.7 years and up to 6.8 years.

Consistent nonlinear patterns emerged, they report. Substantial dysregulation clustered at about age 44 and again at about age 60. Each wave carried distinct molecules and pathways. The 60-year shift involved immune regulation and carbohydrate metabolism. The earlier shift involved cardiovascular disease signals plus lipid and alcohol metabolism. The authors conclude that functions and risks of ageing diseases change nonlinearly across the lifespan.
europmc-pmc11614693:
Gabitto and a very large team build an integrated cell atlas of Alzheimer disease in this 2024 study. Alzheimer disease is the top cause of dementia in older adults. Its progression follows a stereotyped accumulation of protein deposits, but the affected cell populations remained understudied. The team applied multiomics and spatial genomics to one brain region, the middle temporal gyrus, in 84 donors.

Donors averaged 88 years at death and were scored along a disease pseudoprogression scale. Two phases emerged, they report. An early phase showed slow pathology growth, inflammatory microglia, reactive astrocytes, and loss of one inhibitory neuron type. Precursor cells attempted remyelination, meaning repair of nerve insulation. A later phase showed exponential pathology growth and loss of excitatory neurons plus two more inhibitory subtypes. The findings were replicated in other major Alzheimer studies.
europmc-pmc11701593:
Cerezo and a large team describe standards work at the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog in this 2025 paper. The catalog is the most comprehensive database of human genome-wide association study results. GWAS means scanning genomes for variants tied to traits or diseases. The catalog currently holds close to 7,000 publications covering more than 15,000 traits.

Curators have logged over 625,000 lead associations from those publications, the authors report. A further 85,000 full summary statistics datasets are available for downstream work such as meta-analysis, fine-mapping, and building polygenic risk scores. The paper describes the latest data content and interface improvements. A new standard format for summary statistics, GWAS-SSF, was implemented. Shared processes and vocabulary with the PGS Catalog improve interoperability. Sustainability and diversity challenges are addressed directly.
europmc-pmc12367593:
Sati and colleagues updated the WHO priority list for drug-resistant bacteria in 2025. The World Health Organization first issued the list in 2017. It steers policy, research money, and drug development. At least 13 new antibiotics had since gained approval.

The 2024 list scores 24 resistant pathogens on eight criteria. Criteria include deaths, illness burden, and spread trends. A structured decision method weighed expert input. The update fixes limits seen in the first list. Sati aims global effort at the most urgent threats. Antibiotic resistance keeps growing, so priorities need refresh. The list sorts pathogens into critical, high, and medium tiers. Gram-negative bacteria top the critical tier.
europmc-pmc1247193:
Elliott and Wartenberg surveyed spatial epidemiology in 2004. The field maps how disease varies across places. It weighs demographic, environmental, behavior, and genetic factors together. Small-area studies anchor the field, from maps to cluster hunts.

New mapping software and fine-grained data opened fresh chances. Small areas also bring statistical traps. Random noise can dominate rates where case counts are tiny. Social factors can confound local comparisons. A single data error can fake a disease excess. Elliott stresses data quality checks before any cluster claim. It appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2004.
europmc-pmc1297593:
Kinloch and co-authors hunted the targets of arthritis-linked antibodies in 2005. Antibodies against citrullinated proteins are highly specific to rheumatoid arthritis. Their exact protein targets were poorly understood. Cell lysates treated with a converting enzyme were screened with patient serum.

A 47 kilodalton protein reacted with patient samples only. Controls showed no reaction, and only the altered form was recognized. Mass spectrometry identified it as alpha-enolase, a metabolic enzyme. Nine altered sites were mapped in its sequence. In a larger test, 46 percent of patients reacted to it. Kinloch names a concrete candidate target antigen.
europmc-pmc1557993:
Small gene regulators called microRNAs can be edited after they are made. Blow and co-authors surveyed that editing in 2006 across ten human tissues. MicroRNAs, about 20 letters long, mute genes by pairing with their messages. Editing swaps letters in the microRNA itself.

The survey found editing widespread in human microRNAs. Each edit can change which messages a microRNA targets, since pairing depends on the letters. Blow concludes editing expands the diversity of microRNAs and their target range. That extra layer may help tune gene control by tissue.  The edited forms may also help explain how microRNA control shifts during development.
europmc-pmc1637893:
Dirty air during pregnancy may stunt babies before birth. Bobak tested that in 2000 using all registered births in 67 Czech districts in 1991, over 108,000 babies. He estimated each mother's exposure to sulfur dioxide, particles, and nitrogen oxides by trimester.

Low birth weight affected 5.2 percent of babies, prematurity 4.8 percent. Both rose with sulfur dioxide, and slightly less with particles. A 50-unit rise in first-trimester sulfur dioxide raised low-weight odds by 20 percent. Effects were marginally strongest for first-trimester exposure. Growth retardation inside the womb showed no link to any pollutant. Prematurity rose with the same gases.
europmc-pmc1796893: Are MRI-defined fat infiltrations in the multifidus muscles associated with low back pain? — a 2005 science paper on back-muscle fat. It asks if fat links to pain. The paper is the back-fat study: the findings on low back pain, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1864993: Identification of a novel polyomavirus from patients with acute respiratory tract infections. — a 2005 science paper finding a new lung virus. It names the new polyomavirus. The paper is the virus-find study: the findings on respiratory ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1904193: Utilization of the PICO framework to improve searching PubMed for clinical questions. — a 2005 science paper on PICO PubMed searches. It improves the clinical searching. The paper is the PICO guide: the findings on the search tool, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1913093: Liver fluke induces cholangiocarcinoma. — a 2005 science paper on liver-fluke cancer. It shows the fluke induces cancer for labs worldwide. The paper is the fluke study: the findings on cholangiocarcinoma for labs, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc1994993: Force-induced unfolding of fibronectin in the extracellular matrix of living cells. — a 2005 science paper on force-unfolding fibronectin. It finds the force-induced unfolding. The paper is the unfolding study: the findings on fibronectin, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2147593: Dental plaque as a biofilm and a microbial community - implications for health and disease. — a 2005 science paper on dental plaque as germ films. It treats plaque as a biofilm. The paper is the plaque study: the findings on dental ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2258193: PHOSIDA (phosphorylation site database): management, structural and evolutionary investigation, and prediction of phosphosites. — a 2005 science paper on the PHOSIDA tag-map hub. It guides the tag-map hub for labs. The paper is the hub guide: the notes on tag maps, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2262093: The global distribution of fatal pesticide self-poisoning: systematic review. — a 2005 science paper on worldwide bug-spray suicides. It charts the worldwide suicides for labs. The paper is the suicide-chart review: the notes on spray ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2268993: MicroRNA399 is a long-distance signal for the regulation of plant phosphate homeostasis. — a 2005 science paper on a plant phosphate signal. It finds the long-distance signal. The paper is the signal study: the findings on phosphate ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2396793: Spatial relational memory requires hippocampal adult neurogenesis. — a 2008 science paper on memory and new brain cells. It finds the neurogenesis requirement. The paper is the memory study: the findings on brain ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2443193: Mapping the structural core of human cerebral cortex. — a 2008 science paper on the brain's core map. It maps the structural core. The paper is the core study: the findings on cortex ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2505093: Impact of stepping stones on incidence of HIV and HSV-2 and sexual behaviour in rural South Afr — a 2008 science paper on the stepping-stones trial. It measures the program impact. The paper is the impact study: the findings on HIV ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2563693: Inferring pathway activity toward precise disease classification. — a 2008 science paper on pathway-activity inference. It infers the pathway activity. The paper is the inference study: the findings on disease ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
europmc-pmc2600393: Systematic literature review of role of noroviruses in sporadic gastroenteritis. — a 2008 science paper on stomach-bug paper sweeps. It sweeps the stomach-bug papers for labs. The paper is the sweep study: the notes on stomach ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2656493: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. — a 2008 science paper on ALS's slow motor fade. It covers the motor fade for labs. The paper is the ALS study: the findings on ALS ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
europmc-pmc2689393: Adalimumab for the treatment of fistulas in patients with Crohn's disease. — a 2008 science paper on adalimumab for fistulas. It treats the Crohn's fistulas. The paper is the adalimumab study: the findings on Crohn ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2719693: Meningococcal carriage and disease--population biology and evolution. — a 2008 science paper on meningococcal carriage. It studies the population biology. The paper is the carriage study: the findings on meningococcus ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
sallustius-gods-and-world-taylor-1793:
Thomas Taylor translated Sallustius's On the Gods and the World into English in 1793. Sallustius, a fourth-century Roman official, wrote a short catechism of pagan belief. Taylor bundled it with the Pythagoric Sentences of Demophilus and hymns of Proclus.

In brief, clear chapters Sallustius explains the gods, the soul, and proper rites. He answers common objections to pagan worship with calm reasoning. Taylor, the great English Platonist, used such translations to carry Neoplatonism to English readers. The little book remains the best short doorway into late-antique pagan thought. Its clarity surprises readers expecting ancient religion to feel murky.
westcott-collectanea-hermetica-vol-1-189:
W. Wynn Westcott opened his Collectanea Hermetica series in 1893 with d'Espagnet's Hermetic Arcanum. Jean d'Espagnet wrote that alchemical treatise in 1623. Westcott, a founder of the Golden Dawn, added preface and notes.

The Arcanum teaches the secret of the philosophers' stone in riddling prose. It ranks among the most respected texts of serious alchemy. D'Espagnet wraps laboratory work inside philosophy and scripture. Westcott's edition aimed the old text at Victorian occult students. His series reprinted rare Hermetic works that libraries held but readers could not reach. This first volume set the pattern of text, preface, and practical notes.
westcott-sepher-yetzirah-1893:
W. Wynn Westcott translated the Sepher Yetzirah, the Book of Formation, in an 1893 second edition. The Hebrew text is among the oldest works of Jewish mysticism. Westcott added the Fifty Gates of Intelligence and the Thirty-two Paths of Wisdom.

The Sepher Yetzirah describes God creating the world through numbers and letters. Ten numbers and twenty-two Hebrew letters form everything that exists. Its style is brief, cryptic, and endlessly commented upon by later Kabbalists. Westcott's translation brought this cornerstone of Kabbalah to Victorian occultists. Golden Dawn teaching absorbed its paths and gates into ritual grades. Few texts so short have generated so much commentary across so many centuries.
sallustius-gods-world-taylor-1793:
Sallustius wrote On the Gods and the World in the fourth century, a clear statement of pagan theology. Thomas Taylor's 1793 translation is the version preserved here. The Pythagoric Sentences of Demophilus and hymns of Proclus accompany it in Taylor's edition.

Sallustius explains the gods, providence, sacrifice, and the soul in short chapters. He argues that myths teach truths about divine things in symbolic form. His tone stays calm, orderly, and remarkably modern in feeling. Pagans of his generation faced a rising Christian empire around them. The little catechism taught thoughtful pagans what they actually believed. Taylor's English Platonist circle treasured it, and modern readers still find it the cleanest pagan summary.
gifford-dialogue-concerning-witches-engl:
George Gifford, an Essex minister, published his Dialogue Concerning Witches and Witchcrafts in 1593. Villagers in the dialogue debate a local witch scare, and Gifford speaks through them. His subtle claim is that the devil deceives the accusers even more than the accused.

Panicked neighbors see pacts and familiars where malice and melancholy suffice. Gifford does not deny the devil; he relocates his cleverest work into human fear. The result is often called the subtlest Elizabethan demonology. Doubt here wears a pastor's tender heart and a keen eye for village life. Modern readers still admire how Gifford turns a witch panic into a lesson about its makers.
peucer-commentarius-divinationum-latin-1:
Kaspar Peucer, son-in-law to the reformer Melanchthon, wrote his Commentary on the chief kinds of divination in Latin. This edition of 1593 spread the mature Lutheran account of foretelling. Peucer surveys every art that claims to read the future, from stars to dreams to lots.

His task is sorting. Some prediction reads natural signs lawfully, as weather lore does. Other kinds rest on diabolical arts and stand condemned. Peucer draws the fences with a scholar's care and a churchman's firmness. The book is the Lutheran science of divination, complete in one volume. It preserves an age when telling the future was a learned profession with rules.
plos-pone-0004893:
Shinji Fukuda led a team that tested a new way to track how gut bacteria use food and fuel over time for PLOS ONE in 2009. Gut bacteria help keep the gut in balance. They sense food, pump compounds in and out, and compete with each other for what they need to live and grow in a dense shared space.

The new method, called real time metabolotyping, tracks fuel use as it happens. It shows how the whole group reacts when food or drugs change. Live tracks like these beat one time snapshots. They may one day help doctors read gut health from how bacteria respond, not just from which kinds are there.
plos-pone-0004993:
Black-band disease is a destructive infection of coral reefs. It is among the most widespread coral diseases. Yet its transmission mechanisms were poorly understood. Assaf Zvuloni and colleagues mapped its spread in a coral community. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They tracked the disease in space and time.

The patterns show how the disease moves between neighboring corals. That reveals the routes an outbreak follows. Reef managers can use such maps to predict spread. They may also find ways to slow it. The study turns scattered cases into an epidemiological picture. Understanding transmission is the first step toward protecting reefs.
plos-pone-0005093:
Baculoviruses infect insects. They are also being groomed as gene-therapy carriers for humans. Johanna Laakkonen and colleagues studied how they enter human cells. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The entry did not use clathrin, the usual doorway protein. Something else happened instead.

The virus's entry triggered the cells to swallow E. coli bacteria. Non-phagocytic human cells normally ignore such bacteria. The baculovirus changed that behavior. The odd coupling reveals a new entry route. It matters for engineering safer viral carriers. A carrier that makes cells swallow bacteria needs careful handling. The finding shows why entry mechanisms must be mapped before clinical use.
plos-pone-0005193:
Niemann-Pick type C is a rare disease in which cholesterol and other fats build up inside cell compartments. The buildup blocks normal fat handling and harms many organs. Schweitzer and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 that boosting one recycling pathway can reverse the defect in cells.

The pathway centers on ARF6, a protein that helps move material out of endosomes for reuse. Raising that recycling traffic cleared the fat pileup in diseased cells. For a disease with few treatment options, a route that undoes the core cell defect is a strong lead for drug work.
plos-pone-0005293:
Autoimmune inner ear disease causes hearing loss and has no definitive lab test. All suspected patients get steroid drugs during attacks, yet only about half respond at first. Vambutas and colleagues looked for a predictor of that response in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Alternative splicing of the IL1R2 gene, measured in lab tests, correlated with how patients responded to glucocorticoids. A splicing pattern that forecasts response could spare non-responders months of useless steroids. It would also give this poorly defined disease its first practical test. Hearing loss in this disease can come on fast, and each week on the wrong drug is a week of loss that may not come back. So a guide test is worth a great deal.
plos-pone-0005893:
Elías Barquero-Calvo and co-authors compared in 2009 two related bacteria to learn how stealth pathogens evolve. Brucella slips inside cells and causes chronic disease while barely tripping innate immunity. Its cousin Ochrobactrum, by contrast, is readily detected and rarely dangerous.

Differences in how the two meet the immune system point to the traits that make Brucella stealthy. Evolution tuned innate immunity to catch most invaders; these bacteria are the exceptions that reveal the rules. The comparison may expose Brucella's few detectable weak points. That is valuable for vaccines against a germ built to hide.
plos-pone-0005993:
A spawning salmon's heart can stop outright at the key moment. Yuya Makiguchi, Shinya Nagata, Takahito Kojima and colleagues studied that arrest in chum salmon in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper looks at missed heartbeats during gamete release, the act of letting out eggs or sperm, and at the nerve system that controls the pause.

The parasympathetic nerves, the body's brake pedal, regulate the arrest, the team reports. A planned pause differs from the skipped beats of disease, since these beats return. The study shows how far the heart's rhythm can bend for breeding, and it gives fish biology a clear case of the nervous system steering the heart to extremes.
plos-pone-0006093:
HIV can fall silent inside cells, where drugs cannot reach it, and wake years later. Sophie Reuse, Miriam Calao, Kabamba Kabeya and colleagues attacked that hiding place in 2009. Together the two wake the virus far more strongly than either alone, a synergistic activation. Waking the reservoir while treatment holds the virus down is a leading cure strategy. The pairing gives that strategy a concrete recipe to carry into further tests, aimed at the last barrier between treatment and eradication.
plos-pone-0006193:

plos-pone-0006693:

plos-pone-0006793:

plos-pone-0006893:

plos-pone-0006993:

plos-pone-0007093:

plos-pone-0007193:

plos-pone-0007293:

plos-pone-0006293:

plos-pone-0009693:
