In some models of quantum gravity, space can pass from a Euclidean region to a Lorentzian one. That switch was first proposed by Hartle and Hawking to dodge the initial singularity of the standard cosmos.

Lafuente-López gives a one-parameter family of such signature-change models. The family generalizes Kossowski's signature type. He seeks simple local formulas near the surface where the switch happens. Clean local forms make the models easier to test and extend. The work serves theorists who model the birth of spacetime without a hard beginning.
arxiv-2601-11093:
Ashish Raj Shekhar, Shiven Agarwal, Priyanuj Bordoloi, Yash Shah, and Vivek Gupta present Integrity Shield, a system for ethical AI use in assessments. Language models can now solve whole exams from an uploaded PDF. That power threatens the reliability of grades and credentials. Watermarking is a common defense, but token-level marks fail when students use closed, black-box systems.

Integrity Shield aims at authorship transparency under those real conditions. Teachers hand out the documents; students query systems the school does not control. Any shield must work without touching the model's decoding. The work serves educators who want AI use declared and checkable, rather than banned in ways no one can enforce.
arxiv-2601-12093:
Duarte Alexandrino, Ben Moseley, and Pavlos Protopapas speed up physics-informed neural networks for nonlinear systems. Such nets solve equations by adding the law to the training loss. They can model dynamic acts across science and engineering.

Yet they train slowly and move poorly to new problems. The team's method, named in the work, guides transfer learning with perturbation steps. Past runs can then seed new ones with care. Faster PINNs would aid real-time models of fluids, structures, and fields.  Shared starts could cut hours from each new solve task.  Speed gains grow when many like problems must be solved in a row.
arxiv-2601-12193:
Shaunak Halbe, Bhagyashree Puranik, Jayakrishnan Unnikrishnan, and their co-authors build one embedding space for many video search tasks. Users now ask for whole clips, for a brief moment in a clip, and for mixed text-image queries. Past systems train split encoders on vast data for each task.

Their system, named VIRTUE in the work, uses unified embeddings for all these tasks. One space could serve many query forms with less cost. It also lets composed queries mix modes in one search. The work tests that breadth.  One trait space also eases mixed text and clip search.
arxiv-2601-11193:
Peter von Schultzendorff and five coauthors mix physics code with learned models. Their 2026 preprint adds a learned near-well model to OPM Flow. OPM Flow is a tool that simulates flow in rock that holds oil and gas. Flow near a well is one of the hard parts to get right.

Hybrid designs pair old physics-based code with models fit to data. The learned parts can match real effects with high fidelity. They also run fast once they are trained and ready. That speed opens the door to quicker full runs of a field. It also helps model effects that physics alone does not yet explain well.
arxiv-2601-11493:
Lorenzo Lazzarino, Katherine Pearce, and Nathaniel Pritchard grade random matrix shortcuts. Their 2026 preprint deals with Generalized Nystrom approximations. Randomized methods in numerical linear algebra scale to huge matrices. They give accurate low-rank approximations at a fraction of the cost.

A key open task is to judge that accuracy cheaply. Extra passes over the matrix can cost as much as the method saves. Error estimators must work with no new matrix access. The team gives efficient estimators for the generalized case. Trustworthy error bars make random methods safe for pipelines. Engineers can then stop early when the fit is good enough.
arxiv-2601-11693:
Shane Panter and Nasir Eisty review technical lag as latent debt. Their 2026 rapid review consolidates research on the topic. Technical lag builds when systems fail to keep pace. Technology advances, and lagging systems lose quality over time.

The review clarifies definitions of technical lag first. It explores how lag is detected and quantified in code. Underlying causes and consequences come next in the survey. Current management practices for lag are also reviewed. The vision casts lag as passively accumulated technical debt. Debt that accrues by standing still reframes upgrade choices. The method was a rapid review with snowballing. Peer-reviewed studies formed the base of the synthesis.
arxiv-2601-13093:
Gabriel Picavet and Martine Picavet-L'Hermitte study a special class of ideals in ring theory. Ideals are sets inside a ring that stay closed under set rules. The class here is called quasi maximal ideals, first set out by Alan and co-authors.

The pair give a full account of what marks such ideals. They also bring in a linked class, called submaximal ideals. A key tool is the conductor of a small step from one ring to a larger ring. They show that this conductor is quasi maximal in the larger ring. That fact yields a fresh way to mark such small steps. Ring staff get a sharper kit for sorting finite ring growth.
arxiv-2601-13193:
Yuxi Hu, Mengran Yuan, and Jie Zhang study if a wavy flow form stays true for long times. The flow is a one dim squeezed fluid. In this form, two old laws are swapped. Newton's law for thick flow is swapped for Maxwell's law. Fourier's law for heat flow is swapped for Cattaneo's law.

The swap gives the set a finite speed for signals, unlike the old set. The wave form at stake is a rarefaction wave, a smooth spread out fan. The team proves that small shakes of that wave fade and the wave holds for long times. Such proofs set when the new set can be trusted for real flows.
arxiv-2601-13293:
Michael Hinze, Christian Kahle, and John Sebastian Simon track the long time acts of best shape flows. Their task joins shape choice with the time flow laws of Navier and Stokes. The sought shape is held as a phase field, a smooth mark that says where fluid or wall sits.

The flow laws are run through a porous media swap, a known trick to make shape tasks firm. The field that marks shape stays fixed in time, while the flow moves. The team asks where the joint acts settle as time runs long. Such work guides tasks like pipe and wing shape, where the best form must serve a flow that never sits still.
arxiv-2601-12393: Shohei Satake works on Lee codes, a tool from coding theory. He builds a new explicit family of codes of a special near perfect kind. These codes can be made as long as one likes. Long codes with good traits are prized, since explicit families are rare in this area.
arxiv-2601-12693:
Mohoshin Ara Tahera and four co authors build a federated system for real time object detection in traffic. Intelligent transportation systems need detection that is fast, private, and secure at once. Three challenges block that goal. Traffic data differ by place, with some classes missing at some sites. Edge hardware also struggles to run large transformer models within latency limits.

The third challenge is trust: client updates may be hostile, and central aggregation is a risk. Their system, BlocksecRT-DETR, answers with decentralized federated learning. It aims to be privacy preserving and token efficient at the same time. Secure detection at the edge would help smart traffic systems scale safely. The design shows one route to that goal.
arxiv-2601-14393:
Gor Oganesyan leads a team of eleven authors on gamma-ray burst physics in this 2026 paper. Gamma-ray bursts are the most violent explosions known. A small fraction of their X-ray photons behave in a telling way after escaping the source. The abstract in the evidence pack cuts off at that point, so the full photon path is not stated there.

The title names the paper's claim: MeV absorption in gamma-ray bursts can serve as a probe of their progenitor winds. A progenitor wind is gas blown off by the star before it burst. If burst photons are absorbed by that wind, the loss pattern records the wind's traits. Readers get a proposed new use for an absorption signal.
arxiv-2601-14493:
Matthieu Bourguignon and a team of seven co-authors study how glass breaks in this 2026 paper. Shear bands lie at the root of fracture initiation in bulk metallic glasses and amorphous polymers. For silicate glasses, past studies stressed a distinct effect: permanent volumetric strain, often called densification. The team's work tests which picture fits silicate glass.

They systematically investigate indentation-induced fracture in two families of aluminoborosilicate glasses. Indentation presses a hard tip into the surface to start cracks in a controlled way. Their title claims a universal shear localization mechanism behind fracture initiation. The tests are hands-on. A hard tip is pressed into real glass, and the cracks are then read up close. Readers get lab evidence that silicate glass may fail more like its metallic cousins than once thought.
arxiv-2601-14593:
Po-Kai Chiu and Hung-Hsuan Chen work on medical image learning in this 2026 paper. Deep learning for medical image analysis is limited by the requirement for expert annotations. Three-dimensional self-supervised methods like volume contrast learning are powerful. They partially address the labeling scarcity issue. Their high computational cost and memory consumption are barriers, though.

The team moves from volumes to slices, as their title says. They design computationally efficient contrastive learning for sequential abdominal CT analysis. Slices are the single cross-section images that stack into a CT volume. Readers get a lighter self-supervised method that still learns from the order of slices in a scan.
arxiv-2601-15493:
M M Abid Naziri and four co-authors test the libraries behind deep learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Libraries such as PyTorch sit under most AI applications. They are complex, and they contain bugs. Many bug-finding methods exist for them. The authors say much room for improvement remains. One core obstacle is the lack of API specifications.

Without specs, a tester cannot easily tell right output from wrong. The team's answer uses neurosymbolic constraint learning, per the title. That blends neural methods with symbolic rules. Learned constraints can stand in for missing specs. Better library tests matter beyond research. A bug deep in a shared library can quietly corrupt many models built on top of it.
arxiv-2601-15793:
Yuxuan Lei and five co-authors teach language models to simulate people in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is HumanLLM. Models have grown strong at objective tasks like math and coding. Simulating human behavior is a different, newer ambition. It carries large implications. Social science research could run on simulated subjects. Businesses could test ideas on simulated customers before spending.

The title stresses personalized understanding and simulation of human nature. A useful simulator must capture how individuals differ, not just averages. The abstract frames the motivation more than the method. Readers will find design details in the full text. The stakes cut both ways. Good simulators aid research, but shallow ones can mislead it with confident, wrong behavior.
arxiv-2601-14893:
C. Chilarescu examines a production function that he put forward in earlier work. A production function links the inputs a firm uses to the output it makes. His 2026 arXiv paper tests what his new function can and cannot do.

One test concerns elasticity, which gauges how output reacts when an input grows. He proves that, under set limits on the inputs, the elasticity can also fall below one. He also proves that the function meets the Inada conditions under set limits. Those are the classic edge rules for such functions in economics.
arxiv-2601-15093:
Fien Apers asks whether a famous set of string theory vacua can have a holographic dual. Her 2026 arXiv paper deals with the DGKT solutions of massive type IIA string theory. These vacua split their scales apart by using very large fluxes.

Whether any scale-separated anti-de Sitter vacuum has a dual is not known. Apers studies the brane dual proposed for the DGKT case. She also studies its decoupling, the step that should isolate the dual theory. The paper tests how far that proposed brane duality can really be trusted today.
arxiv-2601-15293:
Alva Markelius, Fethiye Irmak Doğan, and co-authors ask how disabled students feel about robot help at university. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with barriers in higher education. Long procedures, poor information, and high social demands can block students from support.

The study tests robot-based support in two roles. One role gives information, a signposting role. The other acts as a sounding board for disclosure. Two embodiment types are compared as well: a physical robot and a disembodied voice agent. Students then judge which form of help they would accept in practice.
arxiv-2601-16293:
Roche reports new tests of how stuff bounces far UV light. The 2026 preprint deals with light past the UV edge, called VUV. True bounce values count for probes that sense light in rare gas. DUNE is one such big probe now in build. Past bounce values clash much from source to source. Test terms drove much of that clash.

Fresh tests under set terms aim to pin true values down. Stuff in the tests is that used in argon and xenon probes. Firm values let teams tune probe light yield with care. They also cut doubt in probe design sums. The work is a lab note for probe builders.
arxiv-2601-16393:
Keidai Iiyama and Grace Gao track moon craft by earth GPS marks. Their 2026 preprint deals with craft that loop the moon. Earth GPS marks are weak at moon range and hard to read. Yet they could guide moon craft with no new moon net. The team builds a filter to draw orbit and clock from those marks.

The filter clones past states to hold time lags in the data. A split form of the filter keeps the sums firm and fast. Firm orbit marks are key for safe moon flight plans. The work tests earth marks as a moon guide path. It seeks high grade from low sight terms.
arxiv-2601-16493:
Yuerang Li, Zipeng Wang and Kenan Zhang bound Shimorin type sum tools. Their 2026 preprint deals with sum tools on the unit disk. Such a tool weighs a map by a fixed weight set on a line. Bounds link the in size and out size of the tool. Those links are named Lp to Lq bounds in the field.

Firm bounds tell for which size pairs the tool stays sound. Sound tools serve sums in wave, heat and chance maths. The team seeks sharp pairs for this tool class. Sharp pairs close gaps left in past bound work. The work is a pure sum study of disk tools.
arxiv-2601-16693:
Javier Sanz Rodrigo, Nicholas Kryger-Nelson, Lena Mittmann, Eugène Bertin, Ivano Castelli, and Andrea Crovetto hunt for new raw stuff to build with. Their 2026 preprint centers on metal phosphosulfides. These mixes of metal, phosphorus, and sulfur can do many jobs. Yet they are hard to cook in a lab. Past work thus stuck to one mix at a time.

The team pairs AI tools with fast lab work. Smart search can cut the trial list down. Quick cooks then test the top picks in days. This loop could open a whole class of stuff. New such mixes may serve cells, chips, and light tools.
arxiv-2601-17093:
Olha Sirikova and Alvin Chan build a three-view frame to set neural nets side by side. Teams need such sets to check and trust their nets. Past gauges gave just one view of net kinship. Their 2026 preprint joins three views in a triangle frame. One view is the still shape of the net's codes.

The next view is how nets act, by calls and links. The third view is how nets hold up when trimmed. Trim tests cut weights and watch skill hold or fall. Three views give a fuller kin map than one. Such maps help pick nets for science work.
arxiv-2601-17293:
Minh-Tâm Quang Trinh and Nathan Williams compute special elements in Hecke algebras. For any finite reductive group, such elements arise from partial Springer resolutions. The team finds them via the Harish-Chandra transform. Partial resolutions come in two kinds. The larger kind holds the deeper story, and the authors treat it with care.

Hecke algebras encode deep symmetry in representation theory. Central elements act as anchors for whole blocks of that theory. Knowing them in closed form saves long case work. It also links geometry to algebra in a tight way. The result serves pure math, where such bridges guide new proofs. Noncrossing combinatorics enters as part of that bridge.
arxiv-2601-17893:
Sarmistha Sarna Gomasta, Mahmood Jasim, Hossein Hadisi, Yvonne Jansen, and Pierre Dragicevic test what music does to data videos. Their 2026 preprint reports a study that was registered before it ran. Data videos pair charts and facts with story and sound to reach wide audiences. Many of them use music, yet no one had pinned down what the music changes for viewers.

The team measures three effects: how well the video persuades, how much it engages, and how it makes viewers feel. Each effect matters to people who make such videos for news, health, or public campaigns. The results can guide when music helps a message land and when it may get in the way.
arxiv-2601-17793:
Robin Ming Chen, Yang Lan, Yue Liu, and Zhong Wang prove a stability result for a classic wave equation. Their 2026 preprint deals with the Camassa-Holm equation, used for shallow water waves. The equation admits smooth solitons, single waves that hold their shape as they travel. It also admits multi-solitons, groups of such waves that pass through each other. The team asks whether these waves are stable in the long run.

They show that solutions starting near a soliton settle toward one as time grows. The settling holds in the energy space, up to a shift in position. The same holds for multi-solitons. Stability proofs tell modelers which wave shapes can be trusted over long spans.
arxiv-2601-18293:
A team including Saverio Braccini tests a beam monitor that never touches the beam. Their 2026 preprint deals with low-energy medical cyclotrons. These machines make isotopes for medicine, and their beams are fragile. Even a thin device placed in the beam can spoil its quality. The team studies an external fiber monitor made of cerium-doped silica fibers that scintillate. The fibers catch secondary radiation thrown off at parts the beam already passes.

They test the monitor on the 18 MeV Bern Medical Cyclotron beam line. Reading stray radiation keeps the beam itself intact. Safer, cleaner beams mean more reliable isotope supply. The work serves hospitals that depend on those isotopes.
arxiv-2601-18993:
Wei Cao and eight co-authors free a camera from the path it first took through a scene. Their method replays a moving scene, shot on one plain camera, from any new path a user picks. Wide turns are hard: one camera sees only a thin slice of a moving world, so most of the scene stays unseen.

The team rebuilds the scene in full 3D plus time, then renders the new view without any training. They call the method FreeOrbit4D. Filling the unseen parts in a sound way is the core trick, and it serves film, games, and replay tools.
arxiv-2601-19193:
Van-Quang Nguyen and Takayuki Okatani teach models to answer table questions with visible reasoning. Tables in images and documents hold much of the world's data. Yet models trained on past table sets give short factual answers with no steps shown. Brief answers hide how the model got there and often miss the mark.

Their method, CoReTab, drives reasoning through code, so each step can be checked as it runs. Code based steps turn a guess into a trace a user can audit. Better table skill matters for finance, science, and any office work where numbers live in grids.
arxiv-2601-19593:
Estèphe Arnaud, Mohamed Daoudi, and Pierre Guerreschi work on planning botulinum toxin injections. These injections are the standard treatment for facial asymmetry and a common tool for facial rejuvenation. Choosing the right dose for each spot, though, still rests mostly on the clinician's intuition. Wrong doses lead to weak or uneven results.

The authors propose a framework that simulates the effect of an injection before it happens. Their method edits a learned latent model of the face in a localised way. By tying the edit size to dose, the system models dose-response: how the face changes as dose changes. Doctors could test a plan on the model first. That promises more predictable outcomes and fewer corrective visits.
arxiv-2601-20093:
Xuanyu Long and Feng Liu ask whether flat-band materials can carry a steady current. Flat bands are energy bands that barely vary, giving electrons unusual quantum geometric properties. Singular flat bands touch another band at a point, which makes their geometry especially rich. The authors study how such bands respond to a steady, uniform electric field.

They build a minimal two-band lattice model. Away from the touching point, the flat band's spectrum in the field is captured by an intraband Berry phase. The question is whether Landau-Zener tunneling between bands enables single-particle direct current. Flat-band systems are candidates for novel electronics and superconductors. Knowing if they conduct under a field is a basic, necessary fact.
arxiv-2601-20293:
Marian Douspis tests the standard picture of the expanding universe without assuming any dark energy model. The test concerns the FLRW metric, which assumes the universe is uniform at large scales, and whether space is flat or curved. He uses the latest data release from the DESI survey to run the check.

Distances come from two supernova collections, Pantheon+ and DESY5. An iterative smoothing method rebuilds the distance modulus, the comoving distance, and the Hubble parameter from the data. A model-free test of this kind can show whether the standard metric itself is failing, before new physics is invoked.
arxiv-2601-20493:
Joan Domingo-Pasarin and Xavier Ros-Oton study the regularity of free boundaries for weak solutions of generalized Alt-Caffarelli type problems. Their work is motivated by the Serrin problem, a classic question about overdetermined boundary conditions. In the problems studied, a solution satisfies one condition inside the domain and an extra gradient condition on its boundary.

Free boundaries, where the solution's regime changes, are where the geometry gets subtle. Lipschitz regularity of that boundary is a key step toward smoother conclusions. Such results feed into shape optimization and the theory of equilibria in physics. The point sounds dry, but it is not: the shape of that edge is where a proof lives or dies.
arxiv-2601-20593:
Chetan Balwe and Nidhi Gupta study the connected components of affine quadrics in A1-homotopy theory. For any smooth quadratic hypersurface over a field, they use iterations of the naive connected-components functor. Their goal is the field-valued sections of the sheaf of A1-connected components of the hypersurface.

A1-homotopy theory imports the ideas of topology into algebraic geometry, where paths are replaced by algebraic curves. Connected components in this sense are far subtler than in ordinary topology. Quadrics are a test case where explicit answers can anchor the general theory. The proofs lean on a tool kit that few fields share, and that is part of their worth.
arxiv-2601-18493:
Sara Tehrani and four colleagues build a test set for AI tools that read maps of harm from space. When floods, fires, or quakes hit, fast reads of sky shots help crews choose where to go first. Past test sets ask for coarse tags, such as which block is hit. Real crews need more: what a site does, and what harm it took.

Their set, named DisasterInsight, asks tools to judge shots by use as well as by harm. It also checks if a tool stays firm when the ask is worded in new ways. A tool that fails on a fresh word may fail in the field. The set aims to grade tools by the needs of real aid work. That could push the field toward tools crews can trust in a crunch.
arxiv-2601-18593:
Felix Ballani studies a maths shape used to draw the grains in metals and rocks. The shape splits a space into cells, one per seed point, but its walls can curve. Curved walls fit real grains more than flat walls do. The shape can also grow or shrink each cell by a weight, to match grains of unlike size.

Ballani pulls its key traits into one place. He shows how the shape acts when the whole space is stretched or sheared. He also shows what its flat cuts look like. Last, he speeds up the way shots of the shape are drawn on a grid. Fast, true shots help staff test grain models on real scans. The work makes a prized shape less hard to use.
arxiv-2601-18793:
Michael Lee and three colleagues fix a flaw that pops up when code that makes code meets code that can pause and steer its own flow. The flaw is called scope escape: made code can name a thing that is out of reach where the code will run. Such code is broke at birth. The flaw can be stopped in two ways. A strict type check can bar it up front. Or a run check can catch it late.

Type checks for this case exist in maths but are hard to build and to use in real tools. Run checks are used in the field, yet their worth was not well mapped. The team set out the run check path in full, in a long form of their work. A clear map could help tool teams pick a guard that fits their needs.
arxiv-2601-21093:
Zhou Fan and Leda Wang study how a common training method behaves when data has far more features than old theory assumed. They follow repeated passes of mini-batch gradient descent on models built from a few hidden directions. Sample size and feature count grow together in their setup.

The authors give an exact long-run picture of the learning path. It holds for a wide range of small batch sizes and a matched learning rate. The results show which hidden directions the method learns first and how fast. That helps explain why repeated passes over data help some tasks and hurt others.
arxiv-2601-21393:
Abhijith S Parackal, Florian Trybel, Felix Andreas Faber, and Rickard Armiento run a giant screen for new crystal materials. Computer surveys can map which crystals are likely to be stable. The team lists all two- and three-element mixes up to a set cell size, which yields a vast pool of candidate structures.

Each candidate gets a fast energy check to weed out hopeless cases. Screening at this scale turns materials hunting into a numbers game with real odds. The survivors form a short list for deeper study and lab work. Such maps can speed the search for better batteries, chips, and catalysts.
arxiv-2601-21693:
Liang Li, Yu Wang, Jin-Jun Geng, Yong-Feng Huang, and Rong-Gen Cai dissect long gamma-ray bursts pulse by pulse. The team studies bursts caught by the Swift satellite that show a clear early pulse before the main event. Each precursor and main burst is measured on its own.

They compare duration, spectral hardness, fastest flicker, and spectral lag between the two parts. Both parts broadly match the class of bursts tied to collapsing massive stars. Whether the early pulse is a true warning or a separate act matters for burst physics. Pulse-level detail helps theorists test what the central engine does before it fully wakes.
arxiv-2601-22193:
Cyriac Antony, Alessio Martino, and Blerina Sinaimeri study a hard puzzle from the study of how species evolve. Their 2026 preprint looks at ways to map a parasite family tree onto a host family tree. Events such as shared splits, copies, host jumps, and losses link the two trees.

The hard part is to find the best map when time facts are not full. The team focus on maps where host jumps stay within a fixed short range. They probe the shape and cost of such maps. Their results guide those who build tools for this task.
arxiv-2601-22393:
Amirhossein Akbar Tabatabai and Raheleh Jalali probe the proof strength of linear logics. Proof complexity asks how long a proof must be. Their 2026 preprint notes that lower bounds for the classic sequent calculus remain a major open problem. They shed new light by isolating the power of structural rules.

They show that the rules, combined, are vastly stronger than any one alone. They prove exponential gaps that make the point sharp. The work helps map what makes proofs blow up. That map guides logic, verification, and automated proof. It is a firm step on a hard road.
arxiv-2601-22593:
Zahra Moslemi, Ziyi Liang, Norbert Fortin, and Babak Shahbaba built a transformer that learns across many kinds of graphs at once. Real graph sets differ in shape, scale, and meaning, with no shared node names. Their 2026 preprint presents the Multi-Graph Meta-Transformer for that messy case.

The frame aims to pull joint signals while keeping each graph's sense clear, so results stay interpretable. Brains, molecules, and social nets could all feed one such learner. The work is a bid for a general graph engine. It values clear reasons as much as raw scores. That breadth is the point of the design.
arxiv-2601-22693:
Jiahao Wu, Yunfei Liu, Lijian Lin, and Ye Zhu built PEAR, a tool that rebuilds a full 3D human mesh from one photo, pixel true. Such meshes drive avatars, film, and motion tools. Their 2026 preprint notes that past tools are slow, coarse in pose, and slip at the face and hands.

PEAR aligns the mesh to the image pixel by pixel, with fine detail where it counts. Expressive, well-fit meshes from a single shot would ease many crafts. The work targets the gap between a photo and a true double. Speed and fit are the tests.
arxiv-2601-21993:
Dhiogo José Correa de Sá, Carlos Pereira Lopes Filho. And Carlos Eduardo Schmiedel argue that software interfaces are too rigid for the age of autonomous agents. Agents reason in adaptive, probabilistic, context-dependent ways. System integration, by contrast, still rests on static interfaces and fixed contracts between programs.

Their 2026 preprint introduces Liquid Interfaces, a coordination paradigm where an interface is not a lasting technical artifact. Instead, interfaces are treated as temporary, formed for the interaction at hand. The idea reframes integration as negotiation rather than plumbing. If it works, systems of agents could connect, cooperate, and part without the brittle hand-built adapters that make today's integrations so costly to maintain.
arxiv-2601-22093:
Fethiye Irmak Dogan and co-authors study bias that passes between models. Social bias in generative systems is usually measured as unequal performance across groups. The authors focus on a subtler form: associational bias, where models learn stereotyped links between concepts and demographic groups even when no group is named.

A model can link doctors with men without ever being told a doctor's gender. Their 2026 preprint investigates how such associations behave when generative models communicate with each other. If bias can amplify as models talk, then multi-agent systems and model-generated training data could quietly entrench stereotypes. Tracing that spread is a step toward interrupting it.
arxiv-2601-21193:
Zecheng Zhao and four co-authors speed up how platforms find the right video for a text query. Their 2026 paper studies text-to-video retrieval. It is a core service in video platforms. Dense retrieval with dual encoders leads in accuracy. Its compute and storage scale poorly with corpus size, though. Real-time systems at scale use two stages. A fast recall model gathers a small pool of candidates. A dense retriever then reranks that pool.

The authors pair generative recall with dense reranking. Their twist is learning multi-view semantic IDs for fast retrieval. Each video gets compact codes a generative model can predict from text. Good IDs make stage one both fast and accurate. The work targets the scale where brute-force search dies.
arxiv-2512-01293:
Joao Amarante and co-authors model how disk galaxies form two groups of stars. Some stars are rich in alpha elements, made in big stars. Others are poor in those elements. Real disk galaxies show both groups side by side.

The team ran many smooth particle models as part of the GASTRO set. Each run mixed dense clumps of new stars with a single big merger event. They then checked which mix could make both star groups. Tests like this help show how mergers and clumps each shaped the disks we see today, ours included.
arxiv-2512-01593:
Muhittin Evren Aydin, Nursemin Cavdar, and Mahmut Ergut study curves of constant curvature in dual planes. Dual numbers add a nilpotent part to real numbers. Curves in dual affine and dual Lorentz-Minkowski planes model motions and lines. Their curvature can be a dual constant.

The team first finds invariants of curves under equiaffine moves. They then give explicit equations for all constant-curvature curves. Full lists like this aid work on kinematics, where dual curves encode rigid motions. They also extend classic curve theory to dual settings. Explicit equations let others plot every case at once, turning a classification claim into pictures that can be checked by eye.
arxiv-2512-01793:
Nagl and co-authors identify a candidate for a vortex crystal in a triangular quantum antiferromagnet. Triangular lattices frustrate magnetic order by geometry. Strong spin-orbit coupling adds bond anisotropy. Merging those two paradigms may yield exotic quantum materials.

Their candidate is an organic antiferromagnet with a stated chemical makeup. In it, a Z2 vortex crystal state may form. Crystals of vortices would be a new magnetic texture. Neutron and lab data on the candidate will test whether that texture truly appears. Organic salts can be grown as clean crystals, which suits neutron scattering tests of the vortex state in large shared facilities.
arxiv-2512-00893:
Kundan Mukhia and six coauthors study how a major election moved crypto markets in a 2025 paper. Their event is the 2024 United States presidential election, treated as a major political risk event. They focus on stablecoins, crypto tokens meant to hold a steady value, and split activity into human and automated kinds.

Human-driven peer-to-peer transactions on Ethereum shifted two days before the election, their structural break analysis finds. Exchange trading volumes, by contrast, reacted only on Election Day itself. That timing gap suggests ordinary users moved early while markets waited. Early-warning signals like these could help track political risk in digital markets.
arxiv-2601-22793:
A team of imaging researchers introduces a much faster way to recover phase data at busy beamline labs. Phase retrieval turns measured light patterns into images of a sample. Their method, called fast Eikonal Phase Retrieval, runs more than a hundred times faster while keeping accuracy under control.

The method grows from a math expansion based on how far light travels. A wave-optics fix and a fast filter step keep the results sharp. Speed matters at shared beamlines, where many teams queue for short slots of beam time. The scheme is built for high-throughput beamlines, where fast scans and many users demand results in minutes, not hours of computing.
arxiv-2601-22993:
Rohan Tangri and Jan-Peter Calliess design a learning method that respects a hard limit on risk. Their algorithm, VaR-CPO, optimizes a Value-at-Risk constraint directly, rather than hoping average rewards stay safe. It is built to be sample-efficient and conservative while an agent learns.

In their tests on feasible settings, the method explored safely with no constraint breaches during training. Rival methods failed to match that record. Safe learning matters where a single bad action, in finance or control, is too costly to allow. Zero violations during training is the headline property, a standard that baseline methods in the study failed to uphold.
arxiv-2512-00193:
AI benchmarks tend to saturate within a few years, sometimes months, as models master them. Anson Ho and co-authors address that problem in a 2025 study they call a Rosetta Stone for AI benchmarks. When tests keep expiring, long-run trends in capability become hard to study.

The authors build a statistical framework that stitches benchmarks together onto a single numerical scale. Model capabilities and benchmark difficulties are placed on that shared scale, like items in one measuring system. The approach could let researchers compare today's models with past ones fairly, instead of guessing across disconnected test scores. A common scale also exposes when a new benchmark is simply too easy.
arxiv-2512-00593:
Spin-Hall oscillators generate microwave signals from magnetic materials and can synchronize with each other. Bechberger and co-authors demonstrate spin-wave emission with current-controlled frequency in 2025, using a spin-Hall oscillator based on a low-damping magnetic garnet. The garnet carries dominant perpendicular magnetic anisotropy.

Mutual synchronization, mediated by propagating spin waves, makes such oscillators candidates for neuromorphic computing hardware. Controlling the emitted frequency with current gives designers a simple tuning knob. Gallium-substituted yttrium iron garnet keeps damping low, which should let the spin waves travel farther between devices. Current control is the simplest knob a circuit designer could ask for. Spin waves carry signals without moving charge, which keeps energy loss low. For folks who dream of chips that think like brains, the gain is a part that can sing at a pitch set by a wire. It can also lock step with its peers.
arxiv-2512-03093:
A classic math object may be easier to compute than thought. Isaac Dobes gives a new formula for Cayley's first hyperdeterminant in this 2025 work. Hyperdeterminants extend the idea of a determinant to arrays with more than two directions.

His formula uses the Levi-Civita symbol, a standard tool for signs in algebra. With it, he shows the value for symmetric arrays can be found in time that grows in a tame way with size. He then discusses uses for boson entanglement in quantum physics. Faster methods widen what researchers can test. Symmetric cases arise in quantum problems, so the faster route has ready uses.
arxiv-2512-03293:
What an agent wants shapes how it plans. Filippo Torresan, Ryota Kanai, and Manuel Baltieri study prior preferences in active inference agents in this 2025 work. Active inference uses expected free energy to balance using what is known and exploring for more.

The authors compare soft and hard preferences and ways to shape goals. How a goal is set can change an agent's choices in subtle ways. Their analysis helps designers build agents that act as intended. It matters for robots and AI systems that must plan under uncertainty. Goal shaping is delicate, since a hard goal can blind an agent to new evidence.
arxiv-2512-03493:
Collisions of gold nuclei probe matter at extreme heat and density. Yige Huang, for the STAR Collaboration, reports precision measurements in this 2025 work. The team studies fluctuations in net-proton counts from event to event.

They measure how those fluctuations depend on the rapidity window, using high-statistics data from RHIC. Protons and antiprotons are identified with improved detector performance. Such cumulants can signal the critical point of quantum chromodynamics. Finding it would map a key feature of the strong force's phase diagram. Cumulants of high order are sensitive probes, but they demand the statistics this run provides.
arxiv-2512-03593:
Digital avatars should stay sharp even in close-up views. David Svitov, Pietro Morerio, Lourdes Agapito, and Alessio Del Bue present CloseUpAvatar in this 2025 work. Their method builds high-fidelity, animatable full-body avatars that handle more general camera motions.

The avatar is represented as a set of textured planes. Two sets of learnable textures capture low and high-frequency detail in a multi-scale mixture. Preserving quality in close views matters for virtual meetings, games, and film. The approach aims to keep faces and clothing crisp as the camera moves. Multi-scale textures aim to keep both silhouette and fine surface detail intact.
arxiv-2512-02293:
Simultaneous localization and mapping with 3D Gaussian Splatting makes dense, photorealistic maps, but purely visual systems stumble on motion blur, weak texture, and changing light. Zihan Zhu and four co-authors present VIGS-SLAM in 2025, which adds inertial sensing to the splatting pipeline.

An inertial unit keeps tracking steady exactly where cameras struggle, during fast motion or in blank corridors. The system aims at robust real-time tracking with high-fidelity reconstruction at once. Reliable dense maps are the raw material for augmented reality, robot navigation, and digital twins of real spaces.
arxiv-2512-02393:
Agentic software systems, built from orchestrated AI modules, behave stochastically: the same request can take many different paths. Shuyang Liu and five co-authors argue in 2025 that judging such systems only by their final outcome misses most of what matters, and propose process-centric analysis instead.

Their trajectories adapt to the problem as they run, unlike the fixed paths of conventional programs. Outcome-only evaluation cannot see wasteful detours, lucky recoveries, or fragile reasoning that happened to end well. Studying the process gives engineers the evidence needed to debug and trust systems whose behavior is a distribution, not a script.
arxiv-2512-02493:
Yunlong Xiao takes a fresh look at superchannels, the rules that transform quantum processes themselves. Quantum channels are the basic operations of quantum theory, describing how a system changes. Superchannels act one level up, turning one channel into another.

The standard framework has real flaws, Xiao argues. Two rival constructions of a key operator coexist, and the theory lacks the firm representations that ground channel theory. Guided by a generalized form of Occam's razor, the 2025 study rebuilds the framework more simply. A cleaner foundation could help physicists reason about quantum devices that process other processes. A base that holds firm makes the rest of the field less prone to drift and doubt as it grows.
arxiv-2512-02593:
Chao-Han Huck Yang, Andreas Stolcke, and Larry P Heck survey spoken conversational agents built on large language models. Voice based models have drawn wide interest from researchers and the public alike. Leading closed models now handle speech recognition, translation, and spoken understanding far better than older open systems.

Their 2025 overview maps where these voice agents stand and what they can do. Speech tasks once handled by separate tools are merging into single conversational systems. A clear map of the field helps builders choose models, spot gaps, and design assistants people can truly talk with. Voice is how most of us talk, so gains here reach folks who type with pain or not at all.
arxiv-2512-02993:
Yifei Zeng and nine co-authors generate textures for 3D objects natively, instead of painting them view by view. Multi view fusion often leaves seams where views disagree, and complex surfaces end up partly uncovered. Those flaws limit how faithful and complete a generated texture can be.

TEXTRIX builds a latent attribute grid for native 3D texture generation. Working in 3D from the start avoids stitched inconsistencies. The framework also supports precise 3D part segmentation downstream. Better textures lift games, product design, and virtual retail, where surfaces must look right from every angle. Full wraps with no seams read as one cloth. That cloth like look is what makes a fake good feel real to the eye at a glance.
plos-pone-0010193:
The authors were Alexandro Rodríguez-Rojas, María Maciá, Alejandro Couce, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study looked at drug resistance in a tough germ. The drug fosfomycin treats simple bladder and gut infections well. Mutants that resist it arise often in lab tests, but they were thought to pay a high cost for that trait.

The team checked how resistance emerges and what it costs in living hosts. Their concern was plain: if there is no cost in the body, resistant germs can persist. That would weaken a useful drug against infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
plos-pone-0010293:
The authors were Eva Kolwijck, Ron Wevers, Udo Engelke, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study found a brain chemical in an unexpected place. N-acetylaspartate, or NAA, had never been detected in human tissue outside the brain. Its job there is still undefined, though it has been suggested to act as a molecular water pump in brain tissue.

The team found large quantities of NAA inside ovarian cyst fluid. The cysts came from serous ovarian tumors, a common tumor type. Finding a brain-only chemical in ovarian fluid raises new questions about what NAA does in the body.
plos-pone-0009893:
Cushing's disease comes from a pituitary tumor that floods the body with stress hormone. Madhavi Bangaru and colleagues tested whether curcumin, the yellow spice compound, can slow such a tumor. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The pituitary is a pea-sized gland under the brain.

The model was mouse pituitary corticotroph tumor cells called AtT20. Curcumin suppressed the growth of those tumor cells in the lab. A food-derived compound that slows the tumor could inspire gentler treatments. The authors present the cells as a model for treating Cushing's disease.
plos-pone-0009993:
Tiling arrays scan whole genomes in fine slices, but their data need heavy software to read. Jason Greenbaum and colleagues packaged that software into one ready tool. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

TiArA is a ready-made software package built for tiling array analysis. A virtual appliance is a prebuilt software bundle that runs as one unit. Tiling arrays probe DNA at regular intervals across the genome. Ready tools spread methods beyond specialist groups. A single ready package lowers the barrier for labs without software teams. Genome-wide scans produce far too much data to read by hand.
